8 Fully Worked Practice Problems: Brachiopod Morphology & Paleobiology
Problem 1: Plane of Bilateral Symmetry in Brachiopods vs. Bivalves
Brachiopods: Plane cuts perpendicularly THROUGH each valve; Bivalves: Plane lies BETWEEN the two valves
In brachiopods, each individual valve is equilateral (symmetric across its midline), but the two valves are unequal (inequivalve). In bivalves, the valves are equal, but each valve is inequilateral.
Problem 2: Diductor Muscle Mechanics in Articulates
Contracts to pull the cardinal process behind the hinge fulcrum, levering the valves open
Because teeth and sockets form a rigid fulcrum, diductor muscles running from the ventral floor to the dorsal cardinal process exert a Class-1 lever action to gape the shell.
Problem 3: The Brachidium (Internal Skeletal Support)
Calcareous loops (Terebratulids) and helical spiralia (Spiriferids) supporting lophophore tentacles
In *Spirifer*, two delicate calcified spiral cones (spiralia) project laterally into the shell interior, supporting the thousands of ciliated filtration tentacles.
Problem 4: Indian Stratigraphic Index Brachiopod of the Lower Carboniferous
Syringothyris cuspidata (Kashmir and Spiti)
Characterized by an exceptionally high, flat triangular interarea on the pedicle valve and a syrinx tube inside the delthyrium, *Syringothyris* defines the Tournaisian Syringothyris Limestone.
Problem 5: Punctate vs. Impunctate Shell Structure
Punctate shells have microscopic radial tubules (punctae) filled with caeca; Impunctate shells are solid calcite
Mantle caeca residing in punctae store proteins and lipids while repelling boring epibionts, providing a key taxonomic thin-section diagnostic.
Problem 6: Morphological Specialization of *Productus*
Convex pedicle valve with long hollow anchoring spines and loss of functional pedicle
Late Paleozoic productids (*Marginifera*, *Productus*) rested directly on soft muddy seabeds, using dense mats of hollow spines for snowshoe-like stabilization.
Problem 7: *Lingula* as the Classic 'Living Fossil'
Continuous burrowing infaunal existence in chitinophosphatic shells from the Cambrian to Recent
*Lingula* inhabits vertical sandy burrows anchored by a long muscular pedicle stalk, maintaining an unchanged bauplan for over 500 million years.
Problem 8: Cardinal Process Function
Posterior calcareous boss on the brachial valve serving as the insertion knob for diductor muscles
Located between the dental sockets, the cardinal process acts as the short lever arm against which diductor muscle contraction pulls to gap the shell open.
Micropaleontology & Conodonts / Question 073
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 • Paper-II • Question 73

Micropaleontology: Conodont as a Phosphatic Microfossil (Carbonate-Apatite)

Official Verification: Option (B) • Primitive Chordate Teeth • Conodont Alteration Index (CAI)
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
Micropaleontology: Conodont Mineralogy, Chordate Affinity & Biostratigraphy

Conodonts are microscopic, tooth-like skeletal elements ($0.1 - 2\text{ mm}$ size) belonging to an extinct group of primitive, soft-bodied, eel-like agnathan marine vertebrates (Class Conodonta, Phylum Chordata). In micropaleontology and petroleum geology, conodonts are premier biostratigraphic index fossils, and mineralogically, a conodont is fundamentally a PHOSPHATIC microfossil.

  • Mineralogical Composition (Phosphatic Nature):
    • Carbonate-Apatite (Francolite): Conodont elements are composed strictly of microcrystalline, fibrous, gem-quality calcium phosphate: $$\text{Ca}_5(\text{PO}_4, \text{CO}_3)_3\text{F} \quad (\text{Carbonate Fluorapatite / Francolite})$$
    • Chemical Resilience: Because they are made of insoluble phosphate rather than calcium carbonate, conodont elements resist dissolution during routine laboratory digestion with dilute acetic acid or formic acid, allowing micro-paleontologists to extract pristine conodont teeth from massive Paleozoic and Triassic limestones.
  • Biological Affinity & Apparatus Anatomy:
    • For over 120 years following their discovery by Christian Pander in 1856, conodonts were enigmatic microfossils of unknown affinity (variously attributed to worms, molluscs, or algae).
    • In 1983, the discovery of complete soft-bodied conodont animal fossils in the Lower Carboniferous Granton Shrimp Bed near Edinburgh, Scotland (*Clydagnathus*) proved they were primitive jawless marine chordates equipped with a notochord, V-shaped myomeres, large paired eyes, and a caudal fin.
    • Conodont elements were biting, grasping, and slicing dental structures arranged in a bilateral pharyngeal apparatus comprising:
      • S elements (Ramiform): Comb-like, multi-denticulate grasping bars.
      • M elements: Falcate (sickle-shaped) grasping cusps.
      • P elements (Pectiniform): Robust, flattened platform teeth used for crushing and grinding food particles.
  • Biostratigraphic & Geothermal Maturity Utility:
    • Conodont Alteration Index (CAI): The organic trace matter trapped within the apatite crystal lattice darkens irreversibly with increasing geothermal burial temperature: $$\text{CAI } 1 (\text{Pale Yellow}, <50^\circ\text{C}) \longrightarrow \text{CAI } 1.5-2 (\text{Brown, Oil Window}) \longrightarrow \text{CAI } 5 (\text{Black, Gas Window}) \longrightarrow \text{CAI } 8 (\text{White, }>600^\circ\text{C})$$ CAI is universally employed in sedimentary basin analysis to map oil and natural gas preservation limits.
"Conodonts: Conodonts are microscopic, tooth-like or plate-like phosphatic microfossils composed of calcium phosphate (apatite). They range from the Cambrian to the Triassic. Because of their rapid evolution, worldwide distribution, and resistance to acid dissolution, they are invaluable for correlating Paleozoic marine strata and assessing organic thermal maturity." — K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Micropaleontology: Conodonts, p. 270)
Figure 73.1: Conodont Anatomy and Geochemical Nature. Phosphatic element morphology (carbonate-apatite composition) and Conodont Alteration Index (CAI) thermal maturation scale.

Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection

OPSC Assistant Geologist 2019 • Paper-II • Question 73
Conodontis a:
(A) Siliceous microfossil
(B) Phosphatic microfossil
(C) Fossilized floral species
(D) Coral shell
✔ OFFICIALLY VERIFIED ANSWER: (B) Phosphatic microfossil
(A) Siliceous microfossil INCORRECT
Forensic Analysis: Siliceous microfossils are composed of biogenic opal/silica ($ ext{SiO}_2 \cdot n ext{H}_2 ext{O}$), exemplified by radiolarians, diatoms, and sponge spicules. Conodonts are composed of calcium phosphate, not silica.
(B) Phosphatic microfossil CORRECT VERIFIED
Forensic Analysis: Conodonts are definitively classified as phosphatic microfossils. Their elements are composed of microcrystalline carbonate-apatite (francolite; calcium phosphate), making them insoluble in dilute acetic acid and globally celebrated for Paleozoic-Triassic biozonation.
(C) Fossilized floral species INCORRECT
Forensic Analysis: Conodonts are the tooth-like pharyngeal elements of primitive predatory chordate animals; they have zero biological relationship to plants or flora.
(D) Coral shell INCORRECT
Forensic Analysis: Corals are macroscopic cnidarians possessing calcareous (calcite or aragonite) thecae, totally distinct from microscopic phosphatic conodont elements.

8 Fully Worked Practice Problems: Conodont Micropaleontology & Applications
Problem 1: Acid Extraction Technique for Conodonts
Dissolving marine carbonate rocks in 10% to 15% Acetic Acid or Formic Acid
Calcium carbonate dissolves into calcium acetate and CO2, while the apatite conodont elements remain insoluble, recovered by heavy-liquid separation (sodium polytungstate).
Problem 2: The Conodont Alteration Index (CAI) Scale
CAI 1.5 to 2.0 corresponds to 60° - 140°C, marking the optimum Liquid Petroleum (Oil) Window
Epstein et al. (1977) calibrated CAI against pyrolysis. Beyond CAI 2, liquid hydrocarbons crack to dry gas (CAI 3-4, 110-200°C); rocks with CAI >5 are overmature.
Problem 3: Extinction of the Conodonta
End-Triassic (Rhaetian) mass extinction (~201 Ma)
Conodonts survived the End-Ordovician, Late Devonian, and End-Permian crises, but perished completely during the End-Triassic CAMP flood basalt volcanic catastrophe.
Problem 4: Indian Conodont Biozones
Permian-Triassic transition in the Spiti Valley (*Hindeodus parvus* zone)
The FAD of the conodont *Hindeodus parvus* defines the base of the Induan stage and the international Permian-Triassic boundary at the Guling and Attargoo sections in Spiti.
Problem 5: Conodont Growth Pattern
Centrifugal appositional lamellae secreted by an outer epithelial pocket
Unlike vertebrate teeth that erupt once, conodonts were periodically retracted into epithelial folds that deposited concentric external phosphatic growth lamellae throughout ontogeny.
Problem 6: Coniform, Ramiform, and Pectiniform Elements
Coniform = simple cone; Ramiform = multi-denticulate bar/blade; Pectiniform = wide platform element
In a complete apparatus (e.g., *Polygnathus*), anterior coniform/ramiform elements grasped prey while posterior platform pectiniform (P) elements crushed it.
Problem 7: Who Discovered Conodonts?
Christian Heinrich Pander (1856)
Pander discovered conodonts in Lower Paleozoic greensands near Saint Petersburg, Russia, naming them 'conodonts' (cone-teeth).
Problem 8: Strontium Isotope Stratigraphy Using Conodonts
⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr ratios preserved in pristine biogenic apatite record ancient seawater chemistry
Because conodont apatite resists diagenetic isotopic exchange, high-precision TIMS measurements of ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr provide global seawater chronostratigraphic calibration throughout the Paleozoic.

Standalone View
OPSC 2019 • Paper-II • Question 74

Bivalve Paleontology: Arca as the Classic Representative of Taxodont Dentition

Official Verification: Option (A) • Comb-Like Alternating Teeth • Taxodont vs Heterodont vs Dysodont
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
Bivalve Paleontology: Hinge Dentition Architecture & The Genus Arca

In the Class Bivalvia (Lamellibranchiata / Pelecypoda, Phylum Mollusca), the shell consists of two lateral, calcareous valves hinged dorsally. The inner dorsal margin features a specialized interlocking system of teeth and sockets known as the hinge dentition, which guides valve closure and prevents lateral shearing. Among the classic dentition types, the genus Arca (ark clams) is the world-renowned textbook archetype of TAXODONT dentition.

  • Characteristics of Taxodont Dentition (Archetypal Genus: Arca):
    • Anatomical Definition: Taxodont dentition consists of a long, straight or gently curved hinge plate bearing a continuous row of numerous, small, similar, comb-like alternating transverse teeth and sockets.
    • Mechanical Function: Because the teeth are uniform, transverse, and tightly interlocking along the entire cardinal margin, they provide exceptional resistance against rotational twisting and shearing, adapted for thick-shelled epifaunal or shallow endobenthic bivalves.
    • Subclass & Orders: Typical of the primitive Subclass Pteriomorphia (Order Arcoida, Family Arcidae: Arca, Barbatia, Anadara) and Subclass Protobranchia (Family Nuculidae: Nucula).
  • Forensic Review of Distractor Genera and Their Dentition:
    • Venus (Heterodont Dentition): Subclass Heterodonta. The hinge is differentiated into a few (typically 3) distinct, radiating cardinal teeth directly beneath the beak (umbone) and elongated anterior/posterior lateral teeth.
    • Mytilus (Dysodont Dentition): Subclass Pteriomorphia (Mussels). Hinge teeth are virtually absent, reduced to tiny, weak denticles near the acute umbone, because the valves are anchored to rocks by strong fibrous byssus threads.
    • Pholadomya (Desmodont Dentition): Subclass Anomalodesmata. True hinge teeth are absent; the hinge mechanism is replaced by a large, internal spatulate plate (chondrophore or resilifer) supporting an elastic internal ligament.
"Bivalve Hinge Dentition (Taxodont): The arrangement of teeth and sockets along the hinge margin is of great taxonomic importance: (1) Taxodont Dentition: Consists of a continuous row of numerous, small, similar teeth arranged in a straight or curved line along the hinge plate. The classic example is Arca. (2) Heterodont: Differentiated into cardinal and lateral teeth (e.g., Venus). (3) Dysodont: Teeth reduced or absent (e.g., Mytilus)." — K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Invertebrate Paleontology: Bivalvia - Dentition, p. 261)
Figure 74.1: Bivalve Hinge Dentition Categories. Comb-like taxodont dentition in *Arca* contrasted with heterodont (*Venus*), dysodont (*Mytilus*), and desmodont (*Pholadomya*) systems.

Which amongst the following is a bivalve genus having taxodont type dentition ?
(A) Arca
(B) Pholadomya
(C) Venus
(D) Mytilus
✔ OFFICIALLY VERIFIED ANSWER: (A) Arca
(A) Arca CORRECT VERIFIED
Forensic Analysis: Arca (the ark clam) is the universally documented textbook archetype of taxodont dentition. Its straight hinge margin bears a continuous comb-like row of numerous, small, uniform, transverse alternating teeth and sockets.
(B) Pholadomya INCORRECT
Forensic Analysis: Pholadomya possesses desmodont dentition, where true teeth are absent and replaced by an internal ligament process (chondrophore).
(C) Venus INCORRECT
Forensic Analysis: Venus possesses heterodont dentition, characterized by differentiated cardinal teeth beneath the beak and lateral teeth along the margin.
(D) Mytilus INCORRECT
Forensic Analysis: Mytilus (marine mussel) possesses dysodont dentition, where teeth are reduced to tiny vestigial denticles or completely absent, with valve closure governed by byssal anchoring.

8 Fully Worked Practice Problems: Bivalve Paleobiology & Shell Anatomy
Problem 1: Ligament Function in Bivalve Opening
Antagonistic passive spring opening the valves when adductor muscles relax
The uncalcified proteinaceous ligament is under compression (internal resilium) or tension (external lamellar ligament) when closed. Relaxation of adductor muscles automatically pops the valves open.
Problem 2: The Byssal Notch in *Arca*
Ventral gap between closed valves for the emergence of tough byssal anchor fibers
Many species of *Arca* (*Arca noae*) anchor to rocky substrates using a stout, chitinous byssus projecting through a broad median ventral hiatus.
Problem 3: Pallial Line and Pallial Sinus Significance
Pallial line marks mantle attachment; Pallial sinus indicates retractable siphons (infaunal burrowers)
Infaunal siphonate bivalves (*Mya*, *Tellina*) have a deep indentation (sinus) in the pallial line. Epifaunal non-siphonate bivalves (*Arca*) have an entire, unbroken pallial line (integripalliate).
Problem 4: Dimyarian vs. Monomyarian Adductor Scars
Dimyarian has 2 adductor muscle scars (anterior & posterior); Monomyarian has only 1 large central scar
*Arca* is isomyarian (two equal-sized adductor scars). Oysters (*Ostrea*) and scallops (*Pecten*) are monomyarian, having lost the anterior adductor.
Problem 5: Cardinal Area (Amphidetic Ligament Area) in *Arca*
Broad, flat, triangular ligament area between the umbones bearing chevron-shaped grooves
The wide dorsal spacing between the recurved umbones exposes a large cardinal area scored with diamond or chevron-shaped ligament attachment furrows (duplivincular ligament).
Problem 6: Pachydont Dentition in Rudists
Extreme specialization with colossal peg-like teeth in conical reef-building Cretaceous bivalves
Cretaceous rudists (*Hippurites*) evolved giant peg teeth and deep sockets, functioning like box lids on horn-coral-like calcite cones.
Problem 7: Mineralogy of the *Arca* Shell
Cross-lamellar aragonite
The shell wall of *Arca* is constructed of interlocking cross-lamellar aragonite laths, providing exceptional mechanical toughness against crushing by durophagous predators.
Problem 8: Modern Indian Occurrence of Arcidae
Anadara granosa (blood clam) in coastal muddy estuaries and mangrove lagoons of Odisha and Bengal
*Anadara granosa* possesses hemoglobin in its blood (giving red flesh) and classic taxodont teeth, harvested commercially along the eastern Indian seaboard.
Ichnology & Trace Fossils / Question 075
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 • Paper-II • Question 75

Ichnology: Ichnofossils as Biological Activity Records (Footprints and Trails)

Official Verification: Option (D) [Footprint] / (C) [Trail] • Greek 'Ichnos' = Footprint • Trace vs Body Fossils
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
Ichnology: Trace Fossils vs. Body Fossils & Ethological Classification

In paleontology and sedimentary facies analysis, fossils are divided into two fundamental categories: Body Fossils (the physical preserved skeletal or soft tissues of the organism) and Trace Fossils (Ichnofossils). An ichnofossil (derived from the Greek ichnos = footprint, track, trace) represents the fossilized geological record of the biological activity, behavior, locomotion, feeding, or dwelling of an organism, rather than the anatomical remains of the organism itself.

  • Etymology & Definitive Examples:
    • The root Ichnos literally translates to "footprint" or "track". Hence, in introductory and competitive examination geology, an ichnofossil is archetypally defined as a fossilized footprint (e.g., Fossilized horse foot print or dinosaur trackway) or a fossilized trail (e.g., Fossilized serpent trail).
    • Unlike body fossils, which can be transported post-mortem by storm currents into foreign environments (taphonomic displacement), ichnofossils are always preserved strictly in situ within the exact sedimentary layer where the organism lived and behaved, making them supreme indicators of paleoenvironment, water depth, and sediment consistency.
  • Seilacher's Ethological (Behavioral) Classification of Ichnofossils:
    1. Repichnia (Locomotion Traces): Tracks, trails, and footprints produced during directed travel across or through sediment.
      Examples: Horse footprints (*Equus* / *Hipparion* tracks), dinosaur trackways, serpent trails, and trilobite walking trails (Cruziana).
    2. Pascichnia (Grazing Traces): Winding, looping, or meandering trails on bedding surfaces produced by mobile deposit-feeders systematically harvesting organic detritus (e.g., Helminthopsis, Scolicia).
    3. Fodinichnia (Feeding Burrows): Three-dimensional mining and feeding burrow systems within the sediment (e.g., Thalassinoides, Planolites, Chondrites).
    4. Domichnia (Dwelling Structures): Permanent vertical or U-shaped cylindrical burrows constructed as shelters by suspension-feeders (e.g., Skolithos pipe-rock, Arenicolites).
    5. Cubichnia (Resting Traces): Impressions left when an animal rested temporarily on soft sediment (e.g., trilobite resting trace Rusophycus, starfish resting trace Asteriacites).
  • Forensic Refutation of Distractor Options:
    • Fossilized lamellibranch shell (Option A): A direct Body Fossil composed of the biomineralized calcium carbonate skeleton of a bivalve mollusc.
    • Fossilized trilobite shell (Option B): A direct Body Fossil composed of the calcified chitinous exoskeleton of an arthropod.
    • Options C & D: Both represent valid trace fossils. However, based on the literal Greek etymology (*ichnos* = footprint) and standard textbook question keys, Option (D) Fossilized horse foot print (or Option C) captures the definitive behavioral trace category.
"Trace Fossils (Ichnofossils): Trace fossils, or ichnofossils (from the Greek word ichnos, meaning a footprint), are indirect evidences of ancient life. They include footprints, tracks, trails, burrows, and borings left by animals in soft mud or sand before it hardened into stone. They represent animal behavior rather than the organism itself (contrasting with body fossils like shells or bones)." — K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Fossils & Their Modes of Preservation: Trace Fossils, pp. 257-258)
Figure 75.1: Ichnology & Trace Fossil Categorization. Behavioral classification (Repichnia footprints/trails, Domichnia burrows, Cubichnia resting marks) versus skeletal body fossils.

Echnofossilis a: (Ichnofossil is a :)

(B) Fossilized trilobite shell

(B) Fossilized trilobite shell INCORRECT (BODY FOSSIL)
Forensic Analysis: A preserved trilobite exoskeleton is a Body Fossil. (By contrast, trilobite walking trails like *Cruziana* and resting marks like *Rusophycus* are ichnofossils).
(D) Fossilized horse foot print [Literal Etymological Key: Greek 'Ichnos' = Footprint] PRIMARY VERIFIED EXAM ANSWER
Forensic Analysis: Ichnofossils (from Greek ichnos = footprint) are trace fossils preserving biological activity. In academic and competitive geology syllabi, a fossilized footprint (such as an *Equus* or dinosaur footprint) represents the prime textbook definition and archetype of an ichnofossil.
(C) Fossilized serpent trail [Locomotion Trace Fossil Alternative] VALID ICHNOLOGICAL TRACE
Forensic Analysis: A serpent trail is also a genuine locomotion trace fossil (Repichnia). Both (C) and (D) are ichnofossils (contrasting sharply with body fossils A and B). Option (D) is prioritized because of the direct etymological root of *ichnos* meaning footprint.

8 Fully Worked Practice Problems: Ichnology & Trace Fossil Facies
Problem 1: Seilacherian Ichnofacies Along a Depth Gradient
Trypanites / Glossifungites (Hardground/Firmground) → Skolithos (High-energy beach) → Cruziana (Subtidal shelf) → Zoophycos (Bathyl slope) → Nereites (Deep abyssal turbidite)
Adolf Seilacher established that recurring trace fossil associations track depositional water depth, substrate firmness, hydrodynamic energy, and oxygen levels.
Problem 2: What is a 'Coprolite'?
Fossilized animal feces classified as an ichnofossil
Coprolites are trace fossils composed of calcium phosphate that preserve digested bone shards, scales, or plant phytoliths, revealing ancient trophic diets.
Problem 3: Calculating Dinosaur Running Speed from Trackways
Alexander's formula: $v = 0.25 \cdot g^{0.5} \cdot \text{Stride}^{1.67} \cdot h^{-1.17}$
R. McNeill Alexander (1976) used footprint length ($L$) to estimate hip height ($h \approx 4L$) and combined it with stride length to calculate accurate walking and sprinting velocities.
Problem 4: Gastroliths as Trace Fossils
Highly polished gizzard stones ingested by dinosaurs and birds to grind tough food
Gastroliths are behavioral trace fossils identified by mirror-like stomach polish and anomalous occurrence inside rib cages away from river gravel sources.
Problem 5: Difference Between Epichnia and Hypichnia
Epichnia occur on top of a bedding surface; Hypichnia occur on the sole (underside) of a bed
Martinsson's (1970) toponomic classification describes trace preservation: Epichnial grooves form on bed tops; Hypichnial casts form as sediment molds beneath sandstones.
Problem 6: The Ichnogenus *Skolithos*
Vertical cylindrical dwelling burrows in high-energy sandy shoreface environments ('Pipe-Rock')
In the Devonian Muth Quartzite and Cambrian quartzites, vertical unbranched *Skolithos* tubes reflect suspension-feeders anchoring in wave-washed sands.
Problem 7: Bioerosion Traces (Borings)
Entobia (boring sponge galleries) and Gastrochaenolites (boring bivalve chambers)
Mechanical or chemical excavation into hard substrates (shells, lithified hardgrounds, coral skeletons) produces bioerosion trace fossils belonging to the *Entobia* ichnofacies.
Problem 8: Why One Organism Can Produce Multiple Ichnotaxa
Different behaviors leave different traces (e.g., trilobite makes *Cruziana* while walking, *Rusophycus* while resting)
Trace fossils classify behavior, not anatomy. A single trilobite individual walking, feeding, or burrowing generates entirely different named ichnogenera.

OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 76 • Igneous Petrology

Acid Igneous Rocks & Quartz Abundance: Chemical vs. Modal Mineralogical Criteria

Topic: Igneous Rock Classification • Key Concept: Total Silica (SiO2 wt%) vs. Free Quartz Modal % • Textbooks: K.M. Bangar (p. 110-112); John D. Winter (Principles of Igneous Petrology)
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Chemical vs. Mineralogical Classification

In igneous petrology, rocks are classified chemically based on their total silica ($SiO_2$) weight percentage, and mineralogically based on the abundance of free quartz ($\alpha$-quartz modal volume percentage):

Rock Class Total Silica ($SiO_2$ wt%) Normative / Modal Free Quartz Characteristic Mineral Assemblage Representative Plutonic & Volcanic Examples
Acidic (Felsic / Silicic) > 66% (or > 65%) ≥ 10% Free Quartz (often 20–40%) Quartz + K-Feldspar (Orthoclase/Microcline) + Sodic Plagioclase ± Biotite/Muscovite Granite, Adamellite, Granodiorite (Plutonic); Rhyolite, Dacite (Volcanic)
Intermediate 52% – 66% < 10% Free Quartz (or silica-saturated) Plagioclase (Oligoclase–Andesine) + Hornblende + Biotite ± minor Pyroxene Syenite, Diorite, Monzonite (Plutonic); Trachyte, Andesite (Volcanic)
Basic (Mafic) 45% – 52% 0% Free Quartz (Silica-undersaturated or quartz-free) Calcic Plagioclase (Labradorite/Bytownite) + Clinopyroxene (Augite) ± Olivine Gabbro, Norite (Plutonic); Dolerite (Hypabyssal); Basalt (Volcanic)
Ultrabasic (Ultramafic) < 45% 0% Free Quartz (Desilicated) Olivine (Forsterite) + Pyroxenes (Enstatite/Augite); Feldspar < 10% Peridotite (Dunite, Lherzolite, Harzburgite), Pyroxenite (Plutonic); Komatiite (Volcanic)
"Acid igneous rocks are characterized chemically by a high silica content exceeding 65 or 66 percent. In mineralogical terms, because all bases (alumina, potash, soda, lime, iron, and magnesia) are completely saturated with silica, the surplus silica crystallizes as free quartz, which generally amounts to 10% or more of the rock's total modal volume. Rocks with more than 60-65% free quartz are rare monomineralic quartz-rocks (silexites/quartzolites) or sedimentary sandstones."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Petrology Section, pp. 110–112)
$$\text{Total Bulk Silica} = \sum (\text{Silica bound in silicates: feldspars, micas, amphiboles}) + \text{Free Modal Quartz} (SiO_2)$$ $$\text{In Acid Granitoids: } \text{Total } SiO_2 \ge 66 \text{ wt\%} \implies \text{Modal Free Quartz } \ge 10\text{ vol\% (typically } 20\text{--}35\%\text{)}$$

Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
2. Official Examination Question & Forensic Option Analysis
QUESTION 76
Generally, acid igneous rocks contain :
A 10% or more free quartz
B 15% or more free quartz
C 60% or more free quartz
D 65% or more free quartz
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION A (10% or more free quartz)
OPTION A • CORRECT
10% or more free quartz

By standard petrological convention (Hatch, Wells & Wells; Bangar; IUGS granitoid field), an igneous rock is classified mineralogically as acidic when it contains at least 10% or more free quartz (modal volume). In the QAPF classification of plutonic rocks, the boundary between silica-saturated intermediate rocks (monzonite, syenite, diorite) and true acid granitoids requires $Q > 5\text{--}10\%$. Free modal quartz in normal granites ranges from 20% to 35%.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
15% or more free quartz

While many granites contain 15% to 30% quartz, 15% is an arbitrary cut-off and not the definition of acid igneous rocks. Rocks containing 10% to 14% free quartz (such as quartz syenites, quartz diorites, and granodioritic transition rocks) are already acid rocks supersaturated in silica.

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
60% or more free quartz

This option confuses free modal quartz with total chemical silica ($SiO_2$). An igneous rock with 60% or more free quartz is an ultra-rare hydrothermal pegmatitic facies known as a silexite or quartzolite. Normal granites contain 60% to 70% feldspar, leaving 20% to 35% quartz.

OPTION D • DISTRACTOR
65% or more free quartz

This is a classic trap: acid rocks contain 65% or more total chemical silica ($SiO_2$), NOT 65% free quartz! In a granite containing 72% bulk $SiO_2$, over 45% of that $SiO_2$ is chemically bound in the crystal lattices of feldspars ($KAlSi_3O_8, NaAlSi_3O_8$) and micas, leaving approximately 25% to 30% as free quartz crystals.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. In the chemical classification of igneous rocks, a rock having 58% bulk $SiO_2$ and 4% free modal quartz is classified as:
Answer: Intermediate igneous rock
Intermediate rocks have bulk silica between 52% and 66% and contain less than 10% free modal quartz.
2. What distinguishes 'total silica' from 'free silica' in petrographic analysis?
Answer: Total silica is all $SiO_2$ present chemically; free silica is uncombined $SiO_2$ crystallizing as quartz/tridymite/cristobalite.
Most silica in igneous rocks is bound in framework and chain silicates (feldspars, amphiboles). Only the excess silica above cation saturation forms free quartz.
3. What is an igneous rock with greater than 90% modal quartz called in the IUGS classification?
Answer: Quartzolite (or Silexite)
Field 1 of the IUGS QAPF double triangle covers rocks where $Q / (Q+A+P) > 90\%$, representing the most quartz-rich igneous extreme.
4. A typical granite has 72 wt% $SiO_2$. What is its expected modal quartz percentage?
Answer: Approximately 25% to 35%
Feldspars (potash feldspar and albite) require ~65% $SiO_2$ in their formula stoichiometry. In a 72% bulk rock, ~25-30% modal quartz precipitates.
5. Why cannot olivine ($Mg_2SiO_4$) and free quartz ($SiO_2$) coexist in equilibrium under normal magmatic conditions?
Answer: Because they react to form orthopyroxene (enstatite): $Mg_2SiO_4 + SiO_2 \rightarrow 2 MgSiO_3$.
Olivine is an unsaturated nesosilicate that is unstable in the presence of free silica melt, immediately reacting peritectically to form enstatite.
6. Which volcanic rock is the compositional equivalent of a granite?
Answer: Rhyolite
Rhyolite is the fine-grained, extrusive/volcanic equivalent of granite, possessing >66% $SiO_2$ and ≥10% free normative quartz.
7. What is the Color Index ($M'$) of acid igneous rocks?
Answer: $M' < 20$ (Leucocratic to extreme leucocratic)
Acid rocks are dominated by felsic minerals (quartz + feldspars > 80%), leaving less than 20% dark ferromagnesian minerals.
8. What is the normative mineral calculated in CIPW norm when a rock has excess silica over all mineral bases?
Answer: Normative Quartz ($q$)
When all alumina, alkalis, lime, iron, and magnesia are saturated to form feldspars, pyroxenes, and magnetite, remaining $SiO_2$ is allocated to normative quartz ($q$).

Andesite Petrography: The Prototypical Intermediate Volcanic Rock

Topic: Volcanic Rock Types • Key Concept: Subduction Zone Magmatism & Intermediate Chemistry • Textbooks: John D. Winter (Principles of Igneous & Metamorphic Petrology); K.M. Bangar (p. 125)
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Petrography & Geological Environment of Andesite

Andesite is a fine-grained, aphanitic to porphyritic intermediate volcanic (extrusive) rock named by Christian Leopold von Buch (1826) after the Andes Mountains of South America, where it forms the dominant volcanic edifice along active subduction zone margins.

Property Petrological Specification Diagnostic Detail
Chemical Class Intermediate (52 – 63 wt% $SiO_2$) Total alkali-silica (TAS) field between basaltic andesite and dacite.
Emplacement Mode Volcanic (Extrusive) Lava flows, block-and-ash flows, pyroclastic breccias, and stratovolcano cones.
Plutonic Equivalent Diorite Shares identical chemical and bulk mineralogical composition; differs in grain size.
Essential Mineralogy Plagioclase Feldspar + Mafics Zoned plagioclase (typically Andesine $An_{30}\text{--}An_{50}$) + Augite / Hypersthene / Hornblende.
Diagnostic Texture Porphyritic with Hyalopilitic Groundmass Prominent phenocrysts of oscillatory-zoned andesine and hornblende/augite in a microcrystalline or glassy groundmass.
"Andesite is the volcanic equivalent of diorite. It is an intermediate, usually porphyritic rock consisting essentially of plagioclase feldspar (principally andesine or oligoclase) together with one or more ferromagnesian minerals such as biotite, hornblende, augite, or hypersthene. Andesites are the characteristic lavas of island arcs and active continental margins bordering the Pacific Ocean (the 'Andesite Line')."
— John D. Winter, Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology (2nd Ed., Chapter 2, pp. 24–28)
Figure 77: Position of Andesite within the IUGS Total Alkali-Silica (TAS) diagram and volcanic rock suite, illustrating its classification as an intermediate extrusive rock (52–63 wt% SiO2).

QUESTION 77
Andesite is :
A A coarse grained acid plutonic rock
B A fine grained hypabyssal rock
C An intermediate volcanic rock
D An ultrabasic volcanic rock
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION C (An intermediate volcanic rock)
OPTION C • CORRECT
An intermediate volcanic rock

Andesite has a silica content of 52% to 63% (intermediate range) and forms as an extrusive (volcanic) lava flow or pyroclastic deposit on planetary crusts. It represents the extrusive counterpart of diorite.

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
A coarse grained acid plutonic rock

A coarse-grained acid plutonic rock is Granite or Adamellite ($SiO_2 > 66\%$, phaneritic texture). Andesite is fine-grained/porphyritic, volcanic, and intermediate.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
A fine grained hypabyssal rock

A fine- to medium-grained hypabyssal rock equivalent to diorite is a microdiorite or porphyrite. Andesite is an extrusive surface lava flow (volcanic).

OPTION D • DISTRACTOR
An ultrabasic volcanic rock

An ultrabasic volcanic rock ($SiO_2 < 45\%$, highly magnesian) is a Komatiite or Meimechite, characterized by spinifex texture. Andesite is neither ultrabasic nor rich in olivine.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. What geological boundary separates the tholeiitic basalt province of the open Pacific basin from circum-Pacific andesitic volcanism?
Answer: The Andesite Line (Marshall Line)
The Andesite Line marks the petrological boundary between intraplate oceanic basalts and subduction-related calc-alkaline andesites.
2. What specific plagioclase composition is diagnostic of andesite?
Answer: Andesine ($An_{30}\text{--}An_{50}$)
By IUGS petrographic rules, the dominant plagioclase in andesite has an anorthite content less than $An_{50}$ (andesine/oligoclase), whereas basalt plagioclase is labradorite ($An_{50}\text{--}An_{70}$).
3. What is the typical magma series that generates the voluminous andesites of volcanic arcs?
Answer: The Calc-Alkaline Magma Series
Hydrous partial melting of mantle wedge peridotite fluxed by slab-derived fluids generates primary hydrous basaltic magmas that differentiate along calc-alkaline pathways to andesite.
4. What texture is commonly observed in andesite phenocrysts indicating magma mixing or fluctuating P-T conditions?
Answer: Oscillatory zoning and sieve (dusty) resorption rims
Repeated magma recharge in sub-volcanic chambers creates abrupt compositional jumps in plagioclase growth zones, forming oscillatory rings and sieve textures.
5. What is the volcanic equivalent of a granodiorite?
Answer: Dacite
Dacite occupies the composition field between andesite and rhyolite ($SiO_2 \approx 63\text{--}68\%$).
6. Which volcanic hazard is most typically associated with viscous andesitic to dacitic lavas?
Answer: Pyroclastic density currents (PDCs) and Peléan / Plinian explosive eruptions
The higher silica content and moderate-to-high volatile ($H_2O$) content make andesitic melts highly viscous, promoting explosive dome-collapse pyroclastic flows.
7. How does basaltic andesite differ from normal andesite in $SiO_2$ content?
Answer: Basaltic andesite has 52% to 57% $SiO_2$, while andesite has 57% to 63% $SiO_2$.
The IUGS TAS diagram formally splits the intermediate volcanic field into basaltic andesite ($52\text{--}57\%$) and andesite ($57\text{--}63\%$).
8. What is the intrusive plutonic equivalent of Andesite?
Answer: Diorite
Diorite crystallizes slowly at depth from the same intermediate magma, producing a phaneritic equigranular texture of plagioclase and amphibole.
Magmatic Crystallization & Bowen's Principles / Question 078
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 78 • Igneous Petrology

Bowen's Reaction Principle: The Continuous Plagioclase Solid-Solution Series

Topic: Magmatic Crystallization Differentiation • Key Concept: Continuous vs. Discontinuous Reaction Series • Textbooks: N.L. Bowen (1928, The Evolution of the Igneous Rocks); John D. Winter
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Bowen's Reaction Principle (1928)

In his seminal work The Evolution of the Igneous Rocks (1928), Canadian experimental petrologist Norman L. Bowen demonstrated that minerals crystallizing from a cooling basaltic magma do not precipitate independently at single freezing points, but rather react continuously with the residual liquid along two distinct branches:

Reaction Series Branch Crystallization Mechanism Sequence from High-T to Low-T Mineral Structural Evolution
Discontinuous Series (Fe-Mg Silicates) Incongruent reaction at fixed temperatures; early crystal reacts with melt to form a new mineral with a fundamentally different crystal structure. $Mg\text{-Olivine} \rightarrow \text{Orthopyroxene} \rightarrow \text{Clinopyroxene} \rightarrow \text{Amphibole (Hornblende)} \rightarrow \text{Biotite}$ Nesosilicate (isolated tetrahedra) $\rightarrow$ Inosilicate (single chains) $\rightarrow$ Inosilicate (double chains) $\rightarrow$ Phyllosilicate (sheets).
Continuous Series (Feldspar Solid Solution) Continuous ionic exchange without changing the underlying crystal lattice (tectosilicate framework); $Ca^{2+} + Al^{3+} \rightleftharpoons Na^+ + Si^{4+}$. Calcic Plagioclase (Anorthite) $\rightarrow$ Bytownite $\rightarrow$ Labradorite $\rightarrow$ Andesine $\rightarrow$ Oligoclase $\rightarrow$ Sodic Plagioclase (Albite) $CaAl_2Si_2O_8$ (pure calcic anorthite at $\sim 1553^\circ\text{C}$) progressively enriches in $NaAlSi_3O_8$ (sodic albite at $\sim 1118^\circ\text{C}$).
"In the continuous reaction series of the plagioclase feldspars, the first mineral to form at the highest temperature from a basaltic liquid is calcic plagioclase (anorthite, $CaAl_2Si_2O_8$). As cooling proceeds, this early-formed calcic plagioclase reacts continuously with the soda-enriched residual liquid, shifting its solid-solution composition gradually through bytownite, labradorite, and andesine toward sodic plagioclase (albite)."
— N.L. Bowen, The Evolution of the Igneous Rocks (Princeton University Press, 1928)
$$\text{Plagioclase Solid-Solution Coupled Substitution: } Ca^{2+} + Al^{3+} \rightleftharpoons Na^+ + Si^{4+}$$ $$T_{\text{crystallization}}(\text{Anorthite } CaAl_2Si_2O_8) = 1553^\circ\text{C} \quad \gg \quad T_{\text{crystallization}}(\text{Albite } NaAlSi_3O_8) = 1118^\circ\text{C}$$ $$\therefore \text{First mineral formed in continuous series} \equiv \mathbf{Calcic\ Plagioclase\ (Anorthite)}$$
Figure 78: Bowen's Reaction Series illustrating the continuous plagioclase solid-solution branch (right) and the discontinuous ferromagnesian branch (left), demonstrating that calcic plagioclase forms first.

2. Official Examination Question & Forensic Option Analysis
QUESTION 78
The first mineral formed in the continuous series of Bowen reaction principle is :
A Sodic-Calcic plagioclase
B Potash feldspar
C Calcic-sodic plagioclase
D Calcic plagioclase
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION D (Calcic plagioclase)
OPTION D • CORRECT
Calcic plagioclase

The continuous series is defined by the plagioclase feldspar binary solid-solution ($An\text{--}Ab$). Because anorthite ($CaAl_2Si_2O_8$) has a much higher melting point ($1553^\circ\text{C}$) than albite ($1118^\circ\text{C}$), the first crystal to precipitate from a cooling basic magma at the highest temperature is calcic plagioclase (anorthite-rich, $An_{90}\text{--}An_{100}$).

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Sodic-Calcic plagioclase

Sodic-calcic plagioclase (such as andesine or oligoclase) forms intermediate to late in the continuous series as the melt becomes progressively depleted in calcium and enriched in sodium.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Potash feldspar

Potash feldspar (orthoclase/microcline) does not belong to the continuous plagioclase series; it precipitates late from the residual felsic liquid at low temperatures ($\sim 700\text{--}650^\circ\text{C}$) after both the continuous and discontinuous series converge.

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
Calcic-sodic plagioclase

Calcic-sodic plagioclase (such as labradorite, $An_{50}\text{--}An_{70}$) represents a middle stage of continuous crystallization, after initial precipitation of pure calcic plagioclase (anorthite/bytownite).

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. What is the first mineral to form in the DISCONTINUOUS series of Bowen's reaction principle?
Answer: Forsteritic Olivine ($Mg_2SiO_4$)
Magnesium-rich olivine (forsterite) has the highest crystallization temperature among mafic silicates ($\sim 1890^\circ\text{C}$ pure, $\sim 1200\text{--}1300^\circ\text{C}$ in basaltic melt).
2. Why does normal zoning in plagioclase phenocrysts always exhibit a calcic core and a sodic rim?
Answer: Because the melt becomes progressively depleted in Ca and enriched in Na during fractional crystallization.
As temperature drops, the plagioclase liquidus and solidus dictate that successive crystal layers become richer in albite ($Na$), leaving the high-T calcic core enclosed by a sodic rim.
3. What happens to early-formed calcic plagioclase crystals if they are rapidly isolated from the melt by sinking?
Answer: Fractional crystallization occurs; the crystals cannot react with the liquid, forming cumulate anorthosite.
Bowen termed this fractional crystallization: removing crystals prevents equilibrium reaction, driving the residual melt toward extreme silicic/alkaline compositions.
4. What is the final mineral to crystallize when both the continuous and discontinuous series converge?
Answer: Quartz ($SiO_2$)
After potash feldspar and muscovite crystallize, residual pure silica precipitates as quartz at $\sim 650\text{--}600^\circ\text{C}$.
5. What type of solid solution occurs in the plagioclase feldspar series?
Answer: Coupled substitution solid solution ($Ca^{2+} + Al^{3+} \rightleftharpoons Na^+ + Si^{4+}$)
Because $Ca^{2+}$ and $Na^+$ have different valencies, charge neutrality is maintained by simultaneously substituting $Al^{3+}$ for $Si^{4+}$ in the tetrahedral framework.
6. Which mineral crystallizes immediately after orthopyroxene in Bowen's discontinuous reaction series?
Answer: Clinopyroxene (Augite), followed by Amphibole (Hornblende)
The discontinuous sequence proceeds: Olivine $\rightarrow$ Orthopyroxene/Clinopyroxene $\rightarrow$ Amphibole $\rightarrow$ Biotite.
7. What is a peritectic reaction in the discontinuous series?
Answer: An incongruent reaction where an early crystal reacts with melt to produce a new crystal phase: Olivine + Liquid $\rightarrow$ Pyroxene.
At the peritectic point ($1557^\circ\text{C}$ in the pure $Mg_2SiO_4-SiO_2$ system), forsterite reacts with silica-rich liquid to form enstatite.
8. Which plagioclase feldspar is most susceptible to chemical weathering under humid surface conditions according to Goldich's Weathering Series?
Answer: Calcic Plagioclase (Anorthite)
Goldich's dissolution series exactly mirrors Bowen's reaction series: high-temperature minerals formed furthest from surface P-T conditions (anorthite, olivine) weather the fastest.

OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 79 • Igneous Petrology

Carbonatites: Primary Mantle-Derived Carbonate Melts & Critical REE Reserves

Topic: Alkaline & Carbonatite Magmatism • Key Concept: IUGS Definition (>50% Carbonate) & Rare Earth Mineralization • Textbooks: Winter (2014); Bell & Rukhlov (Carbonatites); K.M. Bangar
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Carbonatite Petrogenesis & Geochemistry

Carbonatites are unique, mantle-derived igneous rocks defined by the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS) as containing more than 50% modal primary carbonate minerals (calcite, dolomite, ankerite, and siderite) with less than 20% $SiO_2$.

Classification Dominant Carbonate Mineral Chemical Designation Associated Silicate Rocks & Fenitization
Calcio-carbonatite (Sövite / Alvikite) Calcite ($CaCO_3$) Rich in $CaO$; Sövite is coarse plutonic, Alvikite is hypabyssal/volcanic. Surrounded by ijolite, nephelinite, and extensive fenitization (alkali metasomatic halo).
Magnesio-carbonatite (Beforsite) Dolomite ($CaMg(CO_3)_2$) Rich in $MgO$; often forms medium- to fine-grained dykes and cone sheets. Enriched in high-field strength elements (HFSE) and LREEs.
Ferro-carbonatite Ankerite / Siderite ($FeCO_3$) Rich in $FeO + Fe_2O_3 + MnO$; late-stage low-temperature magmatic differentiates. Highest concentration of Rare Earth Elements (monazite, bastnäsite).
Natro-carbonatite Nyerereite / Gregoryite ($(Na,K)_2Ca(CO_3)_2$) Extremely rich in $Na_2O$ and $K_2O$; active lava at Oldoinyo Lengai, Tanzania. Water-soluble, rapidly altering to hydrous carbonates at surface conditions.
"Carbonatites are igneous rocks containing more than 50 percent by volume of carbonate minerals. Although rare, carbonatites are of immense economic importance because they host the world's richest deposits of Rare Earth Elements (REEs: La, Ce, Pr, Nd), Niobium (in pyrochlore), Tantalum, Phosphate (in apatite), and Fluorite. The Amba Dongar complex in Gujarat is India's most famous carbonatite-alkaline ring complex."
— Keith Bell, Carbonatites: Genesis and Evolution (Unwin Hyman)
$$\text{IUGS Classification Criterion: Modal Carbonates } (\text{Calcite} + \text{Dolomite} + \text{Ankerite}) > 50\text{ vol\%}$$ $$\text{Key REE-Bearing Minerals in Carbonatites: Bastn\ddot{a}site } [(\text{Ce},\text{La})CO_3F], \text{ Monazite } [(\text{Ce},\text{La},\text{Nd})PO_4], \text{ Pyrochlore } [(\text{Na},\text{Ca})_2\text{Nb}_2\text{O}_6(\text{OH},\text{F})]$$

QUESTION 79
A magmatic rock rich in calcium carbonate and often containing rare earth minerals is :
A Alkali basalt
B Syenite porphyry
C Carbonatite
D Granodiorite
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION C (Carbonatite)
OPTION C • CORRECT
Carbonatite

Carbonatite is an igneous (magmatic) rock composed of greater than 50% carbonate minerals, predominantly calcium carbonate (calcite in sövite). It is world-renowned as the primary geological host for economic concentrations of Rare Earth Elements (bastnäsite, monazite) and niobium (pyrochlore).

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Alkali basalt

Alkali basalt is a silicate volcanic rock composed of calcic plagioclase, titanaugite, and olivine with normative nepheline. It does not contain primary calcium carbonate minerals.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Syenite porphyry

Syenite porphyry is an intermediate felsic silicate rock dominated by alkali feldspar phenocrysts. While often associated with carbonatite ring complexes, it consists of aluminosilicates, not calcium carbonate.

OPTION D • DISTRACTOR
Granodiorite

Granodiorite is a common acid plutonic silicate rock consisting of quartz, plagioclase (oligoclase/andesine), K-feldspar, and biotite/hornblende. It has negligible carbonate content.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. Which active volcano in the East African Rift erupts natrocarbonatite lava at approximately $500\text{--}600^\circ\text{C}$?
Answer: Oldoinyo Lengai (Tanzania)
Oldoinyo Lengai is the only active volcano on Earth erupting sodium-potassium carbonate lavas (nyerereite and gregoryite).
2. What is the coarse-grained, plutonic variety of calcite carbonatite called?
Answer: Sövite
Coarse-grained plutonic calcite-carbonatite is termed sövite; its fine-grained hypabyssal or volcanic equivalent is alvikite.
3. What is the process of intensive alkali metasomatism of wall rocks surrounding a carbonatite called?
Answer: Fenitization
Fenitization involves pervasive infiltration of hyper-alkaline fluids ($Na, K, Fe^{3+}$), transforming granitic country rocks into fenites rich in aegirine and alkali feldspar.
4. Where is India's most prominent carbonatite complex located, renowned for fluorite and REE mineralization?
Answer: Amba Dongar (Chhota Udepur district, Gujarat)
Amba Dongar is a Cretaceous-Palaeocene ring complex related to Deccan plume magmatism, hosting India's largest fluorite deposit and rich REE reserves.
5. What primary niobium-bearing ore mineral is extracted almost exclusively from carbonatite complexes?
Answer: Pyrochlore [$(Na,Ca)_2Nb_2O_6(OH,F)$]
Over 90% of global niobium production (e.g., Araxá in Brazil) is mined from weathered pyrochlore-bearing carbonatites.
6. How does liquid immiscibility contribute to the origin of carbonatitic magmas?
Answer: A parent carbonated nephelinite/melilitite melt unmixes into two immiscible liquids: a silicate melt and a carbonate melt.
Experimental petrology shows that at crustal pressures, $CO_2$-saturated alkaline silicate melts split into conjugate silicate and carbonate fractions.
7. What is a dolomite-dominated carbonatite termed in classical petrography?
Answer: Beforsite
Beforsite is the magnesio-carbonatite variety, consisting primarily of magmatic dolomite with minor apatite and phlogopite.
8. Which world-class REE deposit in China is hosted within Proterozoic carbonatite dykes?
Answer: Bayan Obo (Inner Mongolia, China)
Bayan Obo is the world's largest known REE deposit, containing massive reserves of bastnäsite and monazite associated with dolomitic carbonatites.
Granulite Facies & Charnockite Series / Question 080
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 80 • Igneous & Metamorphic Petrology

The Charnockite Series: Mineralogy, Granulite Facies, and Hypersthene Signature

Topic: Charnockite Series & Granulite Facies • Key Concept: Orthopyroxene-Bearing Quartzofeldspathic Rocks • Textbooks: Sir Thomas Holland (1900); K.M. Bangar; John D. Winter
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: The Charnockite Series & Holland's Definition (1900)

The term Charnockite was coined in 1900 by Sir Thomas H. Holland, Director of the Geological Survey of India, to designate an orthopyroxene (hypersthene)-bearing quartzofeldspathic rock quarried from St. Thomas Mount in Chennai (formerly Madras) that had been used to construct the tombstone of Job Charnock, the historical founder of Kolkata.

Charnockite Member Essential Mineral Assemblage Granitoid Equivalence Diagnostic Optical Characteristics
Charnockite (sensu stricto) Quartz + K-Feldspar (Perthite) + Plagioclase + Hypersthene Hypersthene Granite Greasy bluish-green or waxy dark-brown lustre; pleochroic hypersthene (pink to green); blue quartz.
Enderbite Quartz + Plagioclase (Anti-perthite) + Hypersthene (± minor K-feldspar) Hypersthene Tonalite / Granodiorite Plagioclase-dominated ($P/(A+P) > 65\%$); common in South Indian granulite terranes.
Mangerite Microperthite + Plagioclase + Hypersthene + minor Quartz (< 20%) Hypersthene Monzonite Intermediate member with roughly equal alkali feldspar and plagioclase.
Jotunite / Norite Calcic Plagioclase + Hypersthene / Orthopyroxene ± Clinopyroxene Hypersthene Monzogabbro / Norite Basic end-member of the charnockitic suite; dark melanocratic appearance.
"Charnockite is a hypersthene granite consisting essentially of quartz, microcline (perthite), plagioclase, and hypersthene, with or without iron ores and garnet. Its most striking physical character is an olive-green, greasy, or resinous waxy luster, imparted by microscopic carbonaceous and fluid inclusions in quartz and feldspar under high-pressure granulite facies metamorphism ($T = 750\text{--}900^\circ\text{C}, P = 5\text{--}10\text{ kbar}$, ultra-low $a_{H_2O}$)."
— Sir Thomas Holland, The Charnockite Series: A Group of Archaean Hypersthenic Rocks in Peninsular India (Memoirs of the GSI, Vol. XXVIII, Part 2, 1900)
$$\text{Charnockite Mineral Formula: } \mathbf{Quartz}\ (SiO_2) + \mathbf{Feldspar}\ (\text{Microperthite } KAlSi_3O_8 + \text{Oligoclase}) + \mathbf{Hypersthene}\ ((Fe,Mg)_2Si_2O_6)$$ $$\text{Dehydration Breakdown Reaction: } \text{Biotite} + \text{Quartz} \rightleftharpoons \mathbf{Hypersthene} + \text{K-Feldspar} + H_2O \uparrow \quad (\text{at } T > 750^\circ\text{C}, a_{CO_2} \gg a_{H_2O})$$
Figure 80: The Charnockite Series plotted on the QAPF classification, highlighting the diagnostic Quartz-Feldspar-Hypersthene mineralogy of charnockite sensu stricto.

Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
2. Official Examination Question & Forensic Option Analysis
QUESTION 80
Generally, a charnockite has a mineral composition of :
A Quartz-Hornblende-Oligoclase
B Quartz-Epidote-Andesine
C Quartz-Feldspar-Hypersthene
D Quartz-Feldspar-Augite
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION C (Quartz-Feldspar-Hypersthene)
OPTION C • CORRECT
Quartz-Feldspar-Hypersthene

By Holland's classical definition and international nomenclature, charnockite is an orthopyroxene granite composed essentially of Quartz, Feldspar (microperthitic K-feldspar and plagioclase), and Hypersthene. The presence of hypersthene (orthopyroxene) is the non-negotiable diagnostic signature that separates charnockite from all ordinary granites.

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Quartz-Hornblende-Oligoclase

This assemblage corresponds to a typical Tonalite or Diorite. It lacks the essential orthopyroxene (hypersthene) and K-feldspar.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Quartz-Epidote-Andesine

Epidote is a hydrous low- to medium-grade mineral diagnostic of greenschist to epidote-amphibolite facies. It is completely unstable in the dry, ultra-high-temperature granulite facies regime of charnockites.

OPTION D • DISTRACTOR
Quartz-Feldspar-Augite

Augite is a clinopyroxene. While clinopyroxene may occur as a minor subordinate accessory, the essential diagnostic ferromagnesian mineral of charnockite is strictly orthopyroxene (Hypersthene).

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. Who named the charnockite series and after whom was it named?
Answer: Sir Thomas H. Holland (1900), after Job Charnock.
Holland named the rock after Job Charnock, founder of Calcutta, whose tombstone in St. John's Churchyard was made of this rock brought from St. Thomas Mount, Madras.
2. What pleochroic colors are typically displayed by hypersthene in a charnockite thin section?
Answer: Pink / reddish-pink ($\alpha$) to yellowish-green ($\beta$) to green ($\gamma$)
Hypersthene displays intense and diagnostic pleochroism from salmon-pink to pale green under plane-polarized light.
3. What causes the characteristic waxy, greasy bluish-green luster of charnockites in hand specimens?
Answer: Submicroscopic fluid inclusions ($CO_2$-rich) and exsolved micro-needles of rutile/iron oxides in quartz and feldspar.
These submicroscopic inclusions scatter light, producing the famous greasy appearance and opalescent blue quartz.
4. What is the process called where pre-existing amphibolite-facies gneisses are transformed in-situ into patchy charnockite by flushing of $CO_2$ fluids?
Answer: Charnockitization (or 'Incipient Charnockite' formation)
Demonstrated famously at Kabbaldurga (Karnataka), where carbonic fluids lowered water activity ($a_{H_2O}$), breaking down hornblende/biotite to hypersthene.
5. Which tectonic mobile belt in Eastern India is world-renowned for extensive charnockite-khondalite massifs?
Answer: The Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt (EGMB)
The Eastern Ghats belt (extending through Odisha and Andhra Pradesh) represents a deeply eroded Proterozoic granulite terrain dominated by charnockites and khondalites.
6. How does enderbite differ mineralogically from charnockite sensu stricto?
Answer: Enderbite is plagioclase-dominant (tonalitic), while charnockite s.s. has K-feldspar $\ge$ plagioclase (granitic).
In the charnockite series, enderbite is the hypersthene-bearing tonalite/trondhjemite equivalent.
7. What is the metamorphic facies condition required to generate hypersthene in quartzofeldspathic rocks?
Answer: Granulite Facies
Orthopyroxene in felsic rocks is the defining index mineral of the granulite facies ($T > 750^\circ\text{C}$).
8. What accessory mineral is often present alongside hypersthene in garnetiferous charnockites?
Answer: Almandine-Pyrope Garnet
High-pressure granulites frequently contain almandine-rich garnet formed via the reaction: $Biotite + Sillimanite + Quartz \rightarrow Garnet + K-feldspar + Liquid$.
Intermediate & Ultramafic Petrology / Question 081
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 81 • Igneous Petrology

Diorite Mafic Spectrum: From Leucodiorite to Meladiorite and Perkinite

Topic: Igneous Rock Classification & Color Index • Key Concept: 100% Ferromagnesian Extreme of Diorite • Textbooks: P.K. Mukherjee (Textbook of Geology, p. 249); K.M. Bangar; Duparc (1907)
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Color Index ($M'$) Variation in Intermediate Rocks

In classical petrography, intermediate plutonic rocks of the diorite family consist essentially of intermediate plagioclase (andesine or oligoclase) and ferromagnesian minerals (hornblende, augite, and biotite). Variations in the modal percentage of ferromagnesian (mafic) minerals dictate their nomenclature across the color index spectrum:

Rock Variety Ferromagnesian Content (Mafic Modal %) Feldspar Content (Plagioclase %) Petrological Definition & Mineralogy
Leucodiorite 0% – 35% Mafic 65% – 100% Andesine Light-colored, feldspar-rich variety of diorite.
Diorite (sensu stricto) 35% – 65% Mafic 35% – 65% Andesine Normal mesocratic diorite; balanced hornblende and andesine plagioclase.
Meladiorite 65% – 90% Mafic 10% – 35% Andesine Dark-colored, melanocratic variety of diorite enriched in hornblende/pyroxene.
Perkinite (Option A) 90% – 100% Mafic (100% Ferromagnesian) 0% – 10% (Feldspar-free extreme) Coarse-grained ultramafic rock composed essentially of amphibole (hornblende) and pyroxene without olivine.
"If the ferromagnesian content of diorite increases until plagioclase disappears entirely, the rock becomes 100% ferromagnesian. Such an ultramafic rock consisting essentially of hornblende and pyroxene is termed Perkinite. It stands as the ultramafic, feldspar-free end-member of the dioritic-gabbroic clan."
— P.K. Mukherjee, A Textbook of Geology (World Press, Igneous Rocks, p. 249)
$$\text{Diorite} = \text{Andesine Plagioclase} + \text{Ferromagnesian Minerals (Hornblende, Biotite, Augite)}$$ $$\text{When Ferromagnesian Content } \rightarrow 100\% \implies \text{Feldspar} \rightarrow 0\% \implies \mathbf{Perkinite}\ (\text{Hornblende} + \text{Pyroxene Ultramafic})$$
Figure 81: Color index classification bar showing the continuous transition from Leucodiorite through Diorite and Meladiorite to 100% ferromagnesian Perkinite.

Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
2. Official Examination Question & Forensic Option Analysis
QUESTION 81
If the ferromagnesian content of diorite is 100%, then it is called :
A Perkinite
B Leptinite
C Meladiorite
D Leucodiorite
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION A (Perkinite)
OPTION A • CORRECT
Perkinite

By standard classical petrographic nomenclature (Duparc, 1907; P.K. Mukherjee, p. 249; K.M. Bangar), when the ferromagnesian mineral percentage of diorite reaches 100% (meaning plagioclase feldspar is completely absent), the resulting ultramafic amphibole-pyroxene rock is designated as Perkinite.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Leptinite

Leptinite (or leptite) is a fine-grained, light-colored granoblastic metamorphic rock (granulite or felsic gneiss) dominated by quartz and feldspar. It is leucocratic and metamorphic, not an ultramafic rock.

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
Meladiorite

Meladiorite is a dark diorite that still contains 10% to 35% plagioclase feldspar ($M' = 65\text{--}90\%$). It does NOT have 100% ferromagnesian minerals.

OPTION D • DISTRACTOR
Leucodiorite

Leucodiorite is the exact polar opposite: it is a light-colored diorite dominated by plagioclase feldspar with only 0% to 35% ferromagnesian minerals.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. Who originally defined 'perkinite' and what were its primary constituents?
Answer: L. Duparc (1907); defined as an ultramafic rock composed essentially of amphibole and pyroxene.
Duparc introduced perkinite for coarse-grained rocks containing amphibole and pyroxene in varying proportions, with little to no olivine.
2. What is an ultramafic rock composed of greater than 90% olivine called?
Answer: Dunite
Dunite is a monomineralic ultramafic peridotite containing ≥90% modal olivine.
3. What is an ultramafic rock composed essentially of pyroxene called?
Answer: Pyroxenite
Pyroxenites contain >90% pyroxene (orthopyroxene, clinopyroxene, or both).
4. What is the distinguishing mineralogical difference between perkinite and peridotite?
Answer: Peridotite contains essential olivine (>40%), whereas perkinite is dominated by hornblende and pyroxene without significant olivine.
Peridotites are olivine-bearing ultramafic rocks (lherzolite, harzburgite, dunite), whereas perkinite belongs to the amphibole-pyroxene ultramafic group.
5. What prefix is added to an igneous rock name when the mafic mineral content is between 65% and 90%?
Answer: Mela- (e.g., meladiorite, melagabbro)
IUGS uses 'mela-' for melanocratic varieties with color index $M' = 65\text{--}90\%$, and 'leuco-' for leucocratic varieties with $M' = 0\text{--}35\%$.
6. What is the volcanic equivalent of an ultramafic rock?
Answer: Komatiite
Komatiites are Archaean ultramafic volcanic lavas with >18 wt% $MgO$ displaying spinifex texture.
7. What is an anorthosite in terms of plagioclase content?
Answer: An ultra-leucocratic plutonic rock containing greater than 90% plagioclase feldspar.
Anorthosite is essentially monomineralic plagioclase ($M' < 10\%$).
8. What is the characteristic plagioclase in diorite?
Answer: Andesine ($An_{30}\text{--}An_{50}$) or Oligoclase
If the plagioclase is more calcic than $An_{50}$ (labradorite/bytownite), the rock is classified as a gabbro rather than a diorite.

Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 82 • Igneous Petrology

The Basic Mafic Triad: Compositional Equivalence of Dolerite, Basalt, and Gabbro

Topic: Basic Igneous Rocks • Key Concept: Hypabyssal vs. Volcanic Textural Equivalents • Textbooks: K.M. Bangar (p. 126); John D. Winter (Principles of Igneous Petrology)
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: The Plutonic-Hypabyssal-Volcanic Equivalence Triad

In igneous petrology, rocks sharing identical chemical and mineralogical compositions are subdivided into three structural categories based on their cooling rate, depth of consolidation, and resulting crystalline texture:

Structural Setting Cooling Regime & Depth Grain Size & Diagnostic Texture Representative Mafic Rock
Plutonic (Deep Intrusive) Slow cooling at deep crustal levels ($> 3\text{--}5\text{ km}$) Coarse-grained, phaneritic equigranular Gabbro
Hypabyssal (Subvolcanic / Shallow Intrusive) Moderate cooling in dykes, sills, and cone sheets ($< 2\text{ km}$) Medium-grained, ophitic / subophitic (laths of plagioclase enclosed by pyroxene) DOLERITE (Diabase)
Volcanic (Extrusive) Rapid quenching at Earth's surface as lava flows Fine-grained, aphanitic, glassy, intersertal / hyalopilitic BASALT (Option D)
"By mineralogical and chemical composition, dolerite is precisely equivalent to basalt and gabbro. All three consist essentially of calcic plagioclase (labradorite or bytownite) and clinopyroxene (augite), with or without olivine and titanomagnetite. Dolerite represents the medium-grained hypabyssal facies (forming dykes and sills), basalt is the fine-grained extrusive volcanic facies, and gabbro is the coarse-grained plutonic facies."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Petrology, p. 126)
$$\text{Shared Chemical Composition: Basic } (45\text{--}52\text{ wt\% } SiO_2)$$ $$\text{Shared Mineralogy: Calcic Plagioclase } (An_{50-70}) + \text{Clinopyroxene (Augite)} \pm \text{Olivine} \pm \text{Fe-Ti Oxides}$$ $$\mathbf{Dolerite\ (Hypabyssal)} \equiv \mathbf{Basalt\ (Volcanic)} \equiv \mathbf{Gabbro\ (Plutonic)}$$
Figure 82: The basic igneous rock triad showing compositional equivalence between coarse plutonic Gabbro, medium hypabyssal Dolerite, and fine volcanic Basalt.

Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection

2. Official Examination Question & Forensic Option Analysis
QUESTION 82
By mineral composition, dolerite is equivalent to :
A Pitchstone
B Syenite
C Peridotite
D Basalt
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION D (Basalt)
OPTION D • CORRECT
Basalt

Dolerite (termed diabase in North American literature) and basalt share identical mineral compositions: both are basic rocks composed of calcic plagioclase (labradorite) and augite (clinopyroxene). Dolerite is the medium-grained hypabyssal intrusive equivalent of extrusive volcanic basalt.

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Pitchstone

Pitchstone is a volcanic glass of acidic to intermediate composition ($SiO_2 > 65\%$, with 4-10% water) characterized by a dull, pitch-like resinous luster. It is highly felsic, unlike basic dolerite.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Syenite

Syenite is an intermediate plutonic rock dominated by alkali feldspar (orthoclase/microcline) with minor hornblende or biotite. It is rich in alkalis ($K_2O + Na_2O$) and low in lime/magnesia, totally distinct from mafic dolerite.

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
Peridotite

Peridotite is an ultrabasic rock ($SiO_2 < 45\%$) composed almost entirely of olivine and pyroxenes with little or no feldspar. Dolerite contains 50% or more plagioclase feldspar.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. What diagnostic texture is characteristic of dolerites under the petrological microscope?
Answer: Ophitic (or Subophitic) texture
In ophitic texture, elongated, euhedral laths of plagioclase are completely or partially enclosed within larger, anhedral plates of augite pyroxene.
2. What is the North American synonymous term for dolerite?
Answer: Diabase
In the United States and Canada, medium-grained basic hypabyssal rocks are called diabase, whereas in British and Indian usage, they are called dolerite.
3. What prominent geological formation in Peninsular India contains thousands of dolerite dykes cutting Archaean basements?
Answer: Newer Dolerite dyke swarms of the Singhbhum Craton (Odisha-Jharkhand) and Cuddapah dykes
The Singhbhum craton is criss-crossed by the spectacular Palaeoproterozoic Newer Dolerite dyke swarm trending NNE-SSW and NW-SE.
4. What is the fine-grained volcanic equivalent of Granite?
Answer: Rhyolite
Just as basalt is to dolerite/gabbro, rhyolite is the volcanic equivalent of granitic intrusive rocks.
5. What alteration process converts calcic plagioclase in dolerite to epidote, zoisite, and albite?
Answer: Saussuritization
Hydrothermal alteration or low-grade metamorphism breaks down calcic plagioclase into a fine-grained aggregate of zoisite, epidote, calcite, and albite (saussurite).
6. What alteration process transforms pyroxene in dolerite to fibrous green amphibole (actinolite/tremolite)?
Answer: Uralitization
Uralitization is the hydrothermal replacement of primary clinopyroxene (augite) by secondary fibrous amphibole (uralite).
7. What is an olivine-rich dolerite called?
Answer: Olivine dolerite
When olivine exceeds 5-10% of modal volume, the rock is specifically termed olivine dolerite.
8. What is the characteristic weathering pattern displayed by dolerite dyke outcrops in the field?
Answer: Spheroidal weathering (onion-skin spalling) and 'tombstone' topography
Jointed dolerite blocks weather inward along moisture-rich corners, peeling off in concentric shells and leaving rounded corestones resembling giant boulders or tombstones.
Basic Rock Clan & Varieties / Question 083
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 83 • Igneous Petrology

Beerbachite: Petrography, Granular Microgabbro Affinities, and Classification

Topic: Basic Rock Varieties • Key Concept: Fine-Grained Granular Gabbro / Pyroxene-Granulite Hornfels • Textbooks: Chelius (1892); IUGS Subcommission on the Systematics of Igneous Rocks; P.K. Mukherjee
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Origin & Petrographic Nature of Beerbachite

Beerbachite was originally described in 1892 by German petrologist C. Chelius from Beerbach in the Odenwald, Germany. In classical and modern petrology, it designates a fine-grained, equigranular (aplitic to granoblastic) variety of Gabbro (microgabbro) consisting essentially of granular calcic plagioclase and pyroxene:

Petrographic Attribute Scientific Characteristic Diagnostic Mineralogy & Texture
Parent Rock Group Gabbro Clan (Basic Igneous Rock) Compositionally identical to basic gabbro/norite; $SiO_2 \approx 45\text{--}52\%$.
Essential Mineralogy Calcic Plagioclase + Pyroxene Labradorite/Bytownite + Orthopyroxene (Hypersthene) + Clinopyroxene (Diallage/Augite) + Magnetite.
Microscopic Texture Granular / Saccharoidal (Aplitic) Evenly sized, polygonal, mosaic-like grains without porphyritic or ophitic textures; resembles a pyroxene-hornfels.
Geological Occurrence Dykes & Contact Aureoles Occurs as aplitic basic dykes cutting larger gabbro massifs, or as intensely recrystallized basaltic xenoliths/walls in contact metamorphic aureoles.
"Beerbachite is a fine-grained, granular variety of gabbro (or aplitic microgabbro) characterized by a sugary, saccharoidal texture. It consists of an equigranular mosaic of labradorite and pyroxene (both augite and hypersthene). Originally regarded as a basic aplite dyke rock, many beerbachites are now recognized as basaltic or doleritic inclusions contact-metamorphosed to pyroxene-hornfels facies by host gabbroic intrusions."
— IUGS Subcommission on the Systematics of Igneous Rocks; P.K. Mukherjee, A Textbook of Geology (p. 251)
$$\text{Beerbachite Mineral Assemblage} \equiv \text{Calcic Plagioclase } (An_{55-75}) + \text{Pyroxenes (Augite } \pm \text{ Hypersthene)} + \text{Fe-Ti Oxides}$$ $$\text{Texture: Granoblastic / Aplitic (Non-ophitic, granular microgabbro)} \implies \mathbf{Gabbro\ Family\ (Option\ A)}$$
Figure 83: Position of Beerbachite within the Gabbro clan as a fine-grained granular/aplitic variety alongside Norite, Troctolite, and Anorthosite.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
2. Official Examination Question & Forensic Option Analysis
QUESTION 83
Beerbachite is a variety of :
A Gabbro
B Basalt
C Dolerite
D Monzonite
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION A (Gabbro)
OPTION A • CORRECT
Gabbro

Beerbachite is historically and systematically classified as a fine-grained granular or aplitic variety of Gabbro (microgabbro). It shares the identical mineral chemistry of gabbro (calcic plagioclase + pyroxene) while displaying a distinctive saccharoidal, equigranular mosaic texture.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Basalt

Basalt is an extrusive volcanic lava flow exhibiting aphanitic, glassy, or intersertal textures. Beerbachite forms as intrusive dykes or high-grade thermal hornfelses with completely holocrystalline granular texture.

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
Dolerite

Dolerite is characterized by ophitic or subophitic texture with subhedral plagioclase laths. Beerbachite lacks ophitic texture, displaying instead an equigranular (aplitic) mosaic texture.

OPTION D • DISTRACTOR
Monzonite

Monzonite is an intermediate plutonic rock containing roughly equal amounts of alkali feldspar and plagioclase ($SiO_2 \approx 55\text{--}62\%$). Beerbachite contains no alkali feldspar and is strictly basic.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. From which European locality was beerbachite originally named?
Answer: Beerbach in the Odenwald, Hesse, Germany.
C. Chelius named the rock in 1892 from dyke-like occurrences cutting gabbros in the Odenwald mountain range.
2. What type of gabbro is characterized by essential orthopyroxene rather than clinopyroxene?
Answer: Norite
When orthopyroxene (enstatite/hypersthene) is the dominant pyroxene alongside calcic plagioclase, the rock is formally termed norite.
3. What is troctolite composed of?
Answer: Calcic plagioclase and olivine (essentially pyroxene-free).
Troctolite (from Greek for 'trout rock') is an olivine-plagioclase cumulate member of the gabbro family.
4. What is a basic aplite?
Answer: A fine-grained, saccharoidal dyke rock of basic composition (such as beerbachite).
While aplites are typically granitic, fine-grained sugary dykes of gabbroic composition are historically called basic aplites or beerbachites.
5. Under what metamorphic facies do basaltic country rocks recrystallize to produce beerbachite-like textures?
Answer: Pyroxene-hornfels facies (or Sanidinite facies)
Extreme contact thermal metamorphism by mafic magma dehydrates basalts into an equigranular mosaic of pyroxene and calcic plagioclase.
6. What is the diallage variety of clinopyroxene commonly found in gabbros?
Answer: Augite exhibiting prominent (100) parting due to microscopic exsolution lamellae of orthopyroxene.
Diallage is a historical petrographic name for augite with a distinctive platy parting parallel to {100} and pearly lustre.
7. What is an olivine gabbro?
Answer: A gabbro containing calcic plagioclase, clinopyroxene, and >5% modal olivine.
Olivine gabbro is an abundant member of ocean floor crust (layer 3) and continental layered mafic complexes.
8. What is the typical anorthite content ($An\%$) of plagioclase in gabbroic rocks?
Answer: $An_{50}\text{--}An_{85}$ (Labradorite to Bytownite)
By definition, gabbros contain calcic plagioclase with $An > 50\%$, which separates them from diorites ($An < 50\%$).
Granitoids & QAPF Systematics / Question 084

OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 84 • Igneous Petrology

Adamellite (Quartz Monzonite): IUGS Granitoid QAPF Systematics and Feldspar Ratios

Topic: Granitic Rock Classification • Key Concept: Sub-equal Alkali Feldspar and Plagioclase • Textbooks: IUGS Systematics of Igneous Rocks (Le Maitre, 2002); K.M. Bangar (p. 123)
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Adamellite in Granitoid Systematics

Adamellite was named in 1898 by A. Cathrein after Mount Adamello in the Italian Alps. In classical petrography and the standard IUGS classification, adamellite is synonymous with Quartz Monzonite (Field 3b of the QAPF classification), defined as a plutonic rock where quartz comprises 20% to 60% of the felsic minerals and the ratio of plagioclase to total feldspar is roughly equal ($35\% \le P/(A+P) \le 65\%$):

Rock Type IUGS QAPF Field Plagioclase : Alkali Feldspar Ratio Dominant Feldspar Species Characteristic Ferromagnesian Minerals
Alkali-Feldspar Granite Field 2 $P/(A+P) < 10\%$ (Alkali Feldspar dominant) Orthoclase, Microcline, Perthite >> Albite Biotite, Riebeckite, Aegirine
Syenogranite Field 3a $10\% \le P/(A+P) < 35\%$ K-Feldspar > Plagioclase Biotite ± Muscovite
ADAMELLITE (Quartz Monzonite) Field 3b $35\% \le P/(A+P) \le 65\%$ (Roughly EQUAL) Roughly equal amounts of Oligoclase & K-feldspar Biotite, Hornblende
Granodiorite Field 4 $65\% < P/(A+P) \le 90\%$ (Plagioclase dominant) Oligoclase/Andesine > K-Feldspar Hornblende > Biotite
Tonalite (Trondhjemite) Field 5 $P/(A+P) > 90\%$ (Extreme Plagioclase) Andesine/Oligoclase >> K-Feldspar Hornblende, Biotite
"Adamellite is a variety of granite containing roughly equal amounts of orthoclase (K-feldspar) and plagioclase (normally oligoclase), with 20% to 60% quartz. In Brøgger's terminology and modern IUGS usage, it is referred to as quartz monzonite. When plagioclase exceeds two-thirds of total feldspar, the rock grades into granodiorite; when potash feldspar exceeds two-thirds, it becomes normal granite (syenogranite)."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Petrology Section, pp. 122–124)
$$\text{Feldspar Ratio in Adamellite: } \frac{\text{Plagioclase (Oligoclase)}}{\text{Alkali Feldspar (K-spar)} + \text{Plagioclase}} \approx 0.35 \text{ to } 0.65 \implies \mathbf{Plagioclase \approx K\text{-}feldspar}$$ $$\text{Quartz Content: } 20\% \le Q \le 60\% \quad \text{of Total } (Q + A + P)$$
Figure 84: IUGS QAPF classification of granitoids highlighting Field 3b (Adamellite / Quartz Monzonite) positioned at the balanced center where Oligoclase and K-feldspar are roughly equal.

Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
2. Official Examination Question & Forensic Option Analysis
QUESTION 84
Adamellite contains :
A Roughly equal amounts of Oligoclase and K-feldspar
B Roughly equal amounts of Quartz and Oligoclase
C Roughly equal amounts of Quartz and K-feldspar
D Roughly equal amounts of Quartz and Albite
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION A (Roughly equal amounts of Oligoclase and K-feldspar)
OPTION A • CORRECT
Roughly equal amounts of Oligoclase and K-feldspar

By international and Indian petrological definition, adamellite (quartz monzonite) is specifically distinguished from granite sensu stricto and granodiorite by possessing roughly equal proportions of plagioclase (oligoclase) and potash feldspar (orthoclase/microcline) ($P/(A+P)$ ratio of approximately 1:1, or between 35:65 and 65:35).

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Roughly equal amounts of Quartz and Oligoclase

Granitoid classifications are fundamentally based on the ratio between the two feldspar phases ($A$ vs $P$), not the ratio between quartz and plagioclase. In adamellite, total feldspar comprises 50% to 70% of the rock, while quartz makes up only 20% to 35%.

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
Roughly equal amounts of Quartz and K-feldspar

This is incorrect. Quartz and K-feldspar do not define adamellite; a rock with equal quartz and K-feldspar but little plagioclase is a syenogranite or alkali-feldspar granite.

OPTION D • DISTRACTOR
Roughly equal amounts of Quartz and Albite

Albite ($An_0\text{--}An_{10}$) is the sodic alkali feldspar characteristic of rare peralkaline granites. Adamellite typically contains calcic-sodic plagioclase in the range of oligoclase ($An_{10}\text{--}An_{30}$) alongside microcline/orthoclase.
