High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. What is the volcanic extrusive equivalent of Adamellite (Quartz Monzonite)?
Answer: Quartz Latite (or Rhyodacite)
Quartz latite contains phenocrysts of both plagioclase and sanidine in roughly equal amounts within a fine-grained silicic groundmass.
2. Who introduced the term 'monzonite' and from which type area is it derived?
Answer: Albert de Lapparent (1864), from Mount Monzoni in the Italian Dolomites.
Monzoni in Northern Italy is the type locality for intermediate plutonic rocks having equal alkali feldspar and plagioclase.
3. What is the difference between monzonite and quartz monzonite (adamellite)?
Answer: Monzonite has <5% modal quartz; quartz monzonite (adamellite) has 5% to 20% (or 20-60% in QAPF) quartz.
Monzonite is silica-saturated/intermediate, while quartz monzonite is oversaturated and acidic.
4. What is the specific composition of oligoclase plagioclase found in adamellites?
Answer: $An_{10}$ to $An_{30}$ ($10\%\text{--}30\%$ anorthite, $70\%\text{--}90\%$ albite).
Oligoclase is the classic intermediate-sodic plagioclase of acid plutonic rocks.
5. Which batholith in North America contains enormous volumes of adamellite/quartz monzonite?
Answer: The Sierra Nevada Batholith and Idaho Batholith
Mesozoic subduction-related cordilleran batholiths are predominantly composed of granodiorite, adamellite, and tonalite.
6. What is the characteristic dark mineral in adamellites?
Answer: Biotite mica ± common hornblende
Adamellites are calc-alkaline rocks typically carrying 10-15% mafics, dominated by brown biotite and dark green hornblende.
7. Why did the IUGS Subcommission recommend replacing 'adamellite' with 'quartz monzonite'?
Answer: To create a consistent, systematic root-name hierarchy based on QAP modal parameters.
IUGS (1973, 2002) preferred 'quartz monzonite' for Field 3b, but recognized adamellite as an established historical synonym.
8. What texture is produced when plagioclase cores in adamellite are mantled by alkali feldspar?
Answer: Anti-rapakivi texture
Rapakivi texture is K-feldspar mantled by plagioclase; the reverse (plagioclase mantled by K-feldspar) is anti-rapakivi.
Igneous Textures & Pegmatites / Question 085
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 85 • Igneous Petrology

Graphic (Runic) Texture: Eutectic Crystallization in Granitic Pegmatites

Topic: Igneous Textures & Pegmatites • Key Concept: Quartz-Feldspar Simultaneous Eutectic Intergrowth • Textbooks: K.M. Bangar (p. 115); John D. Winter (Principles of Igneous Petrology)
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Origin & Morphology of Graphic Texture

Graphic texture (also termed runic texture or micrographic texture) is a distinctive magmatic intergrowth texture where angular, wedge-shaped, or hook-shaped rods of quartz are enclosed within a single optically continuous host crystal of alkali feldspar (microcline or orthoclase). In cross-section, the skeletal quartz crystals strikingly resemble ancient cuneiform, Arabic, or runic writing:

Feature Petrological Characteristic Physicochemical Significance
Host Rock Type Granitic Pegmatite (Option B) Exhibited magnificently in coarse pegmatite border and wall zones (often termed graphic granite).
Host Mineral Microcline / Orthoclase (Alkali Feldspar) Forms large, single-crystal optically continuous background plates (pink, buff, or white).
Intersertal Mineral Quartz (Ichthyoglypts / Skeletal Rods) Parallel three-dimensional rods of quartz that extinguish simultaneously under crossed polars.
Petrogenetic Mechanism Simultaneous Eutectic Crystallization Precipitates at the granite eutectic minimum in volatile-rich, undercooled residual pegmatitic melts.
Phase Ratio $\sim 72\text{--}75\%$ Feldspar : $25\text{--}28\%$ Quartz Matches precisely the eutectic proportions in the binary $SiO_2 - KAlSi_3O_8 - H_2O$ phase system at water-vapor pressures.
"Graphic texture is an intimate intergrowth of quartz and alkali feldspar in which the quartz forms angular, skeletal grains resembling runic inscriptions or ancient cuneiform characters. It is the hallmark texture of pegmatites (graphic granite), resulting from the simultaneous, rapid, eutectic crystallization of quartz and feldspar from a volatile-rich, fluxed residual magmatic liquid."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Petrology Section, p. 115)
$$\text{Eutectic Crystallization: Liquid } (L) \xrightarrow{\Delta T} \text{Alkali Feldspar} + \text{Quartz simultaneously}$$ $$\text{Eutectic Phase Ratio: } \approx 72\text{ wt\% Feldspar} : 28\text{ wt\% Quartz} \quad (\text{Constant across global graphic pegmatites})$$
Figure 85: Schematic thin-section view of graphic texture in granitic pegmatite, showing skeletal quartz rods mimicking runic writing embedded in a single microcline host crystal.

Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
2. Official Examination Question & Forensic Option Analysis
QUESTION 85
Graphic texture is normally exhibited by :
A Komatiite
B Pegmatite
C Phonolite
D Anorthosite
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION B (Pegmatite)
OPTION B • CORRECT
Pegmatite

Graphic texture is the textbook diagnostic feature of granitic pegmatites (often known commercially as graphic granite). It forms by the simultaneous, eutectic precipitation of skeletal quartz rods within large plates of alkali feldspar from volatile-saturated, fluxed residual fluids.

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Komatiite

Komatiite is an Archaean ultramafic volcanic rock characterized by spinifex texture (skeletal, bladed, or platy crystals of olivine and pyroxene caused by rapid surface supercooling). It never contains graphic quartz-feldspar intergrowths.

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
Phonolite

Phonolite is an undersaturated alkaline volcanic rock composed of nepheline, sanidine, and aegirine. Because phonolite is silica-undersaturated (foid-bearing), free quartz cannot form, making graphic texture chemically impossible.

OPTION D • DISTRACTOR
Anorthosite

Anorthosite is a coarse-grained monomineralic plutonic rock consisting of >90% plagioclase feldspar displaying cumulate and adcumulate textures, not graphic intergrowths.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. How does micrographic texture differ from granophyric texture?
Answer: Granophyric texture exhibits a radiating, plumose, or spherulitic intergrowth of quartz and feldspar, often in subvolcanic felsic intrusions.
Granophyric texture occurs at shallower depths and higher undercooling than classic coarse graphic pegmatite.
2. What optical proof confirms that all quartz rods in a graphic granite field belong to a single continuous crystal network?
Answer: They extinguish simultaneously under crossed nicols (birefringence extinction).
Even though cross-sections appear as disconnected angular rods, all quartz units share a single three-dimensional crystallographic orientation.
3. What is the difference between graphic texture and myrmekitic texture?
Answer: Graphic texture is magmatic quartz in K-feldspar; myrmekite is vermicular quartz in sodic plagioclase replacing K-feldspar.
Myrmekite forms by subsolidus fluid-driven metasomatism: $KAlSi_3O_8 + Na^+/Ca^{2+} \rightarrow (Na,Ca)AlSi_3O_8 + SiO_2 (quartz) + K^+$.
4. What is a complex pegmatite with distinct concentric zones called?
Answer: Zoned pegmatite (e.g., Border zone $\rightarrow$ Wall zone $\rightarrow$ Intermediate zone $\rightarrow$ Quartz core)
Cameron et al. (1949) demonstrated that graphic texture typically develops in the intermediate wall zone of zoned pegmatites.
5. What volatile components lower the crystallization temperature of pegmatite melts to $500\text{--}650^\circ\text{C}$?
Answer: Water ($H_2O$), Fluorine ($F$), Boron ($B$), and Lithium ($Li$)
These network-modifying fluxing components depolymerize the silicate melt, reducing viscosity and enabling giant crystal growth.
6. In which Indian state are the world-famous Bihar Mica Belt pegmatites located?
Answer: Jharkhand (Koderma, Giridih, Hazaribagh districts)
The Koderma pegmatite belt is renowned for giant muscovite 'books', beryl, and exquisite graphic granites.
7. What is an aplite in relation to a pegmatite?
Answer: Aplite is a fine-grained, sugary (saccharoidal) felsic dyke rock of identical granitic composition to pegmatite.
Aplites crystallize rapidly due to sudden pressure-release quenching (loss of volatiles), whereas pegmatites crystallize slowly from volatile-rich fluids.
8. What is the term for the skeletal fish-hook shaped quartz grains in graphic texture?
Answer: Ichthyoglypts
Classical petrographers termed the hieroglyphic, hook-shaped quartz rods in graphic granite 'ichthyoglypts' (fish carvings).
Pluton Morphology & Concordant Bodies / Question 086
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 86 • Igneous Petrology

Pluton Morphology: Laccolith Mechanics and Concordant Intrusive Geometry

Topic: Forms of Igneous Rocks • Key Concept: Mushroom-Shaped Pluton with Domed Roof & Flat Floor • Textbooks: G.K. Gilbert (1877); K.M. Bangar (p. 118); G.B. Mahapatra
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Morphology & Mechanics of Concordant Intrusions

In structural and igneous geology, intrusive bodies are classified as concordant when their contacts are parallel to the bedding or foliation planes of the country rock, and discordant when they cross-cut pre-existing planar structures. The classic concordant forms are defined by their geometric cross-sections:

Intrusive Form Roof Geometry Floor Geometry Structural Effect on Host Strata Magmatic Viscosity & Examples
LACCOLITH (Option D) Arched / Convex Upward (Domed) Flat / Planar Horizontal Forces overlying sedimentary beds upward into a gentle to steep structural dome. High-viscosity felsic/intermediate melts (Henry Mountains, Utah; G.K. Gilbert, 1877).
Lopolith Concave Upward (Depressed) Concave Upward (Saucer-shaped) Weight of intrusion sags underlying strata into a central structural basin. Huge basic to ultrabasic layered intrusions (Bushveld, South Africa; Duluth, USA).
Bysmalith Steeply Domed / Plug-shaped Flat Floor bounded by faults Overlying strata lifted vertically like a cylindrical plug along circumscribing piston faults. Extremely viscous silicic magmas (Mt. Holmes, Yellowstone; Iddings, 1898).
Phacolith Crescentic / Lens-shaped Concordant with fold limbs Passive filling of low-pressure crests of anticlines or troughs of synclines. Folded mountain belts (Harker, 1909).
Sill Tabular Planar Parallel Tabular Planar Parallel Injected horizontally along bedding without doming; uniform thickness. Low-viscosity basic basaltic melts (Great Whin Sill, UK; Karoo, S. Africa).
"A laccolith is a concordant, mushroom-shaped or blister-like igneous intrusion that has an approximately flat floor and an arched or domed roof. When viscous magma is injected along bedding planes, instead of spreading laterally as a thin sill, it accumulates locally and pushes up the overlying strata into a magnificent dome or anticline."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Forms of Igneous Bodies, p. 118)
$$\text{Laccolith Mechanics: Magma Overpressure } (P_{\text{magma}}) > \text{Lithostatic Overburden Load } (\rho_{\text{rock}} g z) + \text{Bending Rigidity } (D \nabla^4 w)$$ $$\text{Result: Overlying strata flexed into a dome } \implies \mathbf{Concordant\ Domed\ Pluton \equiv Laccolith}$$
Figure 86: Cross-sectional comparisons of concordant igneous intrusions highlighting the domed-up roof and planar floor of a Laccolith compared to a saucer-shaped Lopolith and faulted Bysmalith.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
2. Official Examination Question & Forensic Option Analysis
QUESTION 86
An igneous body that has doomed up the strata into which it has been inserted is known as :
A Lopolith
B Dyke
C Bysmalith
D Laccolith
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION D (Laccolith)
OPTION D • CORRECT
Laccolith

By standard definition (G.K. Gilbert, 1877; Bangar; Mahapatra), a laccolith (from Greek lakkos = reservoir/cistern, and lithos = stone) is a concordant igneous intrusion characterized by a flat floor and a convex-upward roof that has physically arched or domed up the overlying strata.

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Lopolith

A lopolith is a saucer-shaped intrusion where the floor and roof are concave upward (sagged downward into a basin under magmatic weight), the exact opposite of an upward-domed laccolith.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Dyke

A dyke is a discordant tabular body that cuts perpendicularly or obliquely across bedding planes. It does not dome up strata.

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
Bysmalith

While a bysmalith is an extreme cylindrical plug-shaped offshoot of a laccolith, its roof is lifted vertically along steep bounding peripheral faults like a piston, rather than gently doming continuous flexible strata.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. Who first described and named laccoliths in classical geological literature?
Answer: Grove Karl Gilbert (1877), in his classic report on the Henry Mountains of Utah.
G.K. Gilbert established the fundamental principles of laccolithic intrusion, hydraulic lift, and structural doming.
2. Why do basic (basaltic) magmas typically form sills rather than laccoliths?
Answer: Low viscosity allows basic magma to spread laterally for long distances; viscous felsic magma pools locally, pushing up the roof.
Magma viscosity governs morphology: low-viscosity basalt spreads into thin extensive sills, while high-viscosity dacite/rhyolite bulges into laccoliths.
3. What is a concordant intrusion located along the crest of an anticline or trough of a syncline called?
Answer: Phacolith
Alfred Harker (1909) coined 'phacolith' for lens-shaped intrusions that occupy fold crests or troughs where mechanical pressure is lowest.
4. What is a lopolith, and what famous igneous complex represents the world's greatest example?
Answer: A huge saucer-shaped intrusion with sagging floor; the Bushveld Igneous Complex of South Africa.
The Bushveld lopolith covers over $65,000\text{ km}^2$ and holds world-class platinum group elements (Merensky Reef) and chromite.
5. What is the surface area requirement for an igneous pluton to be classified as a batholith?
Answer: Greater than 100 square kilometers ($> 100\text{ km}^2$)
By definition, discordant plutons with exposed areas $< 100\text{ km}^2$ are termed stocks or bosses; those $> 100\text{ km}^2$ are batholiths.
6. What is a ring-dyke versus a cone-sheet?
Answer: Ring-dykes dip steeply outward/vertically; cone-sheets dip inward toward a common magmatic focus.
Cone-sheets form during upward magmatic pressure; ring-dykes form by cauldron subsidence when the magma chamber roof drops.
7. How can a sill be distinguished in the field from a buried lava flow?
Answer: A sill produces thermal metamorphism (baking) on BOTH its top and bottom contacts and has no vesicular top; a flow only bakes its floor.
Sills bake both upper and lower country rocks and may contain xenoliths from both; lava flows display ropy/vesicular tops and only bake the base.
8. What is a bysmalith?
Answer: A plugged laccolith whose roof has been vertically uplifted along circular fault boundaries.
J.P. Iddings (1898) defined a bysmalith as a cylindrical plug-shaped intrusion where uplift exceeded bending limits, shearing the bounding walls.
Magma Ascent & Emplacement Mechanisms / Question 087
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 87 • Igneous Petrology

Pluton Emplacement Mechanics: R.A. Daly's Theory of Magmatic Stoping

Topic: Magma Ascent & Emplacement Mechanisms • Key Concept: Overhead Stoping & Thermal Shattering • Textbooks: Reginald A. Daly (1903, 1914); K.M. Bangar (p. 119); John D. Winter
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: The Room Problem & Magmatic Stoping

One of the classic conundrums in igneous geology is the 'room problem': how do huge granitic batholiths comprising thousands of cubic kilometers of magma make space for themselves as they ascend through the brittle, solid continental crust? In 1903, Harvard geologist Reginald Aldworth Daly formulated the definitive mechanical theory of Magmatic Stoping (overhead or piecemeal stoping):

Stage Physical / Thermal Process Mechanical Consequence
1. Thermal Shattering Extreme heat from ascending magma ($800\text{--}1100^\circ\text{C}$) establishes steep thermal gradients across the roof rock. Thermal expansion and hydraulic fracturing generate intense jointing and brecciation in country rock walls.
2. Magmatic Wedging Low-viscosity volatile fluids and magma under high pressure inject into open joints and bedding planes. Disarticulates large angular blocks of country rock from the roof (overhead quarrying).
3. Gravitational Sinking (Stoping) Solid country rock blocks ($\rho \approx 2.7\text{--}2.9\text{ g/cm}^3$) are denser than the hydrous granitic melt ($\rho \approx 2.3\text{--}2.5\text{ g/cm}^3$). Blocks (xenoliths) sink downward through the magma chamber, clearing space for the magma to work its way upward.
4. Abyssal Assimilation Sunken xenoliths reach the hotter, deeper base of the chamber where they undergo partial melting and hybrid assimilation. Contaminates magma chemistry (crustal assimilation) leaving restite residues at depth.
"The process whereby magma works its way up into the crust of the earth by mechanically shattering, detaching, and engulfing blocks of the roof and wall rocks—which then sink through the lighter molten magma—is known as Magmatic Stoping (or overhead stoping). Proposed by R.A. Daly in 1903, it explains how batholiths cut cleanly across country rock structures without pushing them aside."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Forms of Igneous Bodies, p. 119)
$$\text{Gravitational Sinking Condition: } \rho_{\text{country rock block (xenolith)}} > \rho_{\text{magma liquid}}$$ $$\Delta \rho = \rho_{\text{solid}} - \rho_{\text{melt}} \approx 2.75 - 2.40 = +0.35\text{ g/cm}^3 \implies \text{Downward Stokes Sinking}$$ $$\mathbf{Upward\ Magma\ Ascent\ via\ Xenolith\ Engulfment \equiv Magmatic\ Stoping\ (Option\ C)}$$
Figure 87: Cross-section of a magmatic chamber demonstrating overhead stoping: thermal fracturing of roof rocks, detachment and gravitational sinking of xenoliths, and upward migration of the intrusion.

Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection

2. Official Examination Question & Forensic Option Analysis
QUESTION 87
A process whereby magma works its way up into the crust of the earth is known as :
A Magmatic injection
B Magmatic thrusting
C Magmatic stoping
D Magmatic intrusion
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION C (Magmatic stoping)
OPTION C • CORRECT
Magmatic stoping

By standard textbook terminology (R.A. Daly, 1903; Bangar, p. 119; Mahapatra), the classic mechanism whereby magma works its way upward through the crust by fracturing and engulfing roof blocks (which sink under gravity) is formally defined as magmatic stoping (or overhead/piecemeal stoping).

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Magmatic injection

Magmatic injection refers simply to the passive or forceful squirt of molten rock into pre-existing fractures or fissures (such as forming dykes and sills), not the continuous crustal penetration process described by Daly.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Magmatic thrusting

Magmatic thrusting is an informal or non-standard term; forceful shouldering aside of country rock is called diapirism or forceful shouldering, not 'thrusting'.

OPTION D • DISTRACTOR
Magmatic intrusion

'Magmatic intrusion' is an umbrella general term denoting any underground entry of magma, whereas the specific process of magma working its way through roof-shattering and block sinking is specifically termed magmatic stoping.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. Who proposed the theory of magmatic stoping and in which year?
Answer: Reginald Aldworth Daly (1903)
Daly published 'The Mechanics of Igneous Intrusion' in the American Journal of Science (1903), detailing overhead stoping.
2. What field evidence directly supports the occurrence of magmatic stoping along pluton roofs?
Answer: Abundant angular xenoliths of country rock frozen in the margins and roof of the intrusion.
Xenolith-rich 'intrusion breccias' at contacts capture roof blocks caught in the act of detaching and sinking.
3. What is the fundamental physical requirement for stoped blocks to sink through the magma?
Answer: The density of the solid country rock must exceed the density of the magma melt.
Silicic melts have densities around $2.3\text{--}2.4\text{ g/cm}^3$, whereas solid country rocks (schists, gneisses, basalts) have densities of $2.6\text{--}3.0\text{ g/cm}^3$.
4. What is piecemeal stoping vs. cauldron stoping?
Answer: Piecemeal stoping involves small individual blocks; cauldron stoping involves a single giant cylindrical block sinking along ring faults.
Cauldron subsidence (Clough, Maufe, & Bailey, 1909) is the large-scale caldera equivalent of overhead stoping.
5. What chemical process occurs when stoped xenoliths dissolve and react with the surrounding magma?
Answer: Magmatic Assimilation (Contamination)
Assimilation modifies the chemical composition of the melt, often enriching it in silica, alumina, and incompatible trace elements.
6. What is the term for a fragment of foreign country rock completely enclosed within an igneous pluton?
Answer: Xenolith (or Accidental inclusion)
Xenolith (from Greek *xenos* = foreign, *lithos* = stone) is a detached piece of wall or roof rock enclosed within an igneous body.
7. Why is magmatic stoping less effective in deep, ductile crustal environments?
Answer: Rocks at high temperature and confining pressure deform ductily rather than fracturing into brittle blocks.
In the lower crust, ductile flow promotes diapirism and ballooning rather than brittle thermal fracturing.
8. What is 'underhand stoping' in mining, and how does it relate to Daly's geological term?
Answer: Daly borrowed the term 'stoping' from mining underground excavations where miners break down rock overhead or underfoot.
Daly adopted 'stoping' as a metaphor for nature's overhead excavation of country rock by magma.

Lamprophyres: Minette Petrography, Mineralogy, and Dyke-Rock Systematics

Topic: Alkaline Dyke Rocks & Lamprophyres • Key Concept: Biotite-Orthoclase Calc-Alkaline Lamprophyre • Textbooks: N.M.S. Rock (1991, Lamprophyres); K.M. Bangar (p. 128); John D. Winter
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: The Lamprophyre Clan & Minette Systematics

Lamprophyres (from Greek lampros = bright/glistening, and phyro = mixed/porphyritic; von Gümbel, 1874) are a distinctive group of melanocratic, volatile-rich ($H_2O, CO_2, F$) hypabyssal dyke rocks characterized by panidiomorphic texture, in which euhedral phenocrysts of ferromagnesian minerals (biotite/phlogopite, amphibole, or pyroxene) are set in a fine-grained groundmass of feldspars ± feldspathoids. Critically, felsic minerals NEVER form phenocrysts in true lamprophyres.

Lamprophyre Group Dominant Mafic Phenocryst Dominant Groundmass Feldspar Lamprophyre Rock Name
Calc-Alkaline Lamprophyres (Shoshonitic) Biotite / Phlogopite Alkali Feldspar (Orthoclase / Sanidine) ★ MINETTE ★ (Option D)
Biotite / Phlogopite Plagioclase Feldspar (Oligoclase/Andesine) Kersantite
Amphibole / Pyroxene-Dominated Hornblende ± Diopside/Augite Alkali Feldspar (Orthoclase) Vogesite
Hornblende ± Diopside/Augite Plagioclase Feldspar Spessartite
Alkaline Lamprophyres Titanaugite, Kaersutite, Biotite Feldspathoids (Nepheline, Analcime) ± Plagioclase Camptonite, Monchiquite, Sannaite
"Minette is a variety of lamprophyre characterized by an abundance of glistening bronze-colored flakes of biotite (or phlogopite) set in a fine-grained groundmass consisting predominantly of orthoclase feldspar. First named from the Vosges Mountains in France, minette forms narrow dykes and sills associated with granitic plutons and continental rift zones."
— N.M.S. Rock, Lamprophyres (Blackie and Son, Glasgow, 1991)
$$\text{Calc-Alkaline Lamprophyre Diagnostic Rule:}$$ $$\mathbf{Minette} \equiv \text{Phenocrysts: } \mathbf{Biotite / Phlogopite} + \text{Groundmass: } \mathbf{Orthoclase\ (K\text{-}Feldspar)}$$ $$\text{Family Affiliation: } \mathbf{Lamprophyre\ (Option\ D)}$$
Figure 88: Standard 2x2 classification matrix of calc-alkaline lamprophyres, showing the exact position of Minette (Biotite + Orthoclase) alongside Kersantite, Vogesite, and Spessartite.

QUESTION 88
Minette is a type of :
A Diorite
B Tonalite
C Aplite
D Lamprophyre
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION D (Lamprophyre)
OPTION D • CORRECT
Lamprophyre

By international IUGS classification (Rock, 1991; Le Maitre, 2002; Bangar), minette is the classic type of calc-alkaline lamprophyre containing essential phenocrystic biotite/phlogopite and groundmass alkali feldspar (orthoclase).

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Diorite

Diorite is a coarse-grained plutonic intermediate rock composed of andesine plagioclase and hornblende. It lacks the distinctive porphyritic-panidiomorphic texture and alkali-rich lamprophyric chemistry of minette.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Tonalite

Tonalite is a quartz-rich, plagioclase-dominated plutonic rock ($Q > 20\%$, $P/(A+P) > 90\%$). Minette is a melanocratic dyke rock dominated by K-feldspar and mica, not a quartz-plagioclase pluton.

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
Aplite

Aplite is a leucocratic (light-colored), fine-grained, equigranular (saccharoidal) dyke rock dominated by quartz and feldspars ($M' < 5\%$). Minette is melanocratic ($M' > 35\text{--}50\%$), dark, and intensely porphyritic.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. What is the fundamental textural rule that distinguishes lamprophyres from all ordinary porphyries?
Answer: In lamprophyres, only mafic minerals form phenocrysts; felsic minerals (quartz and feldspar) are restricted to the groundmass.
In normal porphyries (like granite porphyry), feldspar or quartz form the phenocrysts, whereas lamprophyres exhibit strictly mafic phenocrysts.
2. Which lamprophyre has biotite phenocrysts with PLAGIOCLASE in the groundmass?
Answer: Kersantite
Kersantite is the plagioclase-bearing counterpart of orthoclase-bearing minette.
3. Which lamprophyre has HORNBLENDE phenocrysts with ORTHOCLASE in the groundmass?
Answer: Vogesite
Vogesite is characterized by amphibole/clinopyroxene phenocrysts and alkali feldspar groundmass.
4. What is panidiomorphic texture?
Answer: A texture in which almost all constituent mineral grains possess well-developed crystal faces (euhedral/idiomorphic).
Lamprophyres are renowned for panidiomorphic texture, especially prominently zoned euhedral phlogopite and hornblende.
5. What volatile components are unusually enriched in lamprophyre magmas?
Answer: $H_2O, CO_2, F, Cl, P_2O_5$, and $SO_3$
Abundant primary carbonates, apatite, and hydrous micas reflect deep mantle derivation with metasomatic volatile enrichment.
6. Which Indian coalfield is famous for lamprophyre (mica-peridotite) dykes that have heat-altered coal beds into 'jhama' (natural coke)?
Answer: The Jharia and Raniganj Coalfields (Damodar Valley Basin)
Cretaceous lamprophyre dykes intruded Permian Gondwana coal seams in Jharia, pyrolyzing valuable coal into natural coke (jhama).
7. What is an ocellus (plural: ocelli) in a lamprophyre?
Answer: A small, spherical or rounded leucocratic globule consisting of carbonates, quartz, or feldspar formed by liquid immiscibility or late-stage gas-bubble segregation.
Ocelli are classic diagnostic features of lamprophyric melts, representing separated silicate or carbonate liquid droplets.
8. What is a kimberlite or lamproite in relation to lamprophyres?
Answer: Kimberlites and lamproites are ultra-deep potassic/ultramafic mantle rocks closely related to the lamprophyre clan that host diamonds.
Lamproites and kimberlites share deep volatile-rich mantle genesis and phlogopite-rich mineralogy with lamprophyres.
Magma Generation & Petrogenesis / Question 089
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 89 • Igneous & Metamorphic Petrology

Palingenesis & Anatexis: Complete and Partial Melting of Pre-Existing Rocks

Topic: Magma Generation & Petrogenesis • Key Concept: Rebirth of Magma from Pre-Existing Crustal Rocks • Textbooks: J.J. Sederholm (1907); P.K. Mukherjee (p. 238); K.M. Bangar; Winter
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Origin & Meaning of Palingenesis

The term Palingenesis was coined in 1907 by the renowned Finnish petrologist Johannes Jakob Sederholm from the Greek roots palin (meaning 'again') and genesis (meaning 'birth' or 'creation')—literally translating to the 'rebirth of magma'. In petrology, it designates the geological process of the complete or partial melting (remelting) of pre-existing crustal rocks to generate new magmatic melts:

Magmatic Process Scientific Definition Physical Mechanism & P-T Conditions Resulting Rock / Product
PALINGENESIS (Option D) Complete or partial melting / regeneration of pre-existing rocks to yield new magma. Deep continental subduction, collisional thickening, or mantle plume underplating ($T > 650\text{--}850^\circ\text{C}$). Regenerated S-type granites, batholiths, and mobilised felsic magmas.
Anatexis The ultra-high temperature partial melting of metamorphic rocks in-situ. Water-saturated or dehydration melting of pelites/gneisses across the wet granite solidus. Migmatites (forming leucosome melt and refractory melanosome restite).
Migmatization The transformation of rocks into composite hybrid rocks containing metamorphic and igneous parts. Infiltration of granitic fluids or local in-situ anatectic segregation. Migmatites (banded gneisses with neosome and paleosome).
Assimilation The incorporation, reaction, and dissolution of foreign country rocks into a pre-existing magma. Thermal melting and chemical digestion of stoped xenoliths by hotter surrounding melt. Contaminated hybrid magmas (e.g., crustally contaminated basalts).
Juvenile Magmatism Magma derived directly from the Earth's primordial interior (mantle or core). Direct primary melting of pristine, uncontaminated peridotitic mantle. Mid-Ocean Ridge Basalts (MORB), primary picrites.
"The process of complete or partial melting of pre-existing rocks to form new magma is called palingenesis (literally, magma rebirth). Introduced by Sederholm, it describes the recycling of continental crustal sediments and metamorphic rocks into granitic batholiths during intense orogenic cycles."
— P.K. Mukherjee, A Textbook of Geology (Petrogenesis Section, p. 238)
$$\text{Palingenesis: Pre-existing Crustal Rock } \xrightarrow[\text{Collisional Orogeny}]{T \ge 700^\circ\text{C},\ P \ge 5\text{ kbar}} \text{Partial / Complete Melt} \rightarrow \mathbf{New\ Magma\ (S\text{-}type\ Granite)}$$ $$\text{Etymology: Greek } \pi\acute{\alpha}\lambda\iota\nu\ (\text{again}) + \gamma\acute{\epsilon}\nu\epsilon\sigma\iota\varsigma\ (\text{birth}) \equiv \mathbf{'Rebirth\ of\ Magma' \equiv Palingenesis\ (Option\ D)}$$
Figure 89: The crustal palingenesis cycle: burial of sediment $\rightarrow$ prograde metamorphism $\rightarrow$ anatexis (partial melting) $\rightarrow$ palingenetic magma coalescence and plutonic intrusion.

2. Official Examination Question & Forensic Option Analysis
QUESTION 89
The process of complete or partial melting of a rock is known as :
A Migmatization
B Assimilation
C Juvenile magmatism
D Palingenesis
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION D (Palingenesis)
OPTION D • CORRECT
Palingenesis

By standard petrological definitions (J.J. Sederholm, 1907; P.K. Mukherjee, p. 238; Bangar), palingenesis is the specific geological term for the complete or partial melting of pre-existing continental crustal rocks to generate new magma.

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Migmatization

Migmatization is the process of generating a migmatite—a composite rock retaining both unmelted metamorphic paleosome and newly melted or injected granitic neosome. It does not mean the wholesale or partial melting process that produces mobile magma.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Assimilation

Assimilation is the chemical dissolution and digestion of foreign country rock into an already existing, pre-formed magma. It requires a pre-existing magma host, rather than generating a brand new magma from solid rock.

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
Juvenile magmatism

Juvenile magmatism refers to virgin magma derived directly from the Earth's deep pristine mantle that has never previously been part of the crustal rock cycle. Palingenesis is recycled crustal melting.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. Who introduced the term 'palingenesis' to geology?
Answer: Johannes Jakob Sederholm (1907)
Sederholm coined both 'migmatite' and 'palingenesis' during his pioneering studies of the Precambrian Fennoscandian Shield of Finland.
2. What granite classification corresponds directly to magmas derived by the palingenesis of sedimentary source rocks?
Answer: S-type Granites (Chappell & White, 1974)
S-type (sedimentary source) granites are peraluminous, contain cordierite/garnet/muscovite, and have high initial $^{87}Sr/^{86}Sr$ ratios ($> 0.708$).
3. What is the difference between anatexis and palingenesis?
Answer: Anatexis is the initial physical process of partial melting in-situ; palingenesis is the complete or partial melting viewed as the rebirth of a mobile magma body.
Anatexis describes the melting mechanism; palingenesis emphasizes the regeneration and creation of a new magma from old rock.
4. What is the unmelted, refractory residue remaining after anatectic melting of a crustal rock called?
Answer: Restite (or Melanosome)
The low-melting quartzofeldspathic fraction forms the leucosome (melt), leaving the dark, refractory ferromagnesian residue as restite.
5. At what approximate temperature does water-saturated melting of granitic crust begin?
Answer: Around $650^\circ\text{C}$ to $680^\circ\text{C}$ at crustal pressures ($P \approx 5\text{ kbar}$).
The 'wet granite solidus' marks the minimum temperature required for crustal anatexis in the presence of free $H_2O$.
6. What is dehydration melting in metamorphic rocks?
Answer: Melting triggered by the breakdown of hydrous minerals (muscovite, biotite) without requiring an external water fluid.
Reactions like $Muscovite + Quartz \rightarrow K-feldspar + Sillimanite + Liquid$ release water directly into the melt phase.
7. What is juvenile water vs. palingenetic (resurgent) water?
Answer: Juvenile water is virgin water from the deep mantle; palingenetic water is recycled water released from melted crustal rocks.
Juvenile volatiles originate from Earth's deep interior, while palingenetic volatiles were previously locked in sedimentary or hydrous crustal minerals.
8. What is the Critical Melt Fraction (CMF) or Rheological Transition Threshold in migmatites?
Answer: Around 25% to 40% melt fraction.
When melt exceeds ~30%, the solid crystal framework breaks down and the migmatite behaves as a fluid suspension capable of ascending as a magmatic diapir.

Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 90 • Igneous Petrology

Liquid Immiscibility: Solvus Physics, Liquid-Liquid Unmixing, and Ore Petrogenesis

Topic: Magmatic Differentiation Mechanisms • Key Concept: Two-Liquid Solvus & Unmixing of Melts • Textbooks: John D. Winter (Principles of Igneous Petrology); K.M. Bangar (p. 116); Roedder (1979)
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Physicochemical Basis of Liquid Immiscibility

In chemical thermodynamics and igneous petrology, liquid immiscibility refers to the thermodynamic phenomenon where a single, homogeneous silicate melt cools until it encounters a two-phase liquid boundary (the solvus), causing it to split or unmix into two coexisting, distinct liquids of different composition that cannot dissolve in one another:

Magmatic System Parent Homogeneous Melt Separated Immiscible Liquid 1 Separated Immiscible Liquid 2 Geological / Ore Deposit Consequence
Silicate-Sulfide System Sulfur-saturated basic magma Silicate Melt ($SiO_2$-rich, Fe-poor) Dense Sulfide Melt ($Fe\text{-}Ni\text{-}Cu\text{-}PGE$ liquid) World-class magmatic sulfide deposits (Sudbury, Canada; Norilsk, Russia; Kambalda).
Silicate-Carbonate System $CO_2$-rich alkaline silicate melt Alkaline Silicate Melt (Nephelinite / Ijolite) Carbonate Melt ($Ca\text{-}Mg\text{-}Na$ rich, $SiO_2$-poor) Origin of Carbonatites and associated alkaline ring complexes (Oldoinyo Lengai, Amba Dongar).
Silicate-Iron Oxide System Extreme Fe-rich tholeiitic differentiate Silica-rich Felsic Melt (Granitic / Rhyolitic) Iron-rich Mafic Melt (Magnetite-Apatite liquid) Kiruna-type magnetite-apatite deposits; Skaergaard intrusion late-stage splits.
"Liquid immiscibility is the process by which a single homogeneous liquid phase splits upon cooling into two distinct liquid phases of different compositions that are mutually insoluble, just like oil and water. In silicate systems, this solvus unmixing produces conjugate liquids such as an iron-rich basic melt and a silica-rich felsic melt, or a silicate melt and a sulfide ore melt."
— Edwin Roedder, Silicate Liquid Immiscibility in Magmas (Evolution of the Igneous Rocks, 1979)
$$\text{Thermodynamic Solvus Condition: } \Delta G_{\text{mixing}} = \Delta H_{\text{mixing}} - T \Delta S_{\text{mixing}} > 0 \quad (\text{at } T < T_{\text{solvus}})$$ $$\mathbf{Homogeneous\ Single\ Melt\ (L_0)} \xrightarrow{T \le T_{\text{solvus}}} \mathbf{Liquid\ 1\ (L_1)} + \mathbf{Liquid\ 2\ (L_2)} \quad (\text{Distinct Compositions})$$ $$\therefore \text{Liquid immiscibility results from: } \mathbf{Unmixing\ of\ two\ liquids\ of\ different\ composition\ (Option\ C)}$$
Figure 90: Binary phase diagram illustrating the liquid immiscibility dome (solvus), showing a homogeneous single melt separating into two coexisting immiscible liquids of different composition upon cooling.

Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
2. Official Examination Question & Forensic Option Analysis
QUESTION 90
Liquid imissibility generally results from :
A Mixing of two liquids of two different composition
B Mixing of two liquids of same composition
C Unmixing of two liquids of different composition
D Unmixing of two liquids of same composition
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION C (Unmixing of two liquids of different composition)
OPTION C • CORRECT
Unmixing of two liquids of different composition

By definition in physical chemistry and petrology, liquid immiscibility is the unmixing (separation or exsolution) of a parent homogeneous liquid into two coexisting liquids having different chemical compositions (e.g., a sulfide liquid vs. a silicate liquid, or a carbonate liquid vs. a silicate liquid) because they are mutually insoluble below their solvus temperature.

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Mixing of two liquids of two different composition

This defines magma mixing or hybridization, which is the exact opposite of immiscibility. Mixing combines two melts into one; immiscibility unmixes one melt into two.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Mixing of two liquids of same composition

Mixing identical liquids produces the same liquid without any change, neither creating immiscibility nor generating differentiated phases.

OPTION D • DISTRACTOR
Unmixing of two liquids of same composition

Physically impossible. A liquid cannot 'unmix' into two phases of identical composition; if the compositions were identical, there would be no chemical boundary or interface between them.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. What economic ore deposits owe their origin fundamentally to sulfide liquid immiscibility?
Answer: Magmatic Nickel-Copper-PGE Sulfide Deposits (e.g., Sudbury, Norilsk-Talnakh, Bushveld, Kambalda)
When mafic magma becomes sulfur-saturated, an immiscible sulfide liquid droplets exsolve, scavenge chalcophile metals (Ni, Cu, Pt, Pd), and sink to form massive basal ore pools.
2. What phase boundary in a temperature-composition phase diagram bounds the region of two immiscible liquids?
Answer: The Solvus (Two-Liquid Dome)
Above the solvus, the liquid is completely miscible and homogeneous; below the solvus, it unmixes into conjugate liquids.
3. What petrographic evidence was found in Apollo lunar basalts proving silicate liquid immiscibility?
Answer: High-silica (potassic granite) and high-iron (pyroxferroite) glassy globules in late-stage mesostasis.
Edwin Roedder and Paul Weiblen (1970) proved immiscibility in lunar samples where residual melt split into immiscible felsic and mafic glasses.
4. How does sulfur saturation occur in a basic magma leading to sulfide liquid unmixing?
Answer: By crustal sulfur assimilation, cooling, silica contamination, or fractional crystallization.
Adding crustal sulfur or adding silica drastically lowers sulfide solubility, triggering immediate immiscible sulfide droplet exsolution.
5. What is the Partition Coefficient ($D$) of Platinum Group Elements (PGEs) between immiscible sulfide melt and silicate melt?
Answer: Extremely high ($D_{PGE} \approx 10^3\text{ to } 10^5$)
PGEs strongly partition into the sulfide melt phase, concentrating platinum and palladium by thousands of times relative to silicate magma.
6. What famous layered mafic intrusion in Greenland exhibits late-stage Fe-rich vs. Si-rich liquid immiscibility?
Answer: The Skaergaard Intrusion
Extreme fractional crystallization in the Skaergaard closed magma chamber drove the final melt into the two-liquid immiscibility field.
7. What is the difference between solid solution exsolution and liquid immiscibility?
Answer: Exsolution occurs in the solid state below the solidus; liquid immiscibility occurs entirely within the liquid melt state above the solidus.
Perthite forms by solid-state exsolution; sulfide dropplets and carbonatite melts unmix as distinct liquids above the solidus.
8. What texture is formed when immiscible droplets of sulfide or carbonate are trapped in rapidly solidified volcanic rocks?
Answer: Variolitic, globular, or ocellar texture
Immiscible liquid droplets form spherical globules (ocelli or varioles) preserving the liquid-liquid emulsion texture.
Sedimentary Petrology & Sandstone Petrography / Question 091
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 91 • Sedimentary Petrology

Arkose Sandstone Petrography: The 25% Feldspar Criterion and Provenance

Topic: Sandstone Classification & Petrography • Key Concept: Feldspar-Rich Arenites & Tectonic Provenance • Textbooks: F.J. Pettijohn (1975); R.L. Folk (1968); K.M. Bangar (p. 136)
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Sandstone Classification & Arkose Systematics

In sedimentary petrology, terrigenous clastic sandstones are classified on the ternary QFL Diagram (Quartz – Feldspar – Lithic rock fragments) pioneered by R.L. Folk (1968) and F.J. Pettijohn (1975). A sandstone is formally designated as an Arkose (or arkosic arenite) when its detrital framework contains more than 25% feldspar:

Sandstone Class Quartz Content ($Q\%$) Feldspar Content ($F\%$) Lithic Fragments ($L\%$) Tectonic Provenance & Climatic Significance
ARKOSE (Option C) < 75% > 25% Feldspar ($F / L > 3:1$) < 25% Lithics Rapid erosion of granitic/gneissic basements in fault-bounded rift basins (graben); arid or cold climate.
Subarkose 75% – 95% 5% – 25% Feldspar < 25% Lithics Moderately mature sands; slight chemical weathering or mixed quartzose provenance.
Quartzarenite > 95% < 5% < 5% Ultra-mature stable cratonic platforms; multiple cycles of reworking and chemical leaching.
Lithic Arenite < 75% < 25% > 25% Lithics ($L / F > 3:1$) Active orogenic belts, island arcs, and collision suture zones (recycled orogen provenance).
"An arkose is a sandstone composed of quartz and more than 25 percent feldspar (chiefly orthoclase, microcline, or sodic plagioclase). The grains are generally poorly sorted, angular to sub-angular, and cemented by calcite, iron oxides, or silica. The presence of abundant fresh feldspar indicates that the source rocks (granites or gneisses) underwent rapid mechanical disintegration under arid, semi-arid, or high-relief tectonic conditions before chemical decomposition could destroy the feldspars."
— F.J. Pettijohn, Sedimentary Rocks (3rd Ed., Harper & Row, p. 214)
$$\text{Folk (1968) Arkose Definition: Framework Grains } (Q + F + L = 100\%)$$ $$\mathbf{Feldspar\ (F) > 25\%} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\text{Feldspar}}{\text{Lithics}} > 3 \implies \mathbf{Arkose\ (Option\ C)}$$
Figure 91: Folk (1968) QFL ternary classification of sandstones highlighting the Arkose field defined by > 25% feldspar and F/L > 3:1.

2. Official Examination Question & Forensic Option Analysis
QUESTION 91
Arkose contain more than 25% of :
A Micas
B Amphiboles
C Feldspars
D Chlorite
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION C (Feldspars)
OPTION C • CORRECT
Feldspars

By international consensus across all modern sandstone classifications (Folk, 1968; Pettijohn, 1975; Dickinson, 1985; Bangar, p. 136), an arkose is strictly defined as a sandstone containing more than 25% feldspar (mostly pink potash feldspars such as microcline and orthoclase). This gives arkose its typical pink, red, or salmon-colored appearance.

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Micas

Micas (biotite and muscovite) may occur as subordinate accessories (typically 1% to 5%) in arkosic sandstones, but never exceed 25%. A sandstone rich in micas is termed a micaceous sandstone or flagstone.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Amphiboles

Amphiboles are unstable ferromagnesian minerals that weather rapidly during surface transport. They occur only in trace quantities as heavy mineral accessories, never exceeding 25% in sandstones.

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
Chlorite

Chlorite is a common green sheet-silicate mineral found in the matrix of greywackes and low-grade metamorphic rocks. It does not constitute the framework grain defining an arkose.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. What two climatic/tectonic factors preserve high percentages of feldspar in arkose against chemical weathering?
Answer: Arid / frigid cold climate and high topographic relief with rapid tectonic uplift and burial.
Chemical weathering hydrolyzes feldspars to clay; an arid or freezing climate, combined with rapid erosion and burial, halts hydrolysis.
2. Which potash feldspar is recognized by its distinctive 'tartan' or 'cross-hatched' twinning in arkose thin sections?
Answer: Microcline
Microcline exhibits prominent gridiron (albite + pericline) cross-hatched twinning under crossed nicols, diagnostic of granitic basement provenance.
3. What prominent Indian sedimentary formation contains basal arkosic sandstones overlying Archaean granitic basements?
Answer: The Talchir Formation (basal Gondwana Supergroup) and Cuddapah Basin basal Gulcheru quartzites/arkoses.
Glacial and periglacial erosion of granites during early Gondwana times formed boulder beds and feldspathic arkoses.
4. What is the difference between an arkosic arenite and an arkosic wacke?
Answer: Arkosic arenite has <15% fine matrix; arkosic wacke has 15% to 50% fine matrix.
Gilbert (1954) and Dott (1964) divide all sandstones at the 15% matrix boundary into arenites and wackes.
5. What is 'grus' in weathering petrology?
Answer: Coarse, angular granitic sand produced by in-situ granular disintegration of granite, forming the direct precursor to arkose.
Mechanical spalling of quartz and feldspar crystals in desert granites generates grus, which upon transport lithifies into arkose.
6. What provenance field on the Dickinson (1985) QFL diagram plots typical arkoses?
Answer: Continental Block Provenance (specifically Basement Uplift)
Dickinson's triangular provenance model links arkoses directly to fault-bounded continental basement uplifts exposing granitic plutons.
7. What cement commonly binds arkose grains giving it a red or brownish color?
Answer: Hematite (iron oxide) and Calcite
Oxidizing continental groundwater precipitates iron oxide coatings (hematite) around feldspar grains, producing red-bed arkoses.
8. What is the feldspar threshold for classifying a sandstone as a 'subarkose'?
Answer: 5% to 25% feldspar
Subarkose occupies the transitional field between quartzarenite (<5% feldspar) and true arkose (>25% feldspar).
Clastic Granulometry & Grain Size Scales / Question 092
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 92 • Sedimentary Petrology

The Udden-Wentworth Grain-Size Scale: Silt Grade Detrital Sediments (1/16 to 1/256 mm)

Topic: Clastic Sediment Granulometry • Key Concept: Udden-Wentworth Logarithmic Scale & Phi Units • Textbooks: C.K. Wentworth (1922); W.C. Krumbein (1934); K.M. Bangar (p. 131)
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: The Udden-Wentworth Scale & Silt Fraction

The quantitative classification of detrital (clastic) sediments is based on the geometric particle-size scale formulated by J.A. Udden (1898) and modified by Chester K. Wentworth (1922). In 1934, W.C. Krumbein introduced the logarithmic transformation phi ($\phi$) scale ($\phi = -\log_2 d_{\text{mm}}$) to enable rigorous statistical analysis:

Grain Size Grade Millimeter Range ($d_{\text{mm}}$) Micrometer Range ($\mu\text{m}$) Krumbein Phi Range ($\phi$) Indurated Sedimentary Rock
Gravel / Pebble > 2 mm > 2000 $\mu\text{m}$ $< -1.0\ \phi$ Conglomerate / Breccia
Sand (Very Coarse to Very Fine) 2 mm – 1/16 mm 2000 – 62.5 $\mu\text{m}$ $-1.0\ \phi$ to $+4.0\ \phi$ Sandstone (Arenite / Wacke)
SILT GRADE (Option A) 1/16 mm to 1/256 mm 62.5 to 3.9 $\mu\text{m}$ $+4.0\ \phi$ to $+8.0\ \phi$ Siltstone
• Coarse Silt 1/16 – 1/32 mm 62.5 – 31.2 $\mu\text{m}$ $+4.0\ \phi$ to $+5.0\ \phi$ Coarse Siltstone
• Medium Silt 1/32 – 1/64 mm 31.2 – 15.6 $\mu\text{m}$ $+5.0\ \phi$ to $+6.0\ \phi$ Medium Siltstone
• Fine Silt 1/64 – 1/128 mm 15.6 – 7.8 $\mu\text{m}$ $+6.0\ \phi$ to $+7.0\ \phi$ Fine Siltstone
• Very Fine Silt 1/128 – 1/256 mm 7.8 – 3.9 $\mu\text{m}$ $+7.0\ \phi$ to $+8.0\ \phi$ Very Fine Siltstone
Clay Grade < 1/256 mm < 3.9 $\mu\text{m}$ $> +8.0\ \phi$ Claystone / Shale / Mudstone
"According to the Wentworth grade scale, silt comprises all mineral fragments with diameters between 1/16 mm and 1/256 mm (or 0.0625 mm to 0.0039 mm). Particles larger than 1/16 mm are sand, while particles finer than 1/256 mm are classified as clay. Silt-grade grains are barely visible under a hand lens but feel gritty between the fingers or teeth, distinguishing them from smooth, plastic clays."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Sedimentary Rocks, pp. 130–132)
$$\text{Krumbein Phi Transformation: } \phi = -\log_2 (d_{\text{mm}})$$ $$\text{Upper Limit of Silt: } d = \frac{1}{16}\text{ mm} = 0.0625\text{ mm} \implies \phi = -\log_2(2^{-4}) = \mathbf{+4.0\ \phi}$$ $$\text{Lower Limit of Silt: } d = \frac{1}{256}\text{ mm} = 0.0039\text{ mm} \implies \phi = -\log_2(2^{-8}) = \mathbf{+8.0\ \phi}$$
Figure 92: The Udden-Wentworth grain size scale highlighting the exact Silt Grade range (1/16 mm to 1/256 mm / +4 phi to +8 phi) bounded by Sand and Clay.

QUESTION 92
The silt grade detrital sediments would have a size range of :
A 1/16 mm to 1/256 mm
B Less than 1/256 mm
C 1/16 mm to 2 mm
D 2 mm to 1 mm
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION A (1/16 mm to 1/256 mm)
OPTION A • CORRECT
1/16 mm to 1/256 mm

By international geological standards (Wentworth, 1922; Krumbein, 1934; Pettijohn; Bangar), the silt grade detrital sediment is defined as particles ranging in diameter from 1/16 mm to 1/256 mm (0.0625 mm to 0.0039 mm, or $+4\phi$ to $+8\phi$).

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Less than 1/256 mm

Particles having a diameter less than 1/256 mm ($< 0.0039\text{ mm}$, or $> +8\phi$) belong to the clay grade, which consists of colloidal phyllosilicates and mud.

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
1/16 mm to 2 mm

The size range from 1/16 mm to 2 mm defines the sand grade (from very fine sand at 0.0625 mm up to very coarse sand at 2 mm), not silt.

OPTION D • DISTRACTOR
2 mm to 1 mm

This range corresponds exclusively to very coarse sand (1 mm to 2 mm), which lies near the gravel boundary.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. What is the phi value ($\phi$) of a grain having a diameter of exactly 0.0625 mm (1/16 mm)?
Answer: $+4.0\ \phi$
$\phi = -\log_2(0.0625) = -\log_2(2^{-4}) = -(-4) = +4.0\ \phi$. This marks the exact sand-silt boundary.
2. What aeolian wind-blown deposit consists almost entirely of well-sorted quartz silt?
Answer: Loess
Loess is an unstratified, buff-colored, calcareous deposit of wind-blown glacial or peridesert quartz silt (20 to 50 $\mu\text{m}$).
3. What is the primary mineral constituent of detrital silt?
Answer: Quartz ($SiO_2$)
Quartz is chemically inert and mechanically durable; physical abrasion crushes quartz grains down to a natural cleavage limit of ~20 to 4 $\mu\text{m}$ (silt size).
4. How can a field geologist immediately distinguish siltstone from claystone without a microscope?
Answer: The 'bite test' (chewing a tiny speck): siltstone feels distinctly gritty between the teeth, whereas claystone feels buttery smooth.
Human teeth are exceptionally sensitive tactile sensors capable of detecting particles down to ~10 $\mu\text{m}$ (silt), whereas clay (<4 $\mu\text{m}$) cannot be felt.
5. What physical law governs the settling velocity of silt particles in calm water?
Answer: Stokes' Law ($v = \frac{2}{9}\frac{(\rho_s - \rho_f) g r^2}{\eta}$)
Particles smaller than 0.1 mm (including all silt and clay) settle via laminar viscous drag described by Stokes' Law.
6. What is the millimeter size equivalent of $-1\ \phi$?
Answer: 2.0 mm (the gravel-sand boundary)
$d = 2^{-\phi} = 2^{-(-1)} = 2^1 = 2.0\text{ mm}$.
7. What is mud in sedimentary terminology?
Answer: A mixture of silt and clay grade particles (all detritus finer than 1/16 mm).
Mudrock / mudstone is the collective term for fine-grained clastic rocks containing both silt (1/16-1/256 mm) and clay (<1/256 mm).
8. What is the millimeter diameter of the boundary separating granules from pebbles in Wentworth's scale?
Answer: 4.0 mm
Granules range from 2 mm to 4 mm; pebbles range from 4 mm to 64 mm.
Sedimentary Structures & Intraformational Clasts / Question 093
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 93 • Sedimentary Petrology

Clay Galls (Mud Rip-Up Clasts): Genesis, Morphology, and Sedimentary Significance

Topic: Intraformational Structures • Key Concept: Desiccation, Mud-Flake Ripping & Lenticular Redeposition • Textbooks: F.J. Pettijohn (1975); K.M. Bangar (p. 134); G.B. Mahapatra
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Genesis & Morphology of Clay Galls

In clastic sedimentology, clay galls (also termed mud galls, mud rip-up clasts, or intraformational mud chips) are flat, lenticular, or leaf-like structures of hardened, desiccated clay embedded within beds of sandstone or siltstone. They represent intraformational clasts produced through a distinctive cyclical sedimentary process:

Genesis Stage Physical / Environmental Action Sedimentary Feature Formed
1. Low-Water Deposition Quiescent settling in temporary pools, floodplains, lagoons, or tidal mudflats during low-water stage. Thin lamina of coherent, fine-grained plastic mud/clay.
2. Subaerial Desiccation Subaerial exposure to sun and atmospheric drying; clay contracts, forming polygonal mudcracks. Hardened, curled-up thin flakes resembling dried leaves (leaves of clay).
3. Turbulent Inundation Sudden high-energy flood surge (crevasse splay, storm wave, or flash flood) carrying abrasive sand. Rips up the dried clay flakes, rolls and rounds them slightly, and deposits them in sand.
4. Compaction & Lithification Overburden pressure flattens the soft mud clasts into disc-like or lenticular shapes within the sandstone matrix. ★ CLAY GALLS (Option D) ★ (often weathering out into hollow cavities on exposed rock faces).
"Leaves of hardened clay deposited in a sand or similar sediment as flat or lens-shaped structures are called clay galls (or mud galls). They are formed when mud layers dry out under the sun, crack into curled flakes, and are subsequently torn up and swept away by sudden torrents of sand-laden water. In weathered sandstone outcrops, clay galls easily wash out, leaving characteristic pitted or hollow depressions."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Sedimentary Structures, p. 134)
$$\text{Cycle of Clay Gall Formation: Mud Layer } \xrightarrow{\text{Sun Desiccation}} \text{Curled Clay Leaves} \xrightarrow{\text{Flood Surge}} \mathbf{Clay\ Galls\ (Lenticular\ Clasts\ in\ Sand)}$$ $$\text{Sedimentary Classification: } \mathbf{Intraformational\ Rip\text{-}Up\ Clasts \equiv Clay\ Galls\ (Option\ D)}$$
Figure 93: Schematic cross-section of sandstone containing flat, lens-shaped clay galls (mud rip-up clasts) formed by desiccation, erosion, and rapid redeposition.

QUESTION 93
The leaves of hardened clay deposited in a sand or similar sediment as flat or lense shaped structure are called :
A Clay flakes
B Clay balls
C Clay stones
D Clay galls
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION D (Clay galls)
OPTION D • CORRECT
Clay galls

By standard textbook definition (Pettijohn, 1975; Bangar, p. 134; G.B. Mahapatra), the flat or lens-shaped fragments of hardened, desiccated clay leaves enclosed within a sandstone matrix are formally known as clay galls (or mud galls). They are classic indicators of shallow-water, ephemeral, or subaerially exposed environments.

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Clay flakes

'Clay flakes' refers to the uncompacted, loose microscopic phyllosilicate platelets or desiccated surface crust fragments before being transported and incorporated into an indurated sandstone as galls.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Clay balls

Clay balls (specifically armored mud balls) are spherical or subspherical balls of sticky mud rolled along a streambed that pick up an outer armour of pebbles and sand grains. They are spherical, not flat or lens-shaped.

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
Clay stones

Claystone is an indurated, massive, non-fissile sedimentary rock composed entirely of clay-sized particles, not a discrete lenticular inclusion within sandstone.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. What type of conglomerate is formed when a current tears up semi-consolidated clay galls from its own bed and redeposits them locally?
Answer: Intraformational Conglomerate (or Intraformational Mud-Pebble Conglomerate)
Intraformational conglomerates consist of clasts derived from within the same depositional basin, virtually contemporaneous with the host sediment.
2. What happens to clay galls on exposed weathered sandstone cliffs?
Answer: They weather and wash out rapidly, leaving hollow depressions (pitted sandstone or 'tafoni-like' cavities).
Clay is much softer and more easily eroded by rainwater than the surrounding quartz sandstone, creating a pitted outcrop surface.
3. What environmental condition is conclusively demonstrated by the presence of clay galls in a fluvial sandstone?
Answer: Episodic drying (subaerial exposure) followed by high-energy turbulent flooding.
Clay galls require subaerial desiccation to harden the mud flakes so they do not immediately disaggregate into suspension when flooded.
4. What is an armored mud ball?
Answer: A chunk of sticky clay rolled along a torrential streambed that becomes coated with pebbles, gravel, and coarse sand.
Armored mud balls form in flash floods and mountain streams where cohesive mud rolls across pebble-covered bars.
5. Why do clay galls orient themselves parallel to the bedding planes?
Answer: Hydrodynamic settling and post-depositional lithostatic compaction flatten them horizontally along bedding.
Flat disc-shaped clasts settle with their maximum projection area parallel to flow and are further flattened during burial compaction.
6. What is the difference between an intraformational and an extraformational clast?
Answer: Intraformational clasts originate from within the depositional basin; extraformational clasts are eroded from outside source rocks.
Clay galls are intraformational; granitic or quartzite pebbles transported from mountains are extraformational.
7. What is another common sedimentological term for clay galls in turbidites?
Answer: Rip-up clasts (or shale rip-ups)
High-velocity turbidity currents erode the underlying muddy sea floor, incorporating shale rip-up clasts into the basal $T_a$ division.
8. Which Gondwana formation in India frequently displays clay galls in cross-bedded river sandstones?
Answer: The Barakar Formation (Damodar and Mahanadi Valley basins)
Braided channel Barakar sandstones commonly carry intraformational shale clasts and clay galls derived from cannibalized overbank muds.
Coarse Clastic Granulometry & Conglomerates / Question 094

OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 94 • Sedimentary Petrology

Coarse Clast Granulometry: Classification of Cobbles (64 mm to 256 mm)

Topic: Conglomerate & Gravel Granulometry • Key Concept: Udden-Wentworth Size Limits (Cobble vs Pebble vs Boulder) • Textbooks: C.K. Wentworth (1922); F.J. Pettijohn; K.M. Bangar (p. 131)
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Coarse Clastic Granulometry

In the Udden-Wentworth classification of coarse detrital sediments (Wentworth, 1922), rudaceous (gravel-grade) clasts ($> 2\text{ mm}$) are precisely categorized based on intermediate diameter measurements. A rounded to sub-rounded clast with a diameter between 64 mm and 256 mm is designated as a Cobble:

Clast Grade Millimeter Diameter Range Inches Range (Approx.) Krumbein Phi Range ($\phi$) Lithified Rock Equivalent (Rounded Clasts)
Boulder > 256 mm > 10.1 inches $< -8.0\ \phi$ Boulder Conglomerate
COBBLE (Option C) 64 mm to 256 mm 2.5 to 10.1 inches $-6.0\ \phi$ to $-8.0\ \phi$ Cobble Conglomerate
Pebble 4 mm to 64 mm 0.16 to 2.5 inches $-2.0\ \phi$ to $-6.0\ \phi$ Pebble Conglomerate
• Coarse Pebble 16 mm to 64 mm 0.63 to 2.5 inches $-4.0\ \phi$ to $-6.0\ \phi$ Coarse Pebble Conglomerate
• Fine Pebble 4 mm to 16 mm 0.16 to 0.63 inches $-2.0\ \phi$ to $-4.0\ \phi$ Fine Pebble Conglomerate
Granule 2 mm to 4 mm 0.08 to 0.16 inches $-1.0\ \phi$ to $-2.0\ \phi$ Granule Conglomerate / Grit
"In petrology, coarse detrital fragments are classified by size. A boulder has a diameter greater than 256 mm. A cobble has a diameter ranging from 64 mm to 256 mm (roughly grapefruit to human-head size). A pebble ranges from 4 mm to 64 mm, and a granule from 2 mm to 4 mm. A sedimentary rock formed of consolidated, rounded cobbles is a cobble conglomerate."
— F.J. Pettijohn, Sedimentary Rocks (Gravels and Conglomerates, p. 153)
$$\text{Udden-Wentworth Size Rule: } \mathbf{64\text{ mm} \le \text{Diameter} < 256\text{ mm}} \implies \mathbf{COBBLE\ (Option\ C)}$$ $$\phi = -\log_2(64) = -6\ \phi \quad \text{to} \quad \phi = -\log_2(256) = -8\ \phi$$
Figure 94: Clast size scale comparing Boulder (>256 mm), Cobble (64 to 256 mm), Pebble (4 to 64 mm), and Granule (2 to 4 mm).

QUESTION 94
Rounded to sub-rounded clast with a diameter between 64 and 256 mm is generally known as :
A Gravel
B Pebble
C Cobble
D Boulder
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION C (Cobble)
OPTION C • CORRECT
Cobble

By Wentworth's (1922) authoritative sedimentological scale, clasts having a diameter between 64 mm and 256 mm are uniquely designated as cobbles. Rounded clasts in this size range form cobble conglomerates, typical of high-energy braided rivers and storm-tossed beaches.

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Gravel

'Gravel' is an overarching collective term encompassing all unconsolidated detrital clasts larger than 2 mm in diameter (including granules, pebbles, cobbles, and boulders), not the specific 64–256 mm size class.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Pebble

A pebble is strictly defined as a clast having a diameter between 4 mm and 64 mm. Clasts larger than 64 mm are cobbles.

OPTION D • DISTRACTOR
Boulder

A boulder is defined as a clast with a diameter greater than 256 mm ($> 10.1\text{ inches}$).

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. What is the fundamental difference between a conglomerate and a sedimentary breccia?
Answer: A conglomerate is composed of rounded to sub-rounded clasts; a breccia is composed of sharp, angular clasts.
Rounding reflects prolonged fluvial or beach transport; angularity indicates minimal transport (talus scree, faulting).
2. What hydrodynamic transport regime is required to transport 64 to 256 mm cobbles?
Answer: High-energy upper flow regime (torrential flash floods, steep mountain streams, or severe marine storm breakers).
Hjulström's diagram demonstrates that entraining and rolling cobbles requires bottom current velocities exceeding 2 to 4 m/s.
3. What is an oligomictic conglomerate vs. a polymictic conglomerate?
Answer: Oligomictic contains clasts of a single rock type (e.g., pure vein quartz); polymictic contains diverse clasts (granite, basalt, quartzite).
Oligomictic conglomerates reflect intense chemical weathering destroying unstable clasts; polymictic reflects rapid mechanical erosion.
4. What is the term for a conglomerate where clasts touch each other, with sand/mud filling the interstices?
Answer: Clast-supported (or Orthoconglomerate)
When clasts float in a muddy matrix without touching, it is matrix-supported (paraconglomerate or diamictite).
5. What is imbrication in cobble gravels?
Answer: The preferred shingle-like overlapping alignment of flat cobbles dipping gently upstream against the current.
Imbrication provides a definitive palaeocurrent vector: the long $a-b$ planes dip upstream into the paleoflow.
6. What is the phi ($\phi$) value corresponding to the 64 mm cobble-pebble boundary?
Answer: $-6.0\ \phi$
$\phi = -\log_2(64) = -\log_2(2^6) = -6.0\ \phi$.
7. What famous Siwalik group member in the Himalayan foothills consists of massive boulder and cobble conglomerates?
Answer: The Upper Siwalik Boulder Conglomerate Formation (Pleistocene)
The Upper Siwalik Boulder Conglomerate represents syn-orogenic alluvial fans shed off the rising Greater and Lesser Himalayas.
8. What is Zingg's clast shape classification based on?
Answer: Ratios of the three orthogonal axes: $a$ (long), $b$ (intermediate), and $c$ (short).
Zingg (1935) categorized cobbles into Equant (spherical), Oblate (discoid), Prolate (rod-shaped), and Triaxial (bladed).
Primary Sedimentary Structures & Cross-Stratification / Question 095
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 95 • Sedimentary Petrology

Cross-Stratification: Architecture, Mechanics, and Significance of Current Beds

Topic: Primary Sedimentary Structures • Key Concept: Inclined Foreset Lamination & Palaeocurrent Direction • Textbooks: F.J. Pettijohn (1975); K.M. Bangar (p. 132); Sam Boggs Jr. (2014)
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Mechanics of Current Bedding (Cross-Stratification)

Current bedding (also known as cross-bedding, cross-stratification, or false bedding) is one of the most fundamental primary depositional structures in sedimentary geology. It is defined as a series of inclined internal laminations (foresets) deposited at an angle to the main horizontal or master bedding planes, produced by the migration of ripples, sand waves, or dunes under moving water or wind currents:

Structural Element Morphology & Geometric Attitude Hydrodynamic Mechanism Geological / Geopetal Significance
Topset Beds Gently dipping or sub-horizontal upper strata; frequently truncated by erosion. Transport of bedload across the stoss side of migrating dunes. Top truncation indicates 'younging' / stratigraphic top (geopetal indicator).
CURRENT BEDS (Foresets) (Option B) Inclined planes dipping at angles up to 30–35° (angle of repose) in the direction of current flow. Avalanching and grainfall down the steep lee side of migrating sand dunes or ripples. Dip direction provides the definitive palaeocurrent flow vector.
Bottomset Beds Sub-horizontal lower strata meeting the base tangentially (asymptotic contact). Suspension settling of finer grains in the flow separation zone at the dune toe. Tangential curved base proves the right-side-up (normal) stratigraphic orientation.
"When a series of inclined bedding planes show an angular relationship to the main bedding planes and to the direction of current flow, they are termed current beds (or cross-beds). Formed by the migration of sand waves, dunes, or ripples in flowing water or wind, the inclined foresets dip down-current in the direction of flow. Current bedding is invaluable for determining palaeocurrent directions and identifying overturned beds."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Sedimentary Structures, p. 132)
$$\text{Current Bedding Dip Angle: } \theta \le \theta_{\text{angle of repose}} \approx 30^\circ\text{--}34^\circ \quad (\text{Subaqueous: } 20^\circ\text{--}30^\circ;\ \text{Aeolian: up to } 35^\circ)$$ $$\text{Palaeocurrent Vector} \equiv \text{Down-dip Azimuth of Foreset (Current Bed) Laminae}$$
Figure 95: Cross-sectional architecture of current bedding, showing inclined foreset current beds dipping down-current between horizontal master bedding planes.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
2. Official Examination Question & Forensic Option Analysis
QUESTION 95
If a series of inclined bedding planes showing some angular relationship to the direction of current flow, then they are generally called as :
A Gradient beds
B Current beds
C Dipping beds
D Convolute beds
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION B (Current beds)
OPTION B • CORRECT
Current beds

By classical geological terminology (Bangar, p. 132; Mahapatra, p. 182; Pettijohn), inclined bedding planes formed within a larger sedimentary stratum at an angle to the current flow and the main horizontal bedding are formally termed current beds (or cross-beds / false beds).

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Gradient beds

'Gradient beds' is not a recognized geological term. The vertical variation in grain size is termed graded bedding, which consists of horizontal beds, not inclined cross-strata.

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
Dipping beds

'Dipping beds' is a general structural geology term for any tilted rock stratum inclined to the horizontal plane due to tectonic deformation (tilting or folding), not a primary sedimentary current-formed structure.

OPTION D • DISTRACTOR
Convolute beds

Convolute bedding consists of intensely crumpled, folded, or deformed laminations formed by soft-sediment syn-sedimentary deformation, not regular inclined current beds.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. How can cross-bedding be used as a 'way-up' (geopetal) structure to identify overturned strata?
Answer: Foreset beds are truncated sharply at the top by erosion and curve tangentially (asymptotically) into the bottomset at the base.
If the tangential curves are at the top and the sharp truncations are at the bottom, the bed has been tectonically overturned.
2. What type of cross-bedding is characterized by alternating sets that dip in opposite directions (180° apart)?
Answer: Herringbone cross-bedding
Herringbone structure forms in intertidal environments where flood currents and ebb currents reverse flow directions every 6 hours.
3. What is the maximum dip angle (angle of repose) for subaqueous current beds?
Answer: Approximately $30^\circ$ to $34^\circ$
Avalanching of sand grains down the lee slope cannot exceed the angle of internal friction of submerged sand ($~30-34^\circ$).
4. What is the term for giant cross-bedding sets exceeding 5 to 20 meters in thickness?
Answer: Aeolian Draa / Dune cross-stratification (e.g., Navajo Sandstone, USA)
Desert sand dunes produce colossal cross-bedding sets, far thicker than subaqueous river dunes.
5. What sedimentary structure forms when storm-induced oscillatory waves scour and deposit gently undulating mounds of fine sand?
Answer: Hummocky Cross-Stratification (HCS)
HCS is the diagnostic signature of storm-dominated shelf deposition below fairweather wave base.
6. In a river channel, which direction do the inclined current beds dip?
Answer: Downstream (in the down-current direction of stream flow).
Sediment grains migrate up the stoss side and tumble down the downstream-facing lee face.
7. What is flaser bedding?
Answer: A cross-bedded sand structure in which mud streaks or lenses are preserved in the ripple troughs.
Flaser bedding reflects fluctuating energy in tidal flats: sand ripples migrate during currents, and mud settles in troughs during slack water.
8. What is the difference between planar cross-bedding and trough cross-bedding?
Answer: Planar has flat bounding surfaces; trough cross-bedding has scoop-shaped, curved erosional bounding surfaces.
Planar cross-bedding forms from 2D straight dunes; trough cross-bedding forms from 3D curved/lunate dunes.
Sedimentary Diagenesis & Lithification / Question 096
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 96 • Sedimentary Petrology

Sedimentary Diagenesis: Physical Compaction, Chemical Cementation, and Lithification

Topic: Lithification & Post-Depositional Changes • Key Concept: P-T Boundary of Diagenesis vs. Metamorphism • Textbooks: Sam Boggs Jr. (2014); K.M. Bangar (p. 130); F.J. Pettijohn
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: The Spectrum of Diagenesis

Diagenesis (from Greek dia = through/across, and genesis = origin/creation) encompasses all physical, chemical, and biological processes that affect a sedimentary deposit after its initial deposition and through its progressive burial and lithification, up to the lowest boundary of metamorphism ($T \approx 200\text{--}250^\circ\text{C}, P \approx 1\text{--}2\text{ kbar}$):

Diagenetic Realm Primary Physical / Chemical Process Effect on Porosity & Permeability Diagnostic Mineral Transformations
Mechanical Compaction Overburden loading expels pore water; grains reorient, rotate, and fracture. Primary porosity drops drastically (e.g., from 70% in mud to 20% in shale; 40% to 25% in sand). Dewatering; ductile grains (clay clasts, micas) squeeze into pseudo-matrix.
Chemical Cementation Precipitation of authigenic minerals from supersaturated interstitial pore fluids. Pore throats occluded; loose grains bonded into rigid, consolidated rock (lithification). Calcite cement, quartz overgrowths, hematite coatings, authigenic clays (kaolinite, illite).
Pressure Solution (Chemical Compaction) Intergranular pressure increases solubility at grain contact points. Grains interlock forming sutured, concavo-convex, or stylolitic contacts. Stylolites in carbonates; silica dissolved from contacts reprecipitates as quartz cement.
Dissolution & Leaching Circulation of acidic or undersaturated pore waters dissolves unstable framework grains. Creates secondary porosity (critical for petroleum and groundwater reservoirs). Leaching of feldspars and carbonate fossils leaving moldic and vuggy pores.
"Diagenesis refers to all the physical and chemical changes that sediments undergo after deposition, prior to metamorphism. The two most important processes of diagenesis are compaction (the squeezing together of grains under overburden weight) and cementation (the binding of grains by precipitated mineral matter such as calcite, silica, or iron oxide). Together, compaction and cementation convert loose, unconsolidated sediment into solid rock."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Sedimentary Rocks, p. 130)
$$\text{Athys' Law of Compaction: } \Phi(z) = \Phi_0 e^{-c z} \quad (\text{Porosity } \Phi \text{ decreases exponentially with depth } z)$$ $$\text{Lithification} \equiv \mathbf{Compaction\ (Mechanical\ Dewatering)} + \mathbf{Cementation\ (Chemical\ Authigenesis)} \subset \mathbf{Diagenesis\ (Option\ D)}$$
Figure 96: Progressive stages of sedimentary diagenesis: from uncompacted loose grains at deposition, through mechanical compaction, to mineral cementation producing lithified sedimentary rock.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
2. Official Examination Question & Forensic Option Analysis
QUESTION 96
Compaction and cementation of sediments occur during :
A Transportation
B High temperature and pressure medium
C High water pressure
D Diagenesis
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION D (Diagenesis)
OPTION D • CORRECT
Diagenesis

By unanimous sedimentological definition (Boggs, 2014; Pettijohn; Bangar, p. 130), compaction and cementation are the hallmark processes of diagenesis. They occur post-depositionally during burial at low to moderate temperatures and pressures, transforming loose sediments into solid, indurated sedimentary rocks.

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Transportation

Transportation is the movement of loose sediments by water, wind, or ice. It causes abrasion, rounding, and sorting, but cannot cause compaction or cementation, which require static burial.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
High temperature and pressure medium

High temperature and high pressure ($T > 200\text{--}300^\circ\text{C}, P > 2\text{ kbar}$) define metamorphism (e.g., recrystallization of sandstone into quartzite or shale into schist), exceeding the realm of diagenesis.

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
High water pressure

Excessive pore water pressure (overpressuring) actually prevents compaction by holding grains apart, leading to undercompaction and fluid-escape structures rather than normal lithification.
