High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. What is the minimum crushing strength required for stones used in heavy masonry structures according to Indian Standard codes?
Answer: 100 MPa ($1000\text{ kg/cm}^2$) for heavy structures; 35 MPa for normal building works.
IS: 1905 dictates minimum crushing strength thresholds to ensure safety against structural failure.
2. What shape of laboratory specimen is mandated by IS: 1121 for testing compressive strength of natural stone?
Answer: Either cubes ($70\text{ mm} \times 70\text{ mm} \times 70\text{ mm}$) or cylinders ($L/D = 1.0\text{ to } 2.0$).
Cube specimens must be dressed flat with parallel faces within 0.1 mm tolerance to prevent eccentric edge loading.
3. What is the angle ($\theta$) of the shear rupture failure plane relative to the major principal stress ($\sigma_1$) in Mohr-Coulomb failure?
Answer: $\theta = 45^\circ + \phi / 2$ (typically $55^\circ\text{--}65^\circ$ to the horizontal platen).
Failure planes form inclined shear cones governed by the internal friction angle ($\phi$) of the rock material.
4. What is the conversion factor between MPa ($\text{N/mm}^2$) and $kg/cm^2$?
Answer: $1\text{ MPa} \approx 10.197\text{ kg/cm}^2$ (or $1\text{ kg/cm}^2 \approx 0.098\text{ MPa}$).
For quick estimation: $100\text{ MPa} \approx 1000\text{ kg/cm}^2$.
5. What happens to the compressive strength of a rock if the rate of loading is increased significantly?
Answer: The apparent compressive strength increases (dynamic strength is higher than static strength).
Fast loading gives microcracks insufficient time to propagate, yielding artificially higher peak strengths (IS codes specify 0.5 to 1.0 MPa/sec).
6. Which building stone has the highest crushing strength among common Indian stones?
Answer: Basalt (Deccan Trap) and Fine-grained Dolerite (up to 300-350 MPa).
Dense ophitic micro-crystalline plagioclase-pyroxene intergrowth provides colossal mechanical resistance.
7. What is ductile versus brittle failure in rocks under compression?
Answer: Brittle rocks fracture suddenly with little plastic strain; ductile rocks undergo substantial plastic flow before failure without sudden loss of strength.
Under shallow crustal conditions, intact rocks behave in a brittle manner; deep confining pressure drives the brittle-ductile transition.
8. What is Young's Modulus ($E$) of a rock in compressive stress testing?
Answer: The ratio of axial stress to axial strain within the linear elastic range ($E = \Delta \sigma / \Delta \epsilon$).
Young's modulus represents elastic stiffness; fresh granite has $E \approx 40\text{--}70\text{ GPa}$.

Comparative Rock Mechanics: Why Igneous Rocks Possess Very High Compressive Strength

Topic: Lithological Strength Classification • Key Concept: Interlocking Crystalline Textures vs. Porosity • Textbooks: K.M. Bangar (pp. 286-289); F.G. Bell; Goodman
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Micro-Structural Controls on Compressive Strength

The compressive strength of any rock mass is fundamentally determined by three primary petrographic parameters: (1) interlocking crystalline fabric, (2) mineral hardness and bonding, and (3) void volume (porosity and microcracks). On this basis, Igneous Rocks possess the highest compressive strength among all major rock classes:

Rock Class Fabric & Grain Boundary Architecture Porosity Range Compressive Strength Range (MPa) Engineering Evaluation
IGNEOUS ROCKS (Option A) Interlocking crystalline mosaic (crystallized directly from molten magma without voids). Extremely Low (< 0.5% – 1.5%) ★ VERY HIGH: 150 – 350+ MPa ★ Superlative foundation rocks for mega-dams, high-rise piers, and heavy dimension stone (Basalt, Granite, Dolerite).
Metamorphic Rocks (Non-foliated) Solid-state granoblastic recrystallization (Quartzite, Marble). Very Low (< 1%) High to Very High (100 – 250 MPa) High strength, but foliated varieties (schist, slate) are weakened by directional cleavage planes.
Sedimentary Rocks (Option B) Clastic grains bonded by authigenic cement; grain-to-grain contact points. High (5% to 35%) Low to Moderate (10 – 100 MPa) Weakened by porous matrix, clay content, and soluble cements (Sandstone, Shale, Limestone).
"Among all geological formations, unweathered igneous rocks possess very high compressive strength. Rocks like basalt, dolerite, granite, and diorite have strengths between 1500 and 3000 kg/cm² (150 to 300 MPa). This massive strength stems from their completely crystalline, interlocking fabric of hard silicates (quartz, feldspar, pyroxene) that grew together during solidification from magma, leaving virtually no pore voids."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Properties of Building Stones, pp. 288–289)
$$\text{Ryskewitsch-Duckworth Porosity-Strength Model: } \sigma = \sigma_0 e^{-b \cdot n}$$ $$\text{In Igneous Rocks: Porosity } n \rightarrow 0 \implies \mathbf{Compressive\ Strength\ \sigma \rightarrow Maximum\ (150\text{--}350\text{ MPa})}$$ $$\therefore \mathbf{Rocks\ with\ Very\ High\ Compressive\ Strength \equiv IGNEOUS\ ROCKS\ (Option\ A)}$$

QUESTION 108
Which rocks possess very high compressive strength ?
A Igneous
B Sedimentary
C Metamorphic
D Both sedimentary and metamorphic
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION A (Igneous)
OPTION A • CORRECT
Igneous

Fresh, unweathered igneous rocks (basalt, granite, dolerite, diorite) possess very high compressive strength (routinely exceeding 150 to 300 MPa). Their direct crystallization from silicate melts produces a tightly interlocking mosaic of hard minerals with virtually zero primary porosity ($< 1\%$).

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Sedimentary

Sedimentary rocks (sandstone, shale, limestone) possess low to moderate compressive strength (10 to 80 MPa) because they consist of clastic grains held together by weak cements with high porosity (10% to 30%).

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
Metamorphic

While massive non-foliated metamorphic rocks like quartzite have high strength, the vast majority of metamorphic rocks are foliated (slates, phyllites, schists) and suffer from pronounced directional planes of weakness that shear easily under stress.

OPTION D • DISTRACTOR
Both sedimentary and metamorphic

Sedimentary rocks have the lowest compressive strengths among intact rocks; grouping them with high strength is completely inaccurate.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. Why is fresh Deccan Trap basalt widely regarded as the finest construction aggregate in Western and Central India?
Answer: It possesses colossal crushing strength (>250 MPa), high toughness, low water absorption (<0.5%), and excellent bitumen affinity.
Basalt's fine-grained, interlocking ophitic and intersertal fabric gives it exceptional resistance to traffic abrasion and impact.
2. Which sedimentary rock can occasionally reach high compressive strength comparable to granites?
Answer: Pure orthoquartzite (silica-cemented quartzarenite)
When silica completely fills all pore spaces as syntaxial quartz overgrowths, sandstone converts into a tough, impermeable orthoquartzite.
3. What is the effect of chemical weathering on the compressive strength of granitic rocks?
Answer: Weathering can reduce compressive strength by 80% to 95% (from 200 MPa down to <10 MPa in saprolite).
Hydrolysis alters hard interlocking feldspars into soft, porous kaolinite clay, destroying rock integrity.
4. What is the Deere-Miller Engineering Classification based on?
Answer: Unconfined compressive strength (UCS) and the Modulus Ratio ($E_t / \sigma_c$).
Deere and Miller (1966) plot rock strength classes (A to E) against modulus ratios (High, Medium, Low) for structural rock classification.
5. Why are foliated metamorphic rocks (like mica schists) dangerous as dam abutments despite being crystalline?
Answer: Because mica alignment creates continuous planes of weakness with very low shear strength along foliation.
Water lubrication along schistosity can trigger catastrophic foundation sliding under reservoir thrust.
6. Which volcanic igneous rock possesses LOW compressive strength due to high vesicular porosity?
Answer: Pumice and Scoria (UCS typically < 10-20 MPa).
Extreme trapped gas bubble porosity (>60-80%) makes pumice so weak and light that it floats on water.
7. How does grain size affect the compressive strength within the igneous gabbro-dolerite-basalt family?
Answer: Fine-grained basalt and dolerite are stronger than coarse-grained gabbro.
The Hall-Petch effect in rocks: smaller grain size increases grain boundary area, impeding microcrack propagation and boosting strength.
8. What is the crushing strength threshold below which a rock is classified as 'weak' in engineering practice?
Answer: Less than 25 MPa (ISRM / British Standard)
Rocks with UCS < 25 MPa can be gouged with a geological pick and represent weak foundation conditions.

Pore Physics: Porosity, Void Ratio, and Volumetric Index Properties

Topic: Index Properties of Rocks & Soils • Key Concept: Porosity ($V_v / V_t$) vs. Void Ratio ($V_v / V_s$) • Textbooks: K.M. Bangar (p. 284); Terzaghi & Peck; Sam Boggs Jr.
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Defining Porosity & Volumetric Phase Relations

In hydrogeology, petroleum geology, and rock/soil mechanics, a natural geological material is conceptualized as a multi-phase system consisting of solid mineral grains ($V_s$) and open interstitial pore spaces (voids, $V_v$) occupied by water and/or air. The fundamental volumetric parameters are defined as follows:

Volumetric Property Mathematical Definition Physical Meaning & Reference Base Range of Values
POROSITY ($n$) (Option B) $$n = \frac{V_v}{V_t} \times 100\%$$ Ratio between the total volume of pore spaces ($V_v$) and the TOTAL volume of the rock ($V_t = V_s + V_v$). Always expressed as a fraction ($0 < n < 1$) or percentage ($0\% \text{ to } 100\%$). Cannot exceed 100%.
Void Ratio ($e$) (Option A) $$e = \frac{V_v}{V_s}$$ Ratio between the total volume of pore spaces ($V_v$) and the volume of SOLID mineral grains only ($V_s$). Expressed as a decimal ratio; can exceed 1.0 (or $> 100\%$) in soft clays and loose silts.
Bulk Density ($\rho_b$) (Option D) $$\rho_b = \frac{M_{\text{total}}}{V_t}$$ Total mass of rock (solids + moisture) per unit total volume. Units: $\text{g/cm}^3$ or $\text{kg/m}^3$ (typically 1.8 to 3.0).
"Porosity is the ratio between the total volume of pore spaces (voids) to the total volume of the rock, generally expressed as a percentage. It indicates the storage capacity of the rock for fluids like water, oil, or gas. In contrast, void ratio is the ratio of the volume of voids to the volume of the solid grains alone."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Properties of Building Stones, p. 284)
$$\mathbf{Porosity\ (n)} = \frac{\mathbf{Volume\ of\ Pore\ Spaces\ (V_v)}}{\mathbf{Total\ Volume\ of\ the\ Rock\ (V_t)}} \times 100\% \equiv \mathbf{Option\ B}$$ $$\text{Inter-relationship: } n = \frac{e}{1 + e} \quad \text{and} \quad e = \frac{n}{1 - n}$$
Figure 109: Three-phase diagram of rock volume illustrating the precise difference between Porosity (Vv / Vt) and Void Ratio (Vv / Vs).

QUESTION 109
Ratio between the total volume of pore spaces to the total volume of the rock is a measure of:
A Void ratio
B Porosity
C Pores ratio
D Bulk density
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION B (Porosity)
OPTION B • CORRECT
Porosity

By fundamental definition across physics, hydrogeology, and rock mechanics (IS: 13030; Bangar, p. 284; Todd; Freeze & Cherry), the ratio of the total volume of pore spaces ($V_v$) to the total volume of the rock ($V_t$) is defined as Porosity ($n$).

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Void ratio

Void ratio ($e$) is the ratio of the volume of pore spaces ($V_v$) to the volume of solid mineral grains ($V_s$), NOT to the total volume ($V_t$).

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
Pores ratio

'Pores ratio' is a fictitious non-geological distractor without physical or mathematical definition.

OPTION D • DISTRACTOR
Bulk density

Bulk density is the ratio of mass to volume ($\rho = M/V$), expressed in units of $\text{g/cm}^3$ or $\text{kg/m}^3$, not a dimensionless volume-to-volume ratio.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. If a soil has a void ratio $e = 0.50$, what is its porosity ($n$)?
Answer: $n = 33.33\%$ (or 0.333)
$n = \frac{e}{1 + e} = \frac{0.50}{1 + 0.50} = \frac{0.50}{1.50} = 0.333 \implies 33.33\%$.
2. If a sandstone has a porosity $n = 20\%$, what is its void ratio ($e$)?
Answer: $e = 0.25$
$e = \frac{n}{1 - n} = \frac{0.20}{1 - 0.20} = \frac{0.20}{0.80} = 0.25$.
3. What is the theoretical maximum porosity for an aggregate of uniform spherical grains packed in cubic packing?
Answer: $47.64\%$
In cubic packing, volume of solids in a unit cell of edge $2R$ is $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 / 8 R^3 = \frac{\pi}{6} \approx 0.5236$, leaving $n = 1 - 0.5236 = 47.64\%$.
4. What is the theoretical minimum porosity for uniform spheres in rhombohedral (hexagonal close) packing?
Answer: $25.95\%$ (or $\approx 26\%$)
Rhombohedral packing represents the densest possible geometric packing of uniform spheres without crushing.
5. What is the difference between total porosity and effective porosity?
Answer: Total porosity includes all voids (isolated + interconnected); effective porosity includes only interconnected pores that allow fluid flow.
Pumice and clay have very high total porosity, but low effective porosity because pores are either isolated (pumice) or bound by molecular adhesion (clay).
6. Why does a clay have higher porosity (50-70%) than a well-sorted sand (30-40%), yet far lower permeability?
Answer: Clay has immense total pore volume due to open card-house fabric, but pore throat diameters are sub-microscopic, creating colossal viscous drag.
Permeability is governed by pore throat size ($r^2$), not by total pore volume ($n$).
7. What is secondary porosity in limestone reservoirs?
Answer: Porosity formed after deposition by groundwater dissolution (vugs, caverns) or tectonic fracturing.
Dissolution along joints creates cavernous and karst porosity holding major hydrocarbon reserves.
8. What laboratory instrument is used to measure the grain volume of rock cores for porosity determination?
Answer: Helium Pycnometer (Boyle's Law Porosimeter)
Helium gas penetrates the finest interconnected pores, enabling highly accurate measurement of solid grain volume ($V_s$).

OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 110 • Engineering Geology

Rock Density Mechanics: Bulk Density Retaining In-Situ Natural Moisture

Topic: Index Properties of Building Stones • Key Concept: Bulk Density vs. Dry Density vs. Saturated Density • Textbooks: IS: 13030 (1991); ISRM Suggested Methods; K.M. Bangar (p. 284)
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Density States in Engineering Geology

In geotechnical engineering and rock mechanics (IS: 13030; ISRM), the density of rock is defined as the ratio of mass to total volume. Depending on the moisture state within the pore network, three standardized density parameters are recognized:

Density Parameter Pore Fluid Condition Mathematical Formulation Engineering Significance
BULK DENSITY ($\rho_b$) (Option C) Natural In-Situ Moisture Content ($w_{\text{nat}}$) as excavated from quarry. $$\rho_b = \frac{M_{\text{natural}}}{V_t}$$ The fundamental in-situ unit weight used for calculating overburden stresses, slope stability, and foundation loads.
Dry Density ($\rho_d$) (Option A) Completely dried in oven at $105^\circ\text{C}$ until constant mass; pores contain only air. $$\rho_d = \frac{M_{\text{dry}}}{V_t} = \frac{\rho_b}{1 + w}$$ Baseline parameter for porosity determination and compaction control.
Saturated Density ($\rho_{\text{sat}}$) All pore spaces 100% filled with water under vacuum saturation ($S_r = 1.0$). $$\rho_{\text{sat}} = \frac{M_{\text{sat}}}{V_t} = \rho_d + n \rho_w$$ Used for stability of submerged dam foundations, sea walls, and below-water-table slopes.
True (Grain) Density ($\rho_s$) Solid mineral grains only without voids. $$\rho_s = \frac{M_{\text{dry}}}{V_s}$$ Reflects mineral composition (e.g., pure quartz = $2.65\text{ g/cm}^3$).
"The density of the rock with its natural moisture content is known as its bulk density (or natural wet density). It is the mass of the rock in its natural, in-situ state divided by its total volume. In engineering projects, bulk density governs the dead load of stone masonry and the gravitational driving forces on rock slopes."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Properties of Building Stones, p. 284)
$$\mathbf{Bulk\ Density\ (\rho_b)} = \frac{\mathbf{Mass\ of\ Rock\ with\ Natural\ Moisture\ (M_{\text{natural}})}}{\mathbf{Total\ Bulk\ Volume\ of\ Rock\ (V_t)}} \equiv \mathbf{Option\ C}$$ $$\text{Relationship with Dry Density: } \rho_b = \rho_d (1 + w) \quad (w = \text{Natural Moisture Content})$$
Figure 110: Comparison of the three standard rock density states: Dry Density (pores air-filled), Bulk Density (with natural moisture), and Saturated Density (pores 100% water-filled).

QUESTION 110
The density of the rock with natural moisture content is known as :
A Dry density
B Wet density
C Bulk density
D Natural density
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION C (Bulk density)
OPTION C • CORRECT
Bulk density

By official Indian Standard specification (IS: 13030) and classical textbook definitions (Bangar, p. 284; Mahapatra), the mass per unit total volume of rock containing its natural moisture content is formally designated as Bulk density.

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Dry density

Dry density is measured after driving out all moisture in an oven at $105^\circ\text{C}$ to zero moisture content; it does not contain natural moisture.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Wet density

While casually used, 'wet density' in strict testing usually denotes artificially saturated rock (saturated density); the formal engineering term for natural in-situ moisture state is bulk density.

OPTION D • DISTRACTOR
Natural density

'Natural density' is an informal descriptive phrase; the standardized technical term in Indian and ISRM standards is bulk density.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. If a rock specimen has a total volume of $100\text{ cm}^3$ and weighs 265 grams in its natural moisture state, what is its bulk density?
Answer: $2.65\text{ g/cm}^3$ (or $2650\text{ kg/m}^3$)
$\rho_b = M_{\text{nat}} / V_t = 265\text{ g} / 100\text{ cm}^3 = 2.65\text{ g/cm}^3$.
2. If the same specimen from Problem 1 weighs 260 grams after oven-drying, what is its natural moisture content ($w$)?
Answer: $1.92\%$
$w = \frac{M_{\text{nat}} - M_{\text{dry}}}{M_{\text{dry}}} \times 100 = \frac{265 - 260}{260} \times 100 = \frac{5}{260} \times 100 \approx 1.92\%$.
3. What method is specified by IS: 13030 to measure the total volume ($V_t$) of an irregular porous rock lump?
Answer: The Water Displacement Method with Paraffin Wax Coating (or Mercury Displacement).
Coating the specimen with an ultra-thin layer of melted paraffin wax prevents water from entering the pores during submersion.
4. Why is high bulk density desirable for stones used in breakwaters and harbour sea-walls?
Answer: High density provides greater gravitational submerged weight ($W' = (\rho_b - \rho_w) g V$) resisting displacement by violent storm waves.
Hudson's formula proves that armour stone stability on sea-walls increases with the cube of the submerged unit weight.
5. What is the relation between dry density ($\rho_d$), specific gravity ($G$), and porosity ($n$)?
Answer: $\rho_d = G \cdot \rho_w (1 - n)$
Since dry mass occupies volume $(1 - n) V_t$, the dry density is directly proportional to $(1 - n)$.
6. Which Indian state has extensive quarries of heavy Deccan Trap basalt used for railway ballast?
Answer: Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Western Madhya Pradesh
Deccan basalts have high bulk density ($~2.9\text{ g/cm}^3$), making them ideal for heavy-haul rail beds.
7. What is submerged (buoyant) density ($\rho'$)?
Answer: $\rho' = \rho_{\text{sat}} - \rho_{\text{water}}$
Buoyancy reduces the effective weight of rocks submerged beneath the water table.
8. What temperature is standardized for oven-drying rock specimens to determine moisture content and dry density?
Answer: $105^\circ\text{C} \pm 5^\circ\text{C}$ for at least 24 hours.
This temperature evaporates all free pore water and adsorbed capillary moisture without destroying structural lattice water in gypsum or clays.

OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 111 • Engineering Geology

Building Stone Testing: Impact Testing and the Measurement of Toughness

Topic: Mechanical Testing of Stones • Key Concept: Impact Resistance & Toughness Index • Textbooks: IS: 2386 (Part IV); Page Impact Test; K.M. Bangar (p. 288)
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Mechanical Meaning of Toughness & Impact Testing

In mechanical engineering and stone testing, toughness is defined as the ability of a material to absorb kinetic energy and resist fracturing, shattering, or disintegrating under sudden impact blows. While crushing strength measures resistance to slow, static loads, Impact Testing is conducted specifically to determine a stone's Toughness:

Laboratory Test Method Dynamic Stress Imposed Primary Property Measured Standard Apparatus & Reference
IMPACT TEST (Option D) Sudden dynamic impact blow (falling hammer). ★ TOUGHNESS ★ (Option D) (Resistance to shattering under repeated shock loads). Page Impact Testing Machine / Aggregate Impact Value (AIV) (IS: 2386 Part IV).
Crushing Test Slow, gradually increasing static compressive load. Compressive (Crushing) Strength Universal Testing Machine / Compression Press (IS: 1121 Part I).
Abrasion Test Frictional rubbing and abrasive grinding. Hardness & Wear Resistance Los Angeles Abrasion / Deval Attrition Machine (IS: 2386 Part IV).
Soundness Test Cyclic immersion in sodium or magnesium sulfate salt solutions. Durability (Frost & Weathering resistance) Sodium Sulfate Soundness Apparatus (IS: 2386 Part V).
"The resistance of a stone to impact or shattering under a sudden blow is known as its toughness. It is determined by the impact test using a Page Impact Machine. A steel hammer weighing 2 kg is dropped on a cylindrical stone core from successive heights increasing by 1 cm until the specimen breaks. The height of the blow in centimeters that causes failure is taken as the toughness index of the stone."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Properties of Building Stones, p. 288)
$$\text{Page Impact Toughness Test: } \text{Toughness Index } (T) \equiv \text{Drop Height of 2 kg Hammer at Fracture (in cm)}$$ $$\text{Aggregate Impact Value (AIV): } \text{AIV } (\%) = \frac{W_2 (\text{Fines passing 2.36 mm sieve})}{W_1 (\text{Total sample weight})} \times 100\%$$ $$\mathbf{Impact\ Testing\ of\ Stone} \implies \mathbf{Determines\ TOUGHNESS\ (Option\ D)}$$
Figure 111: Impact testing apparatus and mechanics for determining stone toughness (resistance to sudden impact loads) alongside crushing and abrasion tests.

QUESTION 111
The impact testing of a stone is done to know the:
A Durability
B Porosity
C Density
D Toughness
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION D (Toughness)
OPTION D • CORRECT
Toughness

By standard civil engineering and building stone testing codes (IS: 2386 Part IV; ASTM D3; Bangar, p. 288; Mahapatra), impact testing is conducted specifically to measure the toughness (impact resistance against dynamic shattering) of stones and road aggregates.

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Durability

Durability (weathering resistance) is determined by the soundness test (sodium sulfate cycles), freezing-and-thawing tests, or water absorption tests, NOT by impact testing.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Porosity

Porosity is determined through water absorption saturation methods or helium pycnometry, measuring volumetric voids rather than dynamic shock response.

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
Density

Density is measured by mass-to-volume displacement (pycnometer or water immersion), an intrinsic mass property unrelated to mechanical impact blows.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. In the Page Impact Test, what is the weight of the falling hammer and from what height does the test start?
Answer: The hammer weighs 2.0 kg and drops initially from a height of 1.0 cm.
The drop height increases by 1 cm after each blow (1 cm, 2 cm, 3 cm...) until the specimen fractures.
2. What toughness index value classifies a stone as 'high toughness' according to standard engineering specifications?
Answer: Greater than 19 cm ($T > 19$).
$T > 19$ is high toughness; 13 to 19 is medium toughness; $< 13$ is poor/low toughness.
3. In the Aggregate Impact Value (AIV) test (IS: 2386 Part IV), how many blows are delivered and by what hammer weight?
Answer: 15 blows by a 13.5 to 14.0 kg hammer dropping from a height of 380 mm (38 cm).
AIV is the percentage of crushed fines passing through a 2.36 mm IS sieve after 15 standard blows.
4. What is the maximum permissible Aggregate Impact Value (AIV) for aggregates used in bituminous concrete road wearing courses?
Answer: Maximum 24% (IRC guidelines specify $\le 24\%$ or $\le 30\%$ for base courses).
Lower AIV values signify higher toughness and resistance to shattering under vehicle wheel impacts.
5. Why does dolerite have higher toughness than coarse granite even though both are igneous?
Answer: Dolerite possesses an ophitic texture where flexible plagioclase laths are enclosed in pyroxene, absorbing impact energy without propagating cracks.
Granite contains large brittle quartz crystals that cleave and shatter readily under impact blows.
6. What test determines the resistance of stone to wear caused by mutual rubbing of aggregates against each other?
Answer: The Attrition Test (Deval Attrition Test)
Frictional rubbing of stones against stones is attrition; rubbing of stones against external steel balls/abrasives is abrasion.
7. What is the relationship between toughness and brittleness in rocks?
Answer: Toughness and brittleness are inverse properties; high toughness implies low brittleness.
Brittle rocks fracture with minimal strain energy absorption, whereas tough rocks deform plastically and dissipate energy before failing.
8. What is the Charpy or Izod test used for?
Answer: Measuring the notched impact energy of construction materials (steels and structural composites).
Charpy tests measure the kinetic energy absorbed by a swinging pendulum hammer breaking a notched specimen.
Tunneling & Underground Rock Mechanics / Question 112
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 112 • Engineering Geology

Underground Geomechanics: High In-Situ Stresses and the Hazard of Rock Bursts

Topic: Geological Hazards in Tunneling • Key Concept: Explosive Stress Release & Strainburst Mechanics • Textbooks: E. Hoek & E.T. Brown (1980); K.M. Bangar (p. 305); F.G. Bell
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Geomechanics of Rock Bursts in Deep Excavations

In deep underground civil tunneling and mining excavations (typically at depths exceeding 500 to 1000 meters), rocks exist under colossal lithostatic confining stresses ($\sigma_v = \rho g z$). When an opening is blasted or bored, the confining support is instantly removed, redistributing stress into severe concentrations around the excavation periphery. The sudden explosive release of stored elastic strain energy in massive, brittle rocks causes violent rock ejection known as a Rock Burst:

Tunneling Phenomenon Physical / Mechanical Mechanism Speed of Occurrence Geological Pre-Conditions
ROCK BURST (Strainburst) (Option B) Sudden, violent explosive release of accumulated elastic strain energy as tangential stress ($\sigma_\theta$) exceeds rock strength. Instantaneous (Microseconds to seconds; gunshot-like explosion). Deep overburden (>500 m); hard, brittle, massive crystalline rocks (granites, quartzites, gneisses) with zero open joints.
Rock Fall (Option A) Gravitational detachment of loose, jointed blocks from the tunnel roof. Rapid gravity fall. Shallow tunnels; heavily fractured, blocky, intersecting joint sets.
Squeezing Ground Time-dependent ductile inward plastic creep of overstressed rock. Slow (Days to months). Weak, ductile rocks under high stress (shales, phyllites, fault gouge).
Water Gush (Option D) Sudden inrush of groundwater through karst channels or fault zones. Sudden flooding. Karst limestone cavities or permeable water-bearing shear zones.
"In deep tunnels driven through hard, brittle, massive rocks (like quartzites, granites, or traps), the rock is subjected to colossal in-situ stresses. When the tunnel is excavated, the rock around the boundary expands into the opening. If the elastic strain energy stored in the rock is released suddenly and violently, slabs of rock fly off the walls and roof with explosive force, accompanied by a sound like a cannon shot. This dangerous phenomenon is known as a rock burst."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Tunnels and Underground Works, p. 305)
$$\text{Kirsch Solution for Tangential Stress at Sidewall: } \sigma_\theta = 3\sigma_v - \sigma_h \quad (\text{For hydrostatic stress: } \sigma_\theta = 2\sigma_0)$$ $$\text{Rock Burst Criterion (Hoek): } \frac{\sigma_\theta}{\text{UCS}} > 0.8\text{ to } 1.0 \implies \mathbf{Sudden\ Explosive\ Failure \equiv ROCK\ BURST\ (Option\ B)}$$
Figure 112: Mechanics of rock burst in deep tunneling: concentration of high tangential stresses at tunnel walls triggering explosive failure and ejection of rock slabs.

2. Official Examination Question & Forensic Option Analysis
QUESTION 112
The sudden release of stress in rocks during tunneling will normally result in :
A Rock fall
B Rock bursts
C Blockage
D Water gush
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION B (Rock bursts)
OPTION B • CORRECT
Rock bursts

By unanimous rock mechanics consensus (Hoek & Brown; Barton; Bangar, p. 305; Mahapatra), the sudden, violent, explosive release of stored strain energy in high-stress rock environments during underground tunneling produces rock bursts (spontaneous ejection and shattering of rock slabs from the excavation boundary).

OPTION A • DISTRACTOR
Rock fall

A rock fall is the passive falling of unkeyed, loosened rock blocks under gravity along pre-existing joints, not a dynamic explosion caused by the sudden release of high in-situ strain energy.

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
Blockage

'Blockage' is an informal descriptive consequence of collapsed material in a tunnel, not the geomechanical stress-release process itself.

OPTION D • DISTRACTOR
Water gush

A water gush is a hydrogeological inrush caused by encountering a confined, pressurized aquifer or flooded fault zone, entirely independent of strain energy release in brittle rocks.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. In which famous Indian deep gold mining area were rock bursts a catastrophic historical hazard claiming numerous miners' lives?
Answer: The Kolar Gold Fields (KGF) in Karnataka (Champion Reef Mine down to >3200 m depth).
At depths exceeding 3 km in massive amphibolitic schists, explosive rock bursts registered as local earthquakes on seismographs.
2. What preventive drilling technique is used to alleviate stress concentrations and prevent rock bursts ahead of a tunnel face?
Answer: Destress blasting (or stress-relief drilling).
Drilling large-diameter pilot relief holes or detonating small cushion charges fractured the rock ahead, dissipating strain energy harmlessly.
3. What modern specialized rock reinforcement bolt is designed to absorb colossal kinetic energy during a rock burst without snapping?
Answer: Yielding rockbolts (e.g., D-Bolt, Cone Bolt, or Garford bolt).
Yielding bolts can stretch 15% to 20% plastically while maintaining high load resistance, dissipating the kinetic shock of ejected rock.
4. What is a microseismic monitoring system in deep tunneling?
Answer: A network of acoustic geophones that record high-frequency acoustic emissions generated by propagating microcracks prior to a rock burst.
Spiking microseismic event rates provide early warning of an imminent strainburst, allowing evacuation of tunnel crews.
5. What is the difference between a strainburst and a fault-slip rock burst?
Answer: A strainburst is local explosive spalling at the tunnel skin; a fault-slip burst is an induced earthquake caused by shearing along a nearby major fault.
Fault-slip bursts generate massive seismic magnitudes ($M_L > 2.0\text{--}3.5$) that can destroy hundreds of meters of tunnel.
6. Which Himalayan tunnel project experienced severe rock bursts during excavation through high-cover quartzite massifs?
Answer: The Rohtang (Atal) Tunnel and Nathpa Jhakri Hydroelectric Tunnel (Himachal Pradesh).
Overburden exceeding 1500 to 1900 m in brittle crystalline quartzites triggered intense strainbursting during drilling.
7. Why are heavily jointed, fractured rocks LESS prone to rock bursts than completely intact, massive rocks?
Answer: Joint planes allow the rock mass to deform, slip, and relieve stress gradually, preventing the storage of high elastic strain energy.
Massive, unjointed rocks behave like a giant loaded spring, holding immense strain until catastrophic failure occurs.
8. What is 'overbreak' in tunneling?
Answer: The volume of rock excavated beyond the neat designed perimeter profile of the tunnel.
Rock bursts, unfavorable joint dips, and excessive blasting charges dramatically increase overbreak, requiring costly concrete backfilling.

OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 113 • Structural Geology

Structural Geometry: Classification of Inclined Strata and Dip Angle Limits

Topic: Dip and Strike Systematics • Key Concept: Gentle vs. Moderate vs. Steep Dip Angles • Textbooks: M.P. Billings (Structural Geology); K.M. Bangar (p. 162); G.B. Mahapatra
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Geometric Classification of Inclined Strata

In structural geology and geological mapping, planar sedimentary strata and metamorphic foliations are described by their attitude (strike and dip). The angle of inclination of a bedding plane with the true horizontal plane is termed its true dip ($\theta$). In standard geological engineering classifications (Billings, 1972; Bangar, p. 162), inclined strata are classified based on the magnitude of dip angle:

Inclination Class Dip Angle Range ($\theta$) Outcrop Character & Topographic Expression Engineering Significance (Slopes & Tunnels)
Gently Inclined (Gentle Dip) $0^\circ < \theta < 15^\circ$ (or $0^\circ\text{--}10^\circ$) Forms mesas, buttes, and gentle cuestas; broad outcrop widths in valleys. Extremely stable flat foundations; horizontal tunnel drives.
MODERATELY INCLINED STRATA (Option A) $15^\circ \le \theta \le 45^\circ$ (Angles upto $45^\circ$) Asymmetrical ridges (cuestas) with distinct dip slope and escarpment. Critical dip range for translational planar rockslides (daylighting on slope cuts).
Steeply Inclined Strata (Option B) $45^\circ < \theta < 85^\circ$ Symmetrical razor-backed ridges (hogbacks); narrow outcrop bands. Prone to toppling failures; tunnels cutting normal to strike are most stable.
Vertical Strata $\theta \approx 90^\circ$ Straight linear bands cutting straight across contour lines regardless of topography. No dip-slope sliding; high vertical bearing capacity.
Overturned Strata (Option D) Inverted past $90^\circ$ Oldest beds lie on top of younger beds; confirmed by geopetal structures. Indicates intense recumbent nappe folding.
"According to the angle of inclination (dip), stratified rocks are categorized into: Gently inclined strata (dipping at angles less than 15°), Moderately inclined strata (dipping at angles between 15° and 45°, or angles up to 45°), and Steeply inclined strata (dipping at angles greater than 45°). Plunge (Option C) refers specifically to the inclination of a linear fold axis, not a planar stratum."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Structural Geology, pp. 162–164)
$$\text{True Dip Angle: } \theta = \arctan \left(\frac{\Delta h}{L}\right)$$ $$\mathbf{Dip\ Angle\ Range: } 15^\circ \le \theta \le 45^\circ \implies \mathbf{MODERATELY\ INCLINED\ STRATA\ (Option\ A)}$$
Figure 113: Geometrical classification of bedded strata based on dip angle: Gently Inclined (<15°), Moderately Inclined (15° to 45°), and Steeply Inclined (>45°).

QUESTION 113
Strata dipping at angles upto 45° are called :
A Moderately inclined strata
B Steeply inclined strata
C Plunge
D Overturned
CORRECT ANSWER: OPTION A (Moderately inclined strata)
OPTION A • CORRECT
Moderately inclined strata

By standard structural geology conventions (Billings; Bangar, p. 162; Mahapatra), stratified rock layers dipping at angles between 15° and 45° (or angles upto 45°) are formally designated as moderately inclined strata.

OPTION B • DISTRACTOR
Steeply inclined strata

Steeply inclined strata have dip angles greater than 45° up to nearly vertical ($45^\circ\text{--}85^\circ$), forming symmetrical hogback ridges.

OPTION C • DISTRACTOR
Plunge

'Plunge' is the inclination of a linear feature (such as a fold hinge line or lineation) with the horizontal plane, not the planar dip of a bedding surface.

OPTION D • DISTRACTOR
Overturned

Overturned strata have been rotated through tectonic folding past the vertical (over $90^\circ$), such that original young beds underlie older beds.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. What is the difference between a cuesta and a hogback?
Answer: A cuesta has a gentle dip slope ($< 30^\circ\text{--}40^\circ$) and a steep scarp slope; a hogback has nearly equal steep slopes on both sides ($> 40^\circ\text{--}45^\circ$).
Moderately inclined strata produce cuestas; steeply inclined strata produce symmetrical hogbacks.
2. Why are cut slopes excavated in moderately inclined strata dipping into the roadway exceptionally dangerous?
Answer: If daylighted, the bedding plane acts as a planar slide surface where dip angle ($\theta$) exceeds the friction angle ($\phi$).
Translational planar rockslides occur spontaneously along moderately inclined beds ($20^\circ\text{--}45^\circ$) when the toe is excavated.
3. What is the Strike of an inclined stratum?
Answer: The compass direction of a horizontal line drawn on the bedding plane (perpendicular to true dip).
Strike is always exactly perpendicular to the direction of maximum (true) dip.
4. What is Apparent Dip ($\alpha$) versus True Dip ($\theta$)?
Answer: True dip is the maximum inclination perpendicular to strike; apparent dip is the inclination along any other oblique direction ($\alpha < \theta$).
$\tan \alpha = \tan \theta \cdot \cos \beta$, where $\beta$ is the angle between strike and apparent dip direction.
5. What does the Rule of 'V's state when strata dip upstream?
Answer: The outcrop pattern in the valley forms a 'V' pointing upstream.
Whenever beds dip upstream (against the valley gradient), the outcrop 'V' invariably points upstream.
6. What is the relation between true bed thickness ($T$), outcrop width ($W$), and dip angle ($\theta$) on horizontal ground?
Answer: $T = W \cdot \sin \theta$
As dip angle increases, the outcrop width for the same true bed thickness narrows.
7. In tunnel construction, which alignment relative to strike of inclined strata provides the most stable conditions?
Answer: Tunneling perpendicular to strike (cutting across beds), preferably driving into the dip.
Driving parallel to strike leaves entire sidewalls supported on a single dipping bedding plane, promoting sidewall sliding.
8. What is a clinometer used for in field geology?
Answer: Measuring the angle of dip of a geological plane or the plunge of a lineation.
A Brunton compass combines a magnetic needle for strike azimuth with a spirit-level clinometer for dip angle measurement.
Dam Foundations & Geotechnical Remediation / Question 114
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 114 • Engineering Geology & Dam Foundations

Foundation Treatment: Pressure Grouting for Rectification of Open Rock Joints

Topic: Dam & Tunnel Foundation Treatment • Key Concept: Consolidation & Curtain Grouting of Rock Joints • Textbooks: K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, p. 312); Krynine & Judd (1957); F.G. Bell
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Mechanics of Rock Mass Grouting

In geotechnical and dam foundation engineering, grouting is the process of injecting fluid cementitious, clay-bentonite, asphaltic, or chemical slurries under controlled hydraulic pressure via drilled boreholes into subsurface rock discontinuities. Among the primary geological structures, joints (open, interconnected tensile or shear fractures without displacement) are the principal structural defects routinely and completely rectified by grouting:

Geological Structure Physical Nature of Discontinuity Amenability to Grouting Rectification Primary Engineering Remedy
JOINTS (Open Fractures) (Option A) Discrete, interconnected planar apertures (0.1 mm to several cm) without shear offset IDEAL / DIRECTLY RECTIFIED: Grout penetrates open joint networks, sealing seepage paths and monolithically bonding blocks Consolidation (Blanket) Grouting & Curtain Grouting (IS: 6066)
Folds (Anticlines / Synclines) (Option B) Regional or local ductile-brittle curvature of rock strata Cannot "rectify" curvature of folded strata by grouting; only associated axial-plane tension joints can be grouted Re-align tunnel or dam axis relative to fold limbs and synclinal troughs
Faults & Shear Zones (Option C) Tectonic displacement planes filled with impermeable clay gouge, mylonite, or breccia Clay gouge blocks grout penetration; active faults cannot be stopped by cement injection Dental treatment (excavation of fault zone and backfilling with concrete plug) or seismic design
Inclined Strata (Option D) Regional homoclinal dip of sedimentary beds Attitude (strike and dip) of strata is a geometric property that cannot be altered by grouting Rock bolting, cable anchoring, or orienting dam axis parallel to strike
"Joints are the most universal structural defects encountered in bedrock at dam, reservoir, and tunnel sites. Because open joints drastically reduce the bearing capacity of the rock mass and act as high-velocity conduits for water leakage and uplift pressure, they are systematically rectified by pressure grouting. By pumping cement-water slurry into boreholes intersecting the joint network, the voids are sealed and the jointed rock is transformed into an impervious, monolithic mass."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Standard Publishers, Chapter 15: Dams and Reservoirs, p. 312)
Lugeon Permeability Criterion & Groutability Ratio
$$\text{1 Lugeon (LU)} = \frac{1\text{ Litre of water loss}}{\text{minute} \times \text{metre of borehole}} \quad \text{at } P = 10\text{ bars (1 MPa)}$$ $$\text{Groutability Ratio (Rock Apertures): } N_r = \frac{\text{Fissure/Joint Width } (b)}{\text{Maximum Grain Size of Cement } (D_{95})} > 3$$

When bedrock hydraulic conductivity exceeds $1\text{--}3\text{ Lugeons}$ due to open joints, foundation grouting is mandatory. Ordinary Portland Cement (OPC) grout effectively seals joints wider than $0.1\text{--}0.2\text{ mm}$, while microfine cement or chemical (silicate/acrylamide) grouts penetrate hairline joints down to $0.01\text{ mm}$.

2. Consolidation vs. Curtain Grouting in Jointed Foundations
  • Consolidation (Blanket) Grouting: Executed via shallow holes ($5\text{ to }15\text{ m}$ deep) drilled in a grid pattern across the entire footprint of a dam foundation at low pressures ($1.5\text{ to }3.5\text{ kg/cm}^2$). It seals near-surface relaxation and unloading joints, increases the Young's modulus of deformation ($E_m$), and prevents differential settlement.
  • Curtain (Cutoff) Grouting: Executed via a single or double line of deep boreholes ($30\text{ to }100+\text{ m}$ deep) near the upstream heel of a dam at high pressures ($5\text{ to }20+\text{ kg/cm}^2$). It creates a deep, continuous impermeable barrier across deep-seated joint systems, cutting off under-seepage and dissipating dangerous hydraulic uplift pressure ($U$) beneath the dam base.
  • Contact & Backfill Grouting in Tunnels: Seals open radial joints in the blast-damaged excavation disturbed zone (EDZ) and fills overbreak cavities behind the concrete tunnel lining.
Figure 114.1: Engineering geological cross-section of a concrete gravity dam resting on jointed bedrock, illustrating shallow grid Consolidation Grouting (strengthening jointed rock mass) and deep upstream Curtain Grouting (cutting off seepage and reducing hydraulic uplift pressure).

Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official OPSC 2019 Question & Forensic Option Analysis
Q114. Which type of geological structure can be rectified by grouting ?
(A) Joints
(B) Folds
(C) Faults
(D) Inclined strata
✔ Verified Correct Answer: Option (A) — Joints
A Joints CORRECT ANSWER
Forensic Verification: Joints are divisional planes or fractures in rocks along which there has been no appreciable shear displacement parallel to the fracture surface. Because joints create open apertures that weaken the rock mass and allow water leakage, they are directly and completely rectified by pressure grouting. Injecting cement or chemical grout fills the joint voids, binds individual rock blocks into a rigid monolithic mass, restores compressive strength, and makes the bedrock watertight.
B Folds INCORRECT
Why this is wrong: Folds are macroscopic bends or undulations in layered rocks resulting from compressional tectonic stresses. Grouting cannot unbend or rectify the synclinal or anticlinal geometry of folded strata (though tension joints along a fold crest may be grouted locally).
C Faults INCORRECT
Why this is wrong: Faults are major fracture zones along which relative displacement has occurred, usually containing impermeable clay fault gouge, crushed breccia, or mylonite, and carrying potential for future seismic slip. Fault zones are treated by dental treatment (excavating soft gouge and plugging with reinforced concrete) rather than simple grouting, and active fault displacement cannot be stopped by grouting.
D Inclined strata INCORRECT
Why this is wrong: Inclined strata represent tilted sedimentary beds dipping at an angle to the horizontal. Dip angle is a regional geometric attitude of the formation that cannot be altered or rectified by injecting grout.

Treatment Method Target Geological Defect Injection / Excavation Depth Primary Engineering Objective

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. What is the difference between a Joint and a Fault?
Answer: A joint is a fracture with zero (or negligible) shear displacement parallel to the plane; a fault is a fracture showing measurable shear displacement.
Both are brittle fractures, but displacement across the fracture plane distinguishes a fault from a joint.
2. How is the Lugeon unit defined in dam foundation investigations?
Answer: Water loss of 1 litre per minute per metre length of test borehole under a constant injection pressure of 10 bars (1 MPa or ~10 kg/cm²).
Introduced by Maurice Lugeon (1933), the Lugeonpacker test determines whether rock joints require grouting (typically required when LU > 3).
3. Where is a grout curtain located beneath a concrete gravity dam, and why?
Answer: Near the upstream heel of the dam, just upstream of the foundation drainage curtain.
Placing the grout curtain at the upstream heel blocks reservoir water entry immediately, minimizing hydraulic head and uplift pressure across the entire dam base.
4. What is the "split-spacing" method of drilling and grouting?
Answer: Drilling and grouting primary holes at wide spacing (e.g., 12 m), then halving the interval with secondary (6 m), tertiary (3 m), and quaternary (1.5 m) holes until grout intake drops to zero.
Split-spacing systematically closes first the widest master joints and progressively seals tighter fractures while verifying closure.
5. Why must grouting pressure be carefully limited during shallow consolidation grouting?
Answer: Excessive grouting pressure exceeding the overburden stress causes hydraulic jacking (uplift and heaving of horizontal bedding planes).
Rule of thumb: safe grouting pressure in bars is roughly $0.23\text{ to }0.33\text{ bar per metre}$ of overburden depth in stratified rock.
6. What is "Dental Treatment" (Shasta Formula) in dam foundation engineering?
Answer: Excavating weak fault gouge or weathered shear zones to a calculated depth ($d$) and backfilling with monolithic concrete.
By the USBR Shasta formula, for a fault seam of width $b$ (in metres) under a dam of height $H$: $d = 0.00656 \cdot b \cdot H + 1.5\text{ m}$ (for $H \ge 45\text{ m}$).
7. Which type of grout is used to seal wide solution cavities carrying fast-flowing water in karstic limestone?
Answer: Hot asphalt (bitumen) grout or sanded thick cement-bentonite-accelerating mortar.
Thin cement slurry is washed away by turbulent flowing water; hot asphalt solidifies rapidly on contact with cold water to plug large karst channels.
8. How is Rock Quality Designation (RQD) affected by closely spaced joints?
Answer: Closely spaced joints ($< 10\text{ cm}$ spacing) reduce RQD drastically because only intact core pieces $\ge 10\text{ cm}$ long are summed.
$\text{RQD} = \frac{\sum \text{Length of core pieces } \ge 10\text{ cm}}{\text{Total core run length}} \times 100\%$. Consolidation grouting seals these joints in situ.
Rock Mechanics & Strength Anisotropy / Question 115
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 115 • Rock Mechanics & Strength Anisotropy

Mechanical Anisotropy: Maximum Compressive Strength Normal to Bedding Planes

Topic: Strength Anisotropy of Stratified Rocks • Key Concept: Donath's U-Shaped Curve & Loading Normal to Bedding • Textbooks: K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, p. 287); F.A. Donath (1961); Jaeger, Cook & Zimmerman
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Transverse Isotropy & Strength Anisotropy in Rocks

Stratified sedimentary rocks (sandstones, shales, limestones) and foliated metamorphic rocks (slates, phyllites, schists, gneisses) exhibit pronounced mechanical anisotropy (specifically transverse isotropy). Their compressive strength ($\sigma_c$) varies systematically with the orientation angle ($\beta$) between the major principal compressive stress ($\sigma_1$) and the bedding or foliation planes. In compact stratified rocks, the compressive strength is always greatest when the applied compressive stresses act normal (perpendicular, $\beta = 90^\circ$) to the bedding planes:

Stress Orientation Relative to Bedding Angle $\beta$ (Between $\sigma_1$ and Bedding Plane) Dominant Failure Mechanism Relative Compressive Strength ($\sigma_c$)
STRESSES NORMAL TO BEDDING PLANES (Option A) $\beta = 90^\circ$ (Perpendicular) Shear fracture must cut across intact mineral grains and all strong layers; bedding planes are pressed tightly shut MAXIMUM STRENGTH ($\sigma_{c,\max}$)
Stresses Parallel to Bedding Planes (Option B) $\beta = 0^\circ$ (Parallel) Axial tensile splitting along weak bedding interfaces and Euler buckling of thin individual laminae High-to-Intermediate ($\approx 0.70\text{--}0.85\,\sigma_{c,90^\circ}$), susceptible to splitting
Stresses Inclined at $45^\circ$ to Bedding (Option C) $\beta = 45^\circ$ High resolved shear stress ($\tau = \frac{1}{2}\sigma_1 \sin 2\beta$) directly along weak bedding planes triggers slip Very Low Strength (Near the trough of the U-curve)
Stresses Inclined at $60^\circ$ (or $30^\circ$ to $\sigma_1$) (Option D) $\beta \approx 30^\circ\text{--}45^\circ$ to $\sigma_1$ Critical Mohr-Coulomb slip angle ($\beta_{\text{crit}} = 45^\circ - \phi_j/2 \approx 30^\circ$): pure sliding along bedding ABSOLUTE MINIMUM STRENGTH ($\sigma_{c,\min}$)
"In stratified and laminated rocks, the compressive strength depends strongly on the direction of loading relative to the bedding planes. The strength of a compact rock is always greatest when the compressive stresses are applied normal (perpendicular) to the bedding planes, because the compressive load closes the bedding planes rather than splitting them apart, forcing any rupture surface to shear across the full thickness of the rock layers."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Standard Publishers, Chapter 13: Engineering Properties of Rocks, p. 287)
Jaeger's Single Plane of Weakness Theory (1960) & Anisotropy Index
$$\sigma_1 - \sigma_3 = \frac{2\left(c_j + \sigma_3 \tan\phi_j\right)}{\left(1 - \tan\phi_j \cot\beta\right)\sin 2\beta}$$ $$\text{Minimum Strength Angle: } \beta_{\min} = 45^\circ - \frac{\phi_j}{2} \approx 25^\circ\text{--}35^\circ \quad \text{(to }\sigma_1\text{)}$$ $$\text{Strength Anisotropy Ratio: } R_c = \frac{\sigma_{c(90^\circ)}}{\sigma_{c(\min)}}$$

Here $c_j$ and $\phi_j$ are the cohesion and friction angle of the bedding plane. When $\sigma_1$ is applied normal to bedding ($\beta = 90^\circ$), $\sin 2\beta = 0$, making sliding along the bedding plane impossible ($\sigma_1 \to \infty$ for bedding slip), so failure is governed entirely by the much higher intact rock matrix strength ($c_m, \phi_m$).

2. Engineering Application: Placing Stones on Their "Natural Bed"
  • Masonry & Dam Pier Construction ("Natural Bed" Rule): In civil engineering and stone masonry, dressed sedimentary and metamorphic blocks (sandstone, limestone, gneiss) must always be laid with their bedding planes horizontal (i.e., normal to the vertical compressive gravity load).
  • Consequence of Face-Bedding ($\beta = 0^\circ$): If stone blocks are placed with bedding planes vertical and parallel to load ("face-bedded"), moisture penetration and axial compressive stress cause tensile delamination, buckling, and spalling of outer rock sheets.
  • Consequence of Oblique Bedding ($\beta = 30^\circ\text{--}60^\circ$): Maximum resolved shear stress acts along the bedding planes, leading to premature shear sliding at a fraction ($20\%\text{--}50\%$) of the intact rock strength.
Figure 115.1: Jaeger-Donath U-shaped strength anisotropy curve plotting Unconfined Compressive Strength ($\sigma_c$) against bedding inclination angle ($\beta$), showing peak strength when stress is applied normal to bedding ($\beta = 90^\circ$) and minimum strength at oblique shear inclinations ($\beta \approx 30^\circ\text{--}45^\circ$).
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official OPSC 2019 Question & Forensic Option Analysis
Q115. When is the strength of a compact rock always greater ?
(A) When stresses are normal to bedding planes
(B) When stresses are parallel to bedding planes
(C) When stresses are inclined at 45° to bedding planes
(D) When stresses are inclined at 60° to bedding planes
✔ Verified Correct Answer: Option (A) — When stresses are normal to bedding planes
A When stresses are normal to bedding planes CORRECT ANSWER
Forensic Verification: When compressive stresses act normal (perpendicular, $90^\circ$) to the bedding planes, the normal stress across the bedding interfaces is maximized while resolved shear stress along the bedding planes is zero ($\tau = 0$). The bedding planes are compressed tightly together, preventing delamination or slip, and forcing the rock to fail only by shearing across the strong intact mineral grains. Hence, compressive strength is always greatest normal to bedding.
B When stresses are parallel to bedding planes INCORRECT
Why this is wrong: When compressive stress acts parallel to bedding planes ($\beta = 0^\circ$), lateral Poisson expansion induces tensile stress perpendicular to the bedding planes, causing premature axial splitting (cleavage delamination) and buckling of individual laminae.
C When stresses are inclined at 45° to bedding planes INCORRECT
Why this is wrong: At $45^\circ$ inclination, the resolved shear stress ($\tau = \frac{1}{2}\sigma_1 \sin 90^\circ = 0.5\,\sigma_1$) reaches its theoretical maximum along the weak bedding planes, causing easy shear sliding and very low compressive strength.
D When stresses are inclined at 60° to bedding planes INCORRECT
Why this is wrong: When the normal to the bedding plane is at $60^\circ$ (meaning $\sigma_1$ is inclined at $30^\circ$ to the bedding plane, $\beta = 45^\circ - \phi/2$), Mohr-Coulomb frictional sliding occurs along the bedding plane at the absolute lowest stress on Donath's U-curve.

Synthesis: Ramamurthy (1993) Classification of Rock Strength Anisotropy
Anisotropy Class Anisotropy Ratio $R_c = \sigma_{c(90^\circ)} / \sigma_{c(\min)}$ Typical Rock Lithologies Engineering Behaviour
Isotropic$1.0 - 1.1$Massive Granite, Gabbro, Basalt, Pure QuartziteStrength independent of loading direction
Fairly Anisotropic$1.1 - 2.0$Thick-bedded Sandstone, Massive LimestoneModerate strength peak at $\beta = 90^\circ$

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. What is meant by placing a building stone on its "natural bed" in masonry construction?
Answer: Laying the stone so that its original sedimentary bedding planes are horizontal and perpendicular (normal) to the vertical line of compressive load.
This maximizes compressive strength and prevents exfoliation or splitting of outer stone faces.
2. How should stones be placed in a masonry arch or cornice?
Answer: In an arch, bedding planes should be oriented radial (so that tangential arch thrust acts normal to the bedding planes).
Because the line of thrust in an arch follows the curve of the ring, radial bedding ensures compressive forces always act perpendicular to the bedding planes.
3. At what angle $\beta$ between $\sigma_1$ and a weak cleavage plane does a slate exhibit its minimum compressive strength?
Answer: At $\beta = 45^\circ - \phi_j/2$, which typically lies between $25^\circ$ and $35^\circ$ to the direction of $\sigma_1$.
Proven experimentally by F.A. Donath (1961) on Martinsburg slate and theoretically by J.C. Jaeger (1960).
4. If a laminated sandstone has $\sigma_{c(90^\circ)} = 90\text{ MPa}$ and $\sigma_{c(30^\circ)} = 30\text{ MPa}$, what is its Strength Anisotropy Ratio ($R_c$)?
Answer: $R_c = 90 / 30 = 3.0$ (Moderately Anisotropic).
$R_c = \sigma_{c(90^\circ)} / \sigma_{c(\min)} = 90 / 30 = 3.0$.
5. Why is compressive strength at $\beta = 90^\circ$ consistently higher than at $\beta = 0^\circ$?
Answer: At $\beta = 90^\circ$, failure requires shearing across all layers; at $\beta = 0^\circ$, layers fail at lower stress by tensile axial splitting and buckling of thin laminae.
Even without sliding along bedding, parallel loading ($\beta = 0^\circ$) suffers from column buckling of individual laminations.
6. What happens to the strength anisotropy of a foliated rock as confining pressure ($\sigma_3$) is increased to very high levels?
Answer: Strength anisotropy decreases as high confining pressure suppresses slip along weak planes and induces ductile flow.
Under high $\sigma_3$, frictional resistance ($\sigma_n \tan\phi_j$) across bedding increases markedly, reducing the depth of the U-curve trough.
7. In point load testing ($I_{s(50)}$) of anisotropic rock cores, how is the Point Load Strength Anisotropy Index ($I_{a(50)}$) defined?
Answer: The ratio of mean $I_{s(50)}$ measured perpendicular to planes of weakness (axial test) to mean $I_{s(50)}$ measured parallel to planes of weakness (diametral test).
$I_{a(50)} = I_{s(50)\perp} / I_{s(50)\parallel}$ according to ISRM suggested methods.
8. How does bedding dip affect foundation bearing capacity beneath a dam?
Answer: Horizontal beds (normal to vertical dam weight) provide the highest vertical bearing capacity, though gently upstream-dipping beds ($10^\circ\text{--}30^\circ$) are best for resisting resultant inclined thrust.
Resultant force of dam weight ($\downarrow W$) and horizontal reservoir water thrust ($\rightarrow P$) is inclined downstream, so beds dipping gently upstream meet the resultant force nearly at $90^\circ$ (normal to bedding!).
Dam Site Selection & Foundation Geology / Question 116
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 116 • Dam Site Selection & Foundation Geology

Dam Foundation Geology: Why Massive Granitic Bedrock Is the Premier Site

Topic: Geological Investigation of Dam Sites • Key Concept: Bearing Capacity, Impermeability & Solubility of Bedrock • Textbooks: K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, p. 302); Parbin Singh; Krynine & Judd
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Geological Criteria for Dam Foundations

A major concrete gravity, arch, or embankment dam imposes immense vertical dead loads (up to $3\text{--}6\text{ MPa}$), horizontal reservoir water thrusts, and high hydraulic head gradients on its foundation. An ideal dam site requires bedrock with high unconfined compressive strength (bearing capacity), negligible primary permeability, zero chemical solubility, and high resistance to sliding and erosion. Among the given geological settings, a site with a granitic bedrock (massive plutonic igneous rock) is universally the best site for dam construction:

Candidate Dam Site Bedrock Unconfined Compressive Strength ($\sigma_c$) Permeability & Seepage Hazard Suitability for Dam Construction
SITE WITH GRANITIC BEDROCK (Option A) Very High ($100\text{--}250\text{ MPa}$) Impervious crystalline fabric ($\phi < 1\%$); chemically insoluble in water BEST / IDEAL FOUNDATION: Supports highest concrete gravity and arch dams
Site with Good Shear Fractures (Option B) Severely reduced along shear planes ($c \to 0$) High secondary permeability and piping of fault gouge Hazardous: Prone to sliding failure, differential settlement, and leakage
Lateritic Zone (Option C) Low & variable ($2\text{--}25\text{ MPa}$; softens when saturated) Highly porous, vesicular/vermicular cavities; high seepage Unsuitable for major masonry/concrete dams; requires deep stripping to fresh rock
Site with Limestone Bedrock (Option D) Moderate-to-High intact ($50\text{--}120\text{ MPa}$), but cavernous Severe karstic solution channels, caverns, and sinkholes ($\text{CaCO}_3$ dissolution) Highly problematic: Prone to catastrophic reservoir leakage and foundation collapse
"Massive igneous rocks such as granites, syenites, diorites, and gabbros are the strongest and most desirable foundation rocks for any type of dam. Fresh, unweathered granitic bedrock possesses an interlocking crystalline texture with compressive strength far exceeding any load imposed by the tallest dam, is virtually impervious to water, and is completely immune to solution by percolating reservoir water."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Standard Publishers, Chapter 15: Dams and Reservoirs, p. 302)
Dam Stability Safety Factors on Granitic Bedrock
$$\text{Sliding Safety Factor: } F_s = \frac{c \cdot A + (W - U)\tan\phi}{P_w} > 1.5\text{--}4.0$$ $$\text{Bearing Capacity Check: } \sigma_{\max} = \frac{W}{B}\left(1 + \frac{6e}{B}\right) \le q_{\text{allowable}} \approx \frac{\text{UCS}}{F}$$

Here $W$ is dam weight, $U$ is hydraulic uplift force, $P_w$ is horizontal water pressure, $c$ is concrete-rock bond cohesion, and $\phi$ is friction angle. Fresh granite offers high friction ($\phi \approx 45^\circ\text{--}55^\circ$), strong concrete-to-quartz/feldspar bond cohesion ($c \approx 1.5\text{--}3.0\text{ MPa}$), and allowable bearing capacity $> 5\text{--}10\text{ MPa}$.

2. Why Limestone, Laterite, and Sheared Rock Fail as Ideal Dam Foundations
  • Karstic Limestone Hazard (Option D): Carbonic acid in natural water dissolves calcite ($\text{CaCO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2 \rightleftharpoons \text{Ca}^{2+} + 2\text{HCO}_3^-$), enlarging joints into subterranean caverns and solution conduits. Famous engineering disasters/remediations (e.g., Hales Bar Dam, Camarasa Dam, Kopili Dam) occurred because reservoirs built on limestone drained through underground karst networks.
  • Shear Fractures Hazard (Option B): Shear zones contain slickensided clay gouge with very low residual friction ($\phi_r \approx 12^\circ\text{--}20^\circ$), creating potential sliding planes beneath the dam heel and toe.
  • Lateritic Zone Hazard (Option C): Laterite is a deeply leached tropical residual weathering profile rich in hydrous iron and aluminium oxides with vermicular tubular voids and underlying soft kaolinitic saprolite ("lithomarge" clay) that loses strength upon saturation.
Figure 116.1: Engineering geological evaluation of four candidate dam foundations: (A) Massive Granitic Bedrock (ideal interlocking, high-strength, impervious foundation) vs. hazardous alternatives (B) Sheared fracture zone, (C) Porous lateritic profile, and (D) Cavernous karstic limestone.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official OPSC 2019 Question & Forensic Option Analysis
Q116. Which of the following could be the best site for a dam construction ?
(A) A site with a granitic bedrock
(B) A site with good shear fractures
(C) Lateritic zone
(D) A site with limestone bedrock
✔ Verified Correct Answer: Option (A) — A site with a granitic bedrock
A A site with a granitic bedrock CORRECT ANSWER
Forensic Verification: Granite is a holocrystalline, coarse-grained plutonic igneous rock with an interlocking texture of quartz and feldspar. It provides very high crushing strength ($100\text{--}250\text{ MPa}$), high shear resistance, near-zero primary porosity/permeability, and complete insolubility in water. Hence, a site with granitic bedrock is universally the best and safest site for constructing any major dam.
B A site with good shear fractures INCORRECT
Why this is wrong: Shear fractures represent planes of tectonic rupture with crushed rock and slickensided clay gouge. They drastically lower the shear strength and bearing capacity of the foundation and create pathways for piping and sliding failure.
C Lateritic zone INCORRECT
Why this is wrong: Laterite is a porous, cavernous residual soil/duricrust often underlain by soft, plastic lithomargic clay. It has high permeability, low compressive strength, and undergoes severe settlement under heavy structural loads.
D A site with limestone bedrock INCORRECT
Why this is wrong: Limestone ($\text{CaCO}_3$) is soluble in carbonated water and develops karst topography (solution cavities, sinkholes, and underground channels). Dams built on limestone risk severe reservoir leakage and foundation subsidence unless massive grouting remediation is undertaken.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. What are the two most common modes of failure of a concrete gravity dam resting on weak bedrock?
Answer: (1) Sliding failure along horizontal bedding or shear planes, and (2) Overturning / Toe crushing due to excessive hydraulic uplift pressure.
Granitic bedrock prevents both by providing high frictional resistance against sliding and high crushing strength at the dam toe.
2. Why is limestone bedrock particularly hazardous for reservoir water retention?
Answer: Because limestone dissolves in weak carbonic acid to form interconnected subterranean karst channels, sinkholes, and caverns that drain the reservoir.
Even if intact limestone cores show high UCS, solution-widened master joints can bypass the dam entirely.
3. If a dam must be built across sedimentary strata, which dip direction of beds is safest for the dam foundation?
Answer: Beds dipping gently upstream ($10^\circ\text{ to }30^\circ$).
Upstream dip directs the resultant load nearly perpendicular to bedding and forces any seepage water to travel downward against the hydraulic gradient, preventing both sliding and leakage.
4. Why are beds dipping gently downstream ($10^\circ\text{--}30^\circ$) the most dangerous configuration for a dam foundation?
Answer: The resultant force of dam weight and water pressure acts parallel to the downstream-dipping bedding planes, promoting sliding failure and downstream water leakage.
The tragic Malpasset Dam failure (1959) and Austin Dam failure involved downstream-dipping foliation/bedding planes.
5. What geological precaution must still be checked when selecting a granitic bedrock site for a dam?
Answer: Depth of spheroidal weathering (kaolinized regolith) and presence of sheet joints (unloading fractures) parallel to the valley slopes.
While fresh granite is ideal, weathered granite (grus) and sheet joints must be excavated to fresh rock and consolidated by blanket grouting.
6. Which type of dam requires the strongest, soundest rock not only in the valley floor but also in the valley walls (abutments)?
Answer: Arch Dam (such as Idukki Dam in Kerala, built on massive charnockitic/granitic gneiss).
An arch dam transfers the majority of reservoir water load laterally by arch action into the canyon abutment walls.
7. What is "piping" in dam foundation engineering?
Answer: Progressive backward internal erosion of soil or fault gouge particles beneath a dam caused by high exit hydraulic gradients ($i_{\text{exit}} \ge i_{\text{crit}}$).
Crystalline granitic bedrock is completely immune to piping erosion.
8. Which type of dam is preferred when the foundation consists of deep, unconsolidated alluvial sand and gravel where solid bedrock is too deep to reach?
Answer: Earthfill or Rockfill Embankment Dam with a wide base and an impervious clay core / cutoff trench.
Embankment dams distribute their weight over a very wide footprint, keeping bearing pressures low enough for soil foundations.
Engineering Properties of Building Stones / Question 117
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 117 • Engineering Geology & Building Stones

Granite as a Dimension & Engineering Stone: Crushing Strength, Porosity, and Durability

Topic: Engineering Properties of Building Stones • Key Concept: Interlocking Holocrystalline Texture & Crushing Strength of Granite • Textbooks: K.M. Bangar (p. 296); IS: 3316 (1974); Parbin Singh
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Petrological & Engineering Properties of Granite

Granite is an acid, plutonic (intrusive) igneous rock composed essentially of quartz ($20\%\text{--}40\%$), alkali feldspar (orthoclase/microcline), and sodic plagioclase, with minor biotite or hornblende. Because it crystallizes slowly at depth under high confining pressure, its mineral grains develop a tight, holocrystalline, equigranular interlocking (hypidiomorphic granular) texture. This microstructure gives granite very high crushing (compressive) strength, extremely low porosity, superior durability, and the ability to take a mirror-like polish:

Engineering Property Standard Value for Fresh Granite Governing Mineralogical / Textural Cause Evaluation of Exam Options
CRUSHING (COMPRESSIVE) STRENGTH $1000\text{ to }2500\text{ kg/cm}^2$ ($100\text{--}250\text{ MPa}$) Interlocking 3D framework of hard quartz (Mohs 7) and feldspar (Mohs 6) crystals OPTION (A) IS TRUE: Very high crushing strength
Polishing Quality Takes an exquisite, durable mirror-like polish Uniform high hardness ($H = 6\text{--}7$) and zero intergranular pore cavities Option (B) ("takes poor polish") is FALSE
Porosity ($n$) & Water Absorption Extremely low porosity ($0.1\%\text{ to }0.8\%$); absorption $< 0.5\%$ by weight Holocrystalline plutonic solidification leaves almost no void space Option (C) ("highly porous rock") is FALSE
Weathering Resistance & Durability Exceptionally durable; resists frost, salt, and atmospheric decay for centuries High quartz content (chemically inert) and minimal moisture ingress Option (D) ("weathers out faster") is FALSE
"Granite is one of the strongest, hardest, and most durable of all building stones. Owing to its holocrystalline, interlocking granular texture and the predominance of hard minerals like quartz and feldspar, it possesses a very high crushing strength ranging from $1000\text{ to }2500\text{ kg/cm}^2$ ($100\text{--}250\text{ MPa}$). Its porosity is less than $1\%$, it weathers extremely slowly, and it takes an excellent, lasting polish, making it ideal for bridge piers, dam foundations, heavy masonry, and decorative monumental work."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Standard Publishers, Chapter 14: Building Stones, p. 296)
IS: 3316 (1974) Specifications for Structural Granite
$$\text{Crushing Strength: } \sigma_c = \frac{F_{\max}}{A} \ge 1000\text{ kg/cm}^2 \text{ (100 MPa)} \quad \text{(Typical: } 130\text{--}220\text{ MPa)}$$ $$\text{Specific Gravity: } G = 2.63\text{ to }2.75 \quad \big|\quad \text{Water Absorption (24 hr)} < 0.50\%$$

Fine-grained granites display even higher crushing strength ($180\text{--}250\text{ MPa}$) than coarse-grained pegmatitic varieties ($100\text{--}150\text{ MPa}$) in accordance with the Hall-Petch grain-size strengthening relationship ($\sigma_c \propto d^{-1/2}$).

2. Engineering Applications & One Notable Limitation of Granite
  • Heavy Load-Bearing Structures: Bridge piers, abutments, lighthouses, sea walls, dockyards, and dam foundations where immense crushing loads and hydraulic abrasion act continuously.
  • Dimension & Monumental Facing Stone: Because feldspar and quartz take a brilliant, high-gloss polish and resist acid rain far better than marble or limestone, polished granite slabs are the premier architectural cladding material.
  • Fire Resistance Limitation: The one engineering weakness of granite is poor fire resistance. Under intense fire ($> 573^\circ\text{C}$, the $\alpha \to \beta$ quartz inversion point), quartz undergoes a sudden $0.85\%$ volumetric expansion and differential thermal expansion relative to feldspar, causing granite blocks to crack, spall, and decrepitate when doused with water.
Figure 117.1: Petrological and geotechnical summary of granite, showing its interlocking quartz-feldspar-biotite crystal fabric, superior crushing strength ($100\text{--}250\text{ MPa}$), ultra-low porosity ($< 1\%$), and high resistance to weathering.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official OPSC 2019 Question & Forensic Option Analysis
Q117. Which of the following is true about granite ?
(A) It has very high crushing strength
(B) It takes poor polish
(C) It is a highly porous rock
(D) It weathers out faster
✔ Verified Correct Answer: Option (A) — It has very high crushing strength
A It has very high crushing strength CORRECT ANSWER
Forensic Verification: Granite possesses a very high crushing (unconfined compressive) strength of $1000\text{ to }2500\text{ kg/cm}^2$ ($100\text{--}250\text{ MPa}$). Its interlocking holocrystalline fabric of hard quartz ($H=7$) and feldspar ($H=6$) crystals resists intergranular slip and compressive rupture better than almost any sedimentary rock.
B It takes poor polish INCORRECT
Why this is wrong: Granite takes an excellent, mirror-like, long-lasting polish because of its dense, non-porous interlocking crystals of hard quartz and feldspar. That is why polished granite is used worldwide for countertops, monuments, and building facades.
C It is a highly porous rock INCORRECT
Why this is wrong: Fresh granite is an extremely compact, non-porous rock with total porosity typically under $0.5\%\text{ to }1\%$ and water absorption below $0.5\%$.
D It weathers out faster INCORRECT
Why this is wrong: Granite is rich in quartz (the most stable mineral on Goldich's weathering stability series) and K-feldspar, and has negligible porosity to admit water. Therefore, it weathers very slowly and exhibits outstanding durability.
