High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. According to Indian Standards (IS: 1121), what is the minimum crushing strength required for a stone to be classified as a good structural building stone?
Answer: At least $1000\text{ kg/cm}^2$ ($\approx 100\text{ MPa}$) for heavy-duty masonry; granite easily exceeds this ($1000\text{--}2500\text{ kg/cm}^2$).
Granite, basalt, quartzite, and charnockite all surpass the $1000\text{ kg/cm}^2$ benchmark.
2. Why do fine-grained granites possess higher crushing strength than coarse-grained (porphyritic or pegmatitic) granites?
Answer: Smaller grain size restricts the initial length of Griffith microcracks along grain boundaries and cleavage planes ($\sigma_c \propto d^{-1/2}$).
Fine, equigranular interlocking crystals distribute stress more uniformly and arrest microcrack propagation.
3. Why does granite have poor fire resistance despite its high crushing strength?
Answer: Quartz undergoes sudden volumetric expansion at $573^\circ\text{C}$ ($\alpha\text{-quartz} \to \beta\text{-quartz}$), and unequal thermal expansion of quartz and feldspar shatters the rock.
Compact sandstone (with siliceous cement) has much better fire resistance than granite.
4. What should be the maximum permissible water absorption (by weight after 24 hours immersion) for a first-class building stone like granite?
Answer: Less than $0.5\%\text{ to }1\%$ for granite (and strictly never exceeding $5\%$ for any acceptable building stone).
Low water absorption guarantees immunity against freeze-thaw frost wedging and salt crystallization damage.
5. Why does polished granite retain its exterior gloss in urban atmospheres much longer than polished marble?
Answer: Granite is composed of silicate minerals (quartz and feldspar, $H=6\text{--}7$) immune to weak acids, whereas marble is calcite ($\text{CaCO}_3, H=3$) which is etched by acidic rain ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4, \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$).
Silicate minerals resist both wind-blown quartz dust abrasion and urban acid rain dissolution.
6. What causes dark brown or rusty stains on some inferior granite building blocks over time?
Answer: Oxidation and hydration of accessory iron-bearing minerals such as pyrite ($\text{FeS}_2$) or abundant biotite/magnetite into limonite.
Dimension granites must be free of pyrite nodules to prevent unsightly rust staining and sulphuric acid release.
7. What is the typical specific gravity of granite and what does a lower value ($< 2.55$) indicate?
Answer: Fresh granite has $G = 2.63\text{--}2.75$; a lower value indicates incipient kaolinization (weathering of feldspars) and micro-fracturing.
Weathering alters dense feldspar ($G \approx 2.6$) into porous kaolinite clay ($G \approx 2.2\text{--}2.4$), reducing bulk density and strength.
8. How are Rift and Grain utilized when quarrying massive granite?
Answer: Rift (easiest splitting plane) and Grain (second easiest plane, perpendicular to rift) are microscopic fluid-inclusion microcrack alignments used by quarrymen to split rectangular granite blocks cleanly.
Even though granite lacks sedimentary bedding, orthogonal rift, grain, and hardway planes allow clean dressing of blocks.
Highway Engineering & Road Metal Aggregates / Question 118
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 118 • Engineering Geology & Highway Aggregates

Road Metal (Highway Aggregates): Desirable vs. Undesirable Geotechnical Properties

Topic: Geological Selection of Road Metal & Pavement Aggregates • Key Concept: Crushing Strength, Hydrophobicity, Porosity & Shear Defects • Textbooks: K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, p. 299); Parbin Singh; IRC / IS: 2386
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Desirable vs. Undesirable Properties of Road Metal

Road metal (crushed stone aggregate used in flexible bituminous and rigid concrete highway pavements) is subjected to intense wheel impact loads, mutual inter-particle abrasion, surface tire attrition, and moisture-induced stripping of bitumen. According to standard Indian engineering geology textbooks (e.g., K.M. Bangar and Parbin Singh) and Indian Roads Congress (IRC) specifications, road metal must be strong, tough, hard, hydrophobic (water-repelling, bitumen-loving), and non-porous/impermeable:

Aggregate Property Physical & Engineering Meaning Impact on Highway Pavement Performance Desirable or Undesirable?
Should be Hydrophobic (Option A) Repels water and exhibits strong affinity (adhesion) for asphalt/bitumen binder (e.g., basalt, dolerite, limestone) Prevents moisture "stripping" of bitumen film from aggregate surfaces during monsoon rains HIGHLY DESIRABLE
Sufficient Crushing Strength (Option B) High UCS ($> 100\text{--}150\text{ MPa}$) and Aggregate Crushing Value ($\text{ACV} < 30\%$) Withstands heavy roller compaction and axle wheel loads without pulverizing HIGHLY DESIRABLE
STRONGLY SHEARED / HIGHLY POROUS & PERMEABLE (Options C & D) Option C: Tectonically sheared rock (flaky, pre-fractured, weak)
Option D: High porosity & permeability (absorbs water & wastes bitumen)		 Option C shatters into flaky splinters under rollers; Option D absorbs water, softens, and wastes expensive bitumen NOT DESIRABLE (CORRECT ANSWERS)
"A good road metal must possess: (1) Sufficient crushing strength, hardness, and toughness to resist traffic impact and abrasion; (2) Hydrophobic character (affinity for bitumen over water) so the bituminous binder does not strip off in wet weather; (3) Low porosity and impermeability, because a highly porous and permeable rock absorbs water and excessive bitumen and disintegrates under wheel loads; and (4) Sound, equidimensional cubical breakage, free from strongly sheared, foliated, or flaky planes of weakness."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Standard Publishers, Chapter 14: Road Metals, pp. 299–300)
IS: 2386 & IRC Standard Test Limits for Road Metal Aggregates
$$\text{Aggregate Impact Value (AIV)} \le 30\% \text{ (Wearing Course)} \quad \big|\quad \text{Aggregate Crushing Value (ACV)} \le 30\%$$ $$\text{Los Angeles Abrasion Value (LAAV)} \le 30\% \quad \big|\quad \text{Water Absorption} \le 2.0\% \text{ (Strictly non-porous)}$$ $$\text{Combined Flakiness & Elongation Index} \le 35\% \quad \text{(Rejects sheared/schistose rocks)}$$

Note on OPSC Exam Key & Textbook Verbatim Source: In standard Indian geology MCQ banks (derived verbatim from Bangar/Parbin Singh's list of road metal properties where "Porosity: Road metal should NOT be porous and permeable" is a dedicated heading, alongside structural soundness against sheared/flaky stones), both Option (D) "Should be highly porous and permeable" and Option (C) "Should be strongly sheared" are demonstrably false/undesirable statements. Below we provide complete forensic analysis for both so candidates are 100% covered under either key interpretation.

2. Hydrophobic vs. Hydrophilic Aggregates in Bituminous Roads
  • Hydrophobic Rocks (Basic Rocks & Limestones): Basalt, dolerite (Deccan Trap), gabbro, and compact limestone carry positive surface charges that bond strongly with negatively charged naphthenic acids in bitumen. They repel water and resist binder stripping.
  • Hydrophilic Rocks (Acidic Siliceous Rocks): Pure quartzite, sandstone, and granite have high free $\text{SiO}_2$ ($> 65\%$) carrying negative surface charges. They attract polar water molecules more strongly than bitumen, causing the bitumen film to peel off ("stripping") when submerged in rainwater unless anti-stripping amine additives are used.
Figure 118.1: Engineering comparison of road metal properties: Desirable qualities (hydrophobic bitumen adhesion and high crushing strength) vs. Undesirable defects (strongly sheared/flaky rock and highly porous/permeable rock).
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official OPSC 2019 Question & Forensic Option Analysis
Q118. Which of the following is not a desirable property for a road metal ?
(A) Should be hydrophobic
(B) Should have sufficient crushing strength
(C) Should be strongly sheared
(D) Should be highly porous and permeable
✔ Verified Correct Answer: Option (D) — Should be highly porous and permeable (and Option C — Should be strongly sheared)
A Should be hydrophobic DESIRABLE PROPERTY
Why this IS desirable: A road metal must be hydrophobic (water-repelling, like basalt and dolerite) so that it adheres tightly to bituminous/asphalt binders and resists stripping of the bitumen coating in the presence of rainwater.
B Should have sufficient crushing strength DESIRABLE PROPERTY
Why this IS desirable: A road metal must possess high crushing strength (typically $> 1000\text{ kg/cm}^2$, Aggregate Crushing Value $< 30\%$) to withstand heavy steamrollers and commercial axle loads without crushing into powder.
C Should be strongly sheared UNDESIRABLE (CORRECT)
Forensic Verification (Option C): A strongly sheared rock contains pervasive closely-spaced slickensides, micro-fractures, and foliation planes. When crushed for road aggregate, sheared rocks break into weak, flaky, and elongated splinters (high Flakiness Index) that snap immediately under traffic loads. Therefore, being strongly sheared is completely undesirable.
D Should be highly porous and permeable UNDESIRABLE (CORRECT)
Forensic Verification (Option D): A road metal must never be highly porous and permeable (IRC limits water absorption to $\le 2\%$). Highly porous and permeable aggregates absorb rainwater (losing mechanical strength and causing freeze-thaw or pore-pressure failure) and soak up large quantities of expensive liquid bitumen into internal pores without contributing to inter-particle binding.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. Distinguish between "Hydrophobic" and "Hydrophilic" road aggregates with examples.
Answer: Hydrophobic aggregates (basalt, dolerite, limestone) have stronger affinity for bitumen than water; hydrophilic aggregates (quartzite, granite, sandstone) attract water over bitumen, causing binder stripping.
Basic igneous rocks and carbonate rocks are naturally hydrophobic and superior for bituminous pavements.
2. Which rock type in India is considered the single best all-round road metal and why?
Answer: Basalt and Dolerite ("Deccan Trap") because they are fine-grained, tough, hard, non-porous, break into angular cubical fragments, and are strongly hydrophobic.
Fine-grained basic igneous rocks combine high toughness (low AIV) with excellent bitumen adhesion.
3. What is the difference between "Attrition" and "Abrasion" in road aggregates?
Answer: Attrition is the mutual rubbing of aggregate stones against each other under traffic vibration (tested by Deval Attrition Test); abrasion is wear caused by external vehicle tires (tested by Dorry/Los Angeles Test).
The Los Angeles test measures combined abrasion, attrition, and impact.
4. Why are flaky and elongated aggregate particles (formed from sheared or schistose rocks) rejected in road construction?
Answer: They orient horizontally during rolling and fracture easily across their thin dimension under traffic wheel loads, reducing pavement stability and interlock.
A particle is flaky if its least dimension is less than $0.6\times$ its mean dimension; elongated if its greatest dimension exceeds $1.8\times$ its mean dimension.
5. Why is highly porous rock doubly disadvantageous in bituminous road construction?
Answer: (1) It has low mechanical crushing/impact strength, and (2) its open pores absorb large quantities of expensive bitumen that does not contribute to surface bonding.
Additionally, absorbed water causes freeze-thaw disintegration and hydraulic pore-pressure stripping under fast wheel loads.
6. What is the ideal particle shape for road metal aggregates?
Answer: Angular and approximately equidimensional (cubical / tetrahedral) with rough micro-texture.
Angular cubical fragments provide maximum mechanical interlocking (high angle of internal friction $\phi$) and high surface area for binder adhesion.
7. Why are rounded river gravels unsuitable for the wearing course of heavy-duty roads unless crushed?
Answer: Smooth, rounded pebbles lack angular edges for mechanical interlocking and slip past one another under horizontal wheel braking forces.
Crushing river boulders creates fresh, rough, angular fracture faces required for stability.
8. What is the "Polished Stone Value" (PSV) of a road aggregate and why is pure limestone avoided in the top skid-resistant surface of expressways?
Answer: PSV measures resistance of aggregate to polishing under rubber tires; pure monomineralic limestone ($H=3$) polishes smooth quickly, reducing wet skid resistance.
Rocks composed of minerals with contrasting hardness (e.g., dolerite or gritstone) maintain micro-roughness and high PSV as they wear differentially.
Building Stones & Quarry Economics / Question 119
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 119 • Engineering Geology & Dimension Stones

Workability of Building Stones: Ease of Quarrying, Extraction, Dressing, and Carving

Topic: Selection Criteria for Dimension & Building Stones • Key Concept: Workability vs. Hardness & Economic Cost • Textbooks: K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, p. 295); Parbin Singh; R.K. Rajput
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Workability of Building Stones

In engineering geology and masonry construction, the ease with which a stone can be extracted (quarried) from its natural outcrop and subsequently dressed (cut, chiseled, shaped, and planed) into required dimensions and architectural forms is formally defined as its Workability:

Term in Options Technical Definition in Geology / Civil Engineering Relevance to Stone Quarrying & Dressing
WORKABILITY (Option B) The ease and economy with which a stone can be extracted from the quarry, split, chiseled, dressed, and carved into desired shapes and sizes EXACT DEFINITION (Correct Answer)
Consistency (Option A) Degree of firmness or resistance to deformation of cohesive soils/clays (Atterberg limits: liquid, plastic, semi-solid, solid states) or fresh concrete slump Applies to cohesive soils and wet concrete paste, not hard rock dressing
Easability (Option C) Non-standard colloquial distractor term; not an established geotechnical or rock mechanics property Invalid distractor
Permeability (Option D) Capacity of a porous rock or soil to transmit fluids under a hydraulic gradient (Darcy's coefficient $k$) Hydraulic flow property, unrelated to mechanical dressing
"Workability: A stone is said to be workable when the effort required in its extraction (quarrying), dressing, cutting, and shaping into blocks of required size is small and economical. The ease with which a stone can be extracted and dressed is called its workability. Notice that workability and strength/hardness often oppose each other: very hard, compact igneous rocks like granite and basalt have poor workability (expensive to dress), whereas softer, bedded rocks like sandstone, limestone, and laterite possess high workability."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Standard Publishers, Chapter 14: Building Stones, p. 295)
Geological Controls on Stone Workability & Cost Optimization
$$\text{Workability} \propto \frac{\text{Regularity of Bedding / Cleavage / Rift-Grain}}{\text{Mineral Hardness } (H) \times \text{Interlocking Toughness } (T_i)}$$ $$\text{Total Masonry Cost} = C_{\text{quarrying}} + C_{\text{dressing}} + C_{\text{transport}}$$

A phenomenon known as "Quarry Sap" (natural pore moisture present in freshly quarried sandstone, limestone, and laterite) significantly enhances workability: stones are much softer and easier to dress and carve immediately after extraction while still moist with quarry sap; once the quarry sap evaporates and dissolved silica/calcite precipitates in the outer pores ("seasoning"), the stone becomes hard, durable, and weather-resistant.

2. Comparative Workability of Major Indian Dimension Stones
  • High Workability Stones (Freestones): Thick-bedded, uniform-grained Sandstones (e.g., Vindhyan sandstone of Chunar, Agra, and Jodhpur; Athgarh/Khandolite stones in Odisha) and Limestones/Marbles (e.g., Makrana marble) that cut cleanly in any direction without splintering are called "freestones". Laterite when freshly quarried is cut easily with a pickaxe and hardens on exposure to air.
  • Low Workability Stones: Granite, Basalt, Trap, and Quartzite are extremely hard and tough; dressing them with hand chisels is slow and costly, restricting their traditional use to rubble masonry or mechanically sawed/polished slabs.
Figure 119.1: Engineering concept of Stone Workability, illustrating extraction along natural joints/bedding, ease of chisel dressing while containing fresh "quarry sap", and the inverse trade-off between mechanical hardness/strength and workability across rock types.

Q119. Ease with which a stone can be extracted and dressed is called :
(A) Consistency
(B) Workability
(C) Easability
(D) Permeability
✔ Verified Correct Answer: Option (B) — Workability
A Consistency INCORRECT
Why this is wrong: Consistency refers to the relative ease with which a cohesive soil (clay) can be deformed (quantified by Atterberg limits: Liquid Limit, Plastic Limit, Shrinkage Limit) or the fluidity/slump of freshly mixed concrete.
B Workability CORRECT ANSWER
Forensic Verification: In building stone technology and engineering geology, Workability is the exact technical term for the ease and economy with which a stone can be extracted from its quarry bed and dressed (cut, chiseled, shaped, and carved) into desired building blocks.
C Easability INCORRECT
Why this is wrong: "Easability" is a coined distractor word and not a valid engineering or geological term.

Why this is wrong: Permeability measures the ability of interconnected pores or fractures in a rock to transmit fluids under a hydraulic gradient.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. What is "Quarry Sap" and why must stones be dressed before it dries out?
Answer: Quarry sap is the natural ground moisture containing dissolved mineral salts present in freshly quarried stone; the stone is much softer and more workable while moist, and hardens permanently once the sap evaporates at the surface.
Seasoning of stone (6 to 12 months in open air sheds) is performed *after* dressing so the hardened outer crust is never chiseled off.
2. Why should a seasoned building stone never be re-dressed after seasoning is complete?
Answer: Evaporation of quarry sap deposits a tough, weather-resistant mineral crust on the outer surface; re-dressing strips away this protective skin and exposes the softer interior to rapid decay.
All cutting, carving, and dressing must be completed while the stone is green (fresh from the quarry).
3. What is a "Freestone" in masonry terminology?
Answer: Any fine-grained, thick-bedded sandstone or limestone that can be cut, sawed, and chiseled freely in any direction without splitting or splintering.
Vindhyan sandstones (Chunar, Mirzapur, Dholpur) and Gondwana Athgarh sandstones are classic Indian freestones.
4. How does the relationship between Workability and Durability create an optimization problem in civil engineering?
Answer: Soft, clayey, or porous stones have high workability (cheap to dress) but low durability and strength, whereas dense igneous stones have high durability/strength but poor workability (expensive to dress).
Engineers select intermediate freestones (like siliceous/ferruginous sandstone or marble) when intricate dressing and durability are both required.
5. Which rocks were famously used in the construction of the Sun Temple at Konark and Lingaraj Temple in Bhubaneswar, Odisha?
Answer: Khondalite (quartz-manganese-garnet-sillimanite gneiss) for the main structure and carving, Laterite for core foundations/enclosures, and Chlorite/Serpentinite (Muguni stone) for fine doorway sculptures.
Chlorite schist/serpentinite is soft ($H = 2.5\text{--}3$) with exceptional workability for intricate statuary, while laterite served for foundation blocks.
6. What is the difference between "Quarrying by Wedging" and "Quarrying by Blasting"?
Answer: Wedging uses steel plugs and feathers along natural joints/bedding to extract intact, crack-free dimension blocks; blasting uses explosives to shatter rock into irregular fragments for road metal or aggregate.
Blasting induces internal micro-cracks and ruins dimension building blocks, so wedging or wire-sawing is used for building stones.
7. Why is laterite exceptionally popular as a local building block in coastal Odisha, Malabar, and Konkan?
Answer: In the quarry bed, moist laterite is soft and sectile (easily cut into rectangular bricks with a spade/axe), and upon exposure to air, dehydration of iron hydroxides irreversibly hardens it into stone.
Francis Buchanan-Hamilton coined the term "Laterite" (from Latin *later* = brick) in 1807 in southern India specifically because of this property!
8. Which test checks whether a stone contains soluble clay or mud that reduces its durability despite high initial workability?
Answer: Smith's Test (agitating stone chips in clear water to check for muddy turbidity).
If the water remains clear, the stone is free of soluble earthy matter; if cloudy, it contains poorly cemented clay.
Metamorphic Building Stones & Roofing Materials / Question 120
Standalone View
OPSC 2019 Geology Paper-II • Question 120 • Engineering Geology & Metamorphic Building Stones

Roofing Slate: Low-Grade Metamorphism, Slaty Cleavage, and Impervious Roofing Slabs

Topic: Metamorphic Building Materials • Key Concept: Slaty Cleavage, Splits into Thin Impervious Sheets & Roofing Slabs • Textbooks: K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, p. 298); IS: 6250 (1981); Parbin Singh
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geomorphic mechanics
1. Theoretical Foundation: Why Slate Is the Universal Natural Roofing Slab

Slate is a fine-grained, low-grade regionally metamorphosed pelitic rock derived from shale or mudstone under directed tectonic compression (greenschist/sub-greenschist facies). During metamorphism, clay minerals recrystallize into microscopically aligned, parallel flakes of muscovite (sericite), illite, and chlorite oriented perpendicular to the maximum compressive stress ($\sigma_1$). This imparts an extraordinary penetrative fabric known as slaty cleavage, enabling slate to be split effortlessly into thin ($4\text{--}10\text{ mm}$), flat, smooth, light, and completely impervious sheets ideal for roofing slabs (roofing tiles):

Rock Material Fabric & Splitting Behaviour Weight & Water Absorption Suitability as a Roofing Slab
SLATE (Option A) Perfect penetrative slaty cleavage; splits into thin ($4\text{--}10\text{ mm}$), flat, uniform sheets Lightweight in thin sheets; extremely low water absorption ($< 0.4\%$), high transverse flexural strength UNIVERSAL ROOFING SLAB / TILE (Correct Answer)
Granite (Option B) Massive, non-foliated interlocking plutonic fabric; cannot be split into thin sheets Heavy massive blocks ($2.65\text{--}2.75\text{ g/cm}^3$); zero cleavage Unsuitable for pitched roofing tiles; used for heavy foundations & piers
Marble (Option C) Granoblastic (non-foliated) interlocking calcite mosaic; lacks cleavage planes Heavy slabs; soluble in acid rain and prone to thermal warping Used for interior flooring, wall cladding, and statuary
Gneiss (Option D) Coarse gneissic banding (segregated quartzo-feldspathic and mafic bands); poor splitting Breaks into thick, rough slabs ($> 5\text{--}15\text{ cm}$); too heavy for roof trusses Used for heavy masonry, paving setts, and road aggregates
"Slate is an extremely fine-grained metamorphic rock formed from shales and clays. Its most valuable engineering property is its perfect slaty cleavage, by virtue of which it can be split into very thin, smooth, tough, and flat sheets of uniform thickness. Because slate also possesses negligible porosity (water absorption $< 0.5\%$), high transverse bending strength, and complete resistance to frost and atmospheric weathering, it is universally used as a roofing slab, damp-proof course (DPC), electrical switchboard panel, and school slate."
— K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Standard Publishers, Chapter 14: Building Stones, p. 298)
IS: 6250 (1981) Specifications for Roofing Slate Tiles
$$\text{Water Absorption (after 24 hr boiling)} \le 0.30\%\text{ to }0.40\% \quad \text{(Virtually Impervious)}$$ $$\text{Modulus of Rupture (Flexural Bending Strength): } \sigma_f = \frac{3PL}{2bd^2} \ge 40\text{--}70\text{ MPa}$$ $$\text{Specific Gravity: } G = 2.75\text{ to }2.89 \quad \big|\quad \text{Acid Immersion Test: Zero Delamination in } \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$$

Because a roofing slab spans between wooden or steel purlins/battens and supports wind uplift, snow loads, and maintenance foot traffic as a thin plate ($d \approx 5\text{--}8\text{ mm}$), a high Modulus of Rupture (flexural tensile strength) along the cleavage plane is essential.

2. Key Indian Occurrences & Quality Tests of Roofing Slate
  • Famous Indian Slate Belts:
    • Himachal Pradesh: Kangra (Dharamshala, Khaniara), Mandi, and Chamba districts (premier Himalayan roofing slates).
    • Haryana & Rajasthan: Rewari, Kund, and Alwar (Delhi Supergroup slates).
    • Andhra Pradesh: Markapur belt in Prakasam district (Cumbum Formation, Nallamalai Group of Cuddapah Supergroup).
    • Bihar: Munger (Kharagpur Hills).
  • Field Quality Ring Test: A first-class roofing slate gives a sharp, clear metallic ringing sound when struck lightly with a knuckle or hammer, does not feel greasy to the touch, and shows zero free carbonate ($\text{CaCO}_3$) effervescence with dilute $\text{HCl}$ (since calcite dissolves in acid rain and ruins the roof).
Figure 120.1: Formation of penetrative slaty cleavage by tectonic alignment of mica/chlorite platelets perpendicular to $\sigma_1$, allowing slate to be split into thin, impervious, high-flexural-strength roofing slabs, contrasted with massive granite, granoblastic marble, and coarse-banded gneiss.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official OPSC 2019 Question & Forensic Option Analysis
Q120. Which of the following materials is generally used as a roofing slab ?
(A) Slate
(B) Granite
(C) Marble
(D) Gneiss
✔ Verified Correct Answer: Option (A) — Slate
A Slate CORRECT ANSWER
Forensic Verification: Slate is universally used as a natural roofing slab (roofing tile) because its perfect slaty cleavage allows it to be split into very thin ($4\text{--}10\text{ mm}$), flat, light, and smooth rectangular sheets that are completely impervious to rainwater (absorption $< 0.4\%$) and possess high transverse bending strength.
B Granite INCORRECT
Why this is wrong: Granite is a massive, unfoliated plutonic rock lacking cleavage planes. It cannot be split into thin sheets and is far too heavy for pitched roofing tiles.
C Marble INCORRECT
Why this is wrong: Marble is a non-foliated granoblastic metamorphic rock composed of interlocking calcite crystals. It lacks rock cleavage, cannot be split into thin tiles, and dissolves/etches in acid rain.
D Gneiss INCORRECT
Why this is wrong: Gneiss is a coarse-grained, high-grade metamorphic rock with discontinuous compositional banding (gneissosity). Its foliation is rough and poorly fissile, breaking only into thick, heavy slabs unsuitable for roofing tiles.

High-Yield Practice Problems (8 Exam-Standard Questions)
1. What is the fundamental difference between sedimentary "Fissility" in shale and metamorphic "Slaty Cleavage" in slate?
Answer: Fissility in shale is always parallel to original depositional bedding; slaty cleavage in slate is formed by tectonic recrystallization perpendicular to $\sigma_1$ and usually cuts across the original bedding planes at an angle.
Furthermore, shale softens and slakes in water, whereas metamorphism binds slate into a hard, waterproof sheet.
2. Why is slate also widely used for electrical switchboards and laboratory tabletops?
Answer: Pure slate (free of magnetite or pyrite veins) is an excellent electrical insulator, chemically inert to acids, non-absorbent, and easily machined into perfectly flat panels.
Wait-free flatness and high dielectric resistance make non-metallic slate ideal for precision benches and switchboards.
3. What causes the different natural colors of roofing slates (black, grey, purple, green)?
Answer: Black/dark grey is caused by finely disseminated carbonaceous matter; red/purple by ferric oxide (hematite, $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$); and green by ferrous iron silicate (chlorite).
Mineralogical pigments in the parent mudstone control the color of the resulting slate.
4. Why are calcareous slates (containing $\text{CaCO}_3$) and pyritiferous slates (containing $\text{FeS}_2$) rejected by IS: 6250 for roofing?
Answer: Pyrite oxidizes in rain to form sulphuric acid ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$) and rusty holes, while calcite reacts with the acid to form gypsum ($\text{CaSO}_4\cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$), which swells and delaminates the slate.
The IS: 6250 sulphuric acid immersion test specifically detects calcareous and pyritic impurities.
5. Which sedimentary stone in Rajasthan is also widely split along bedding planes for flooring and flat-roof slabs ("Patti")?
Answer: Kota Stone (fine-grained flaggy siliceous limestone from the Semri/Bhander Group of the Vindhyan Supergroup) and Jodhpur/Karauli flaggy sandstone.
While flaggy sandstones/limestones are used for thick flat-roof beams ("pattis"), true thin pitched roofing tiles are made of metamorphic **Slate**.
6. What is a "Damp-Proof Course" (DPC) in building construction and why is slate ideal for it?
Answer: A horizontal barrier placed at plinth level in brick/stone walls to stop capillary rise of ground moisture; slate is ideal because its water absorption is under $0.4\%$ and its crushing strength exceeds wall loads.
Two overlapping courses of slate laid in cement mortar form a permanent, indestructible damp-proof barrier.
7. Along which plane of the strain ellipsoid ($X \ge Y \ge Z$) does slaty cleavage develop?
Answer: Parallel to the $XY$ plane of maximum flattening, which is strictly perpendicular to the shortest principal strain axis ($Z$, parallel to $\sigma_1$).
Deformed reduction spots in Welsh and Himalayan slates confirm approximately $60\%\text{--}70\%$ shortening along $Z$ perpendicular to slaty cleavage.
8. Which famous stratigraphic formation in Andhra Pradesh yields the Markapur roofing slates?
Answer: The Cumbum Formation of the Nallamalai Group (Proterozoic Cuddapah Supergroup).
The Cumbum slates and phyllites around Markapur (Prakasam district) are one of Peninsular India's largest commercial slate deposits.
